meta.title: What it costs a GB supplier to win a customer, and to keep one
meta.subtitle: Acquisition is a commission you pay someone else. Retention is margin you give up yourself. They are different kinds of thing, and since 2022 the law says so.
meta.wall_placement: Public-reality commons only. Every figure here is from a published source — Ofgem licence conditions, the CMA Energy Market Investigation, or a cited industry rate. No figure produced by this project's simulation appears on this page, and no number on this page was chosen because a number was needed.

claim_freshness.source: Ofgem SLC 22B (Ban on Acquisition-only Tariffs) and its Market-wide Derogation, consultation of 27 August 2025; CMA Energy Market Investigation 2016, Appendix 9.10 paragraphs 64 and 74; Ofgem price cap EBIT methodology consultation May 2023, paragraphs 4.24-4.25; PCW commission rates as cited in docs/market_research/B2_CATEGORY6_CAC_ANCHORS.md; for the save on a loss notice: Ofgem SLC 22B market-wide derogation and its November 2025 renewal decision, CMA Energy Market Investigation final report summary 2016 paragraph 279, and docs/market_research/a_save_offer_against_the_switching_rules_and_the_seam.md section 7; for how far a renewal discount may go: Ofgem SLC 4B (Financial Responsibility Principle), as quoted from the Electricity and Gas Supply Standard Consolidated Licence Conditions in docs/market_research/ofgem_licence_readiness.md section 1, and this supplier's own rule in company/pricing/renewal_desk.py; for whether a retention cut may go below cost: the retention guard's value test in company/interfaces/growth_desk.py (retention_value_protected) and the tier floor landed and measured in commit 5c137eb5b; for what the portfolio premium's target counts: Ofgem's EBIT allowance decision of 25 August 2023 as held in docs/domain_artefact_library/regulatory/price_cap_ebit_allowance.md, and the cap's nil-consumption construction in docs/domain_artefact_library/regulatory/ofgem_cap_standing_charges.json

headline.heading: The claim, in one sentence
headline.body: Winning a domestic customer costs a GB supplier a commission paid to whoever introduced them — around £25 to £30 per fuel through a comparison site — while keeping one costs margin the supplier gives up in the price it charges, not cash it pays out; and since April 2022 a licence condition has made the second the only lawful way to offer a better deal to someone who is already yours.

plain.heading: In plain terms
plain.body:
There are two quite different money flows and it is easy to model them as one. ACQUISITION is money leaving the business: a comparison site or a broker introduces a customer and invoices for it. You can point at the payment. RETENTION is money never arriving: you offer the customer a lower price than they would otherwise have paid, they stay, and the gap shows up as revenue you did not earn. Nobody sends an invoice for a retention offer.

The distinction is not bookkeeping pedantry. A cash cost and a foregone margin behave differently in every direction that matters: one hits the P&L at signup and the other bleeds across the whole term; one is the same whatever the customer consumes and the other scales with their volume; one weakens the balance sheet immediately and the other never appears on it at all. A model that charges a flat cash sum for a retention offer will get the timing, the size and the balance-sheet consequence all wrong at once, and each error will look small on its own.

theory.heading: How it works
theory.body:
ACQUISITION. The CMA set out what the cost is made of: 'Customer acquisition costs comprise doorstep/energy advisers' costs, telesales, commissions payable to brokers or PCWs, sales support, proposition development and other similar costs' (Energy Market Investigation 2016, Appendix 9.10 paragraph 64). The same paragraph records that both UK GAAP and IFRS require firms to expense those costs as incurred, so a customer relationship a supplier built itself never appears on its balance sheet — only one it bought from someone else does.

That accounting treatment is not how the economics work, and the CMA said so. For its return-on-capital analysis it amortised acquisition costs over the average customer lifespan reported by the six large suppliers: those 'varied significantly (from around four to ten years), but with a concentration of values around six years', and the CMA used six years as its base case and eight as a sensitivity (paragraph 74). Ofgem later adopted the same six-year figure in the price cap's EBIT methodology, describing it as 'in line with the CMA's approach to amortising customer acquisition costs'.

RETENTION. Since April 2022 this has been a matter of licence law rather than commercial preference. Standard Licence Condition 22B, the Ban on Acquisition-only Tariffs, stops a supplier offering a fixed-term deal to new customers that it does not also offer its existing ones. Introduced alongside the Market Stabilisation Charge as a temporary response to wholesale volatility, the MSC ended on 31 March 2024 and the BAT was kept, extended annually; Ofgem's consultation of 27 August 2025 proposes extending it to 31 March 2027.

What makes retention possible under that ban is a specific carve-out. In Ofgem's own words, 'The BAT's Market-wide Derogation, which was introduced at the same time as the BAT, enables suppliers to offer bespoke, retention-only deals to their existing customers when they are coming to the end of a fixed-term deal.' A retention offer is therefore a TARIFF — a price, offered at a defined moment in the customer's contract — and the derogation exists precisely because it is a price rather than a payment.

CHANNELS. Comparison sites are the largest single route to a domestic customer and they are paid per switch, at a rate independent of what the customer goes on to consume. Business customers mostly arrive through brokers, and brokers are not paid that way at all: the commission is an ongoing per-unit adder embedded in the customer's own unit rate for the life of the contract, typically 0.5 to 2.0 pence per kWh for a small business and less for larger sites. A broker-introduced customer therefore costs more the more they use, and costs nothing at signup.

The save on a loss notice. Since the Central Switching Service went live in July 2022 a losing supplier can be told of a pending switch, and may offer the household a Fixed Retention Tariff to stay. The licence (SLC 22B's market-wide derogation) says who such a tariff may be sold to and that it must be notified; it says nothing about its price. Ofgem said in November 2025 that it had seen no substantial evidence of the derogation's effect on pricing. The nearest published measurement of how deep retention pricing runs is the CMA's 2016 finding that renegotiated retention tariffs sat 25 to 36 per cent below rollover tariffs for electricity and 25 to 28 per cent for gas, for microbusinesses in 2012 to 2014: a discount off the supplier's own default, not a match to a rival's price.

This project's supplier sizes its save as a match to the cheapest deal on the market, using Ofgem's own published gap between the cheapest tariff and the default, and never below its own cost for the term. That is a design choice with no published basis. The reasoning is a retention desk's: a household on a loss notice is leaving for something cheaper, matching it is the least that answers the reason, and the cost floor stops a guaranteed loss. The evidence would equally allow a fixed discount off the supplier's own default, the supplier's own cheapest tariff, or no standing size at all.

How far a renewal discount may go. Nothing in the licence sets a floor under a domestic fixed tariff. The default tariff cap is a ceiling on default products, not a minimum on anything, and SLC 4B, the Financial Responsibility Principle added after the 2021 supplier failures, asks a supplier to manage responsibly the costs that would be mutualised if it failed: Renewables Obligation and Feed-in Tariff shortfalls and Supplier of Last Resort costs. That condition is a principle about risk and capital. It does not say a supplier may not sell a tariff below cost, and none of the published sources read for this page says so either. A below-cost price is lawful. What 4B makes plain is who pays when a supplier makes a habit of it.

So the limit on a discount is the supplier's own rule, and this project's supplier states it in one place: its renewal desk may undercut to meet the market, and an undercut 'may cost margin, it may never force a sale below cost'. The cost is the term's own: the forward price the supplier priced the term off, the policy and network costs it locked when it struck the rate, and the capital charge the strike prices in for holding collateral against the unhedged part of the term (about 1.2% of the forward before 2023 and 3.7% after, at the stressed volatility the desk prices with). The capital charge was left out of the floor until 2026-10-13, and a discount then stopped above the other three but below the term's cost: on one full-record seed, 496 of 698 renewals entered the value arm in that band. A rate at the floor still recovers nothing towards operating cost or bad debt, so the floor is the least a supplier could hold itself to, not a margin. The supplier holds every adjustment it chooses to make to that floor, the portfolio learning premium included. Only the cap may take a rate lower, because the cap is the law. A rate that the cost of a wholesale spike has already put above the market is not lifted or lowered by this rule: the rule stops a discount, it does not add a price rise.

When the renewal already sits at the floor. On fresh seeds every held electricity renewal sat at this supplier's own cost floor to the penny, so neither the risk-tier cut nor a save could move it. The floor was the problem, not the market: it charged the whole network allowance per unit, while Ofgem's cap construction puts only the per-kWh share in the unit rate and recovers the fixed share once through the standing charge, which the floor ignored. A renewal at that floor was not loss-making, and the market's best deal sat above the true unit cost and below the inflated floor. The fix is in order: the supplier's margin measured on the unit rate, then the world's network charge split into per-unit and per-day shares (a separate fidelity change), and only then is the save re-graded. Still a gap: how real retention desks split margin between proactive renewal pricing and a reserve for a reactive save. Detail: docs/market_research/a_save_offer_against_the_switching_rules_and_the_seam.md section 8.

The same floor holds for a retention offer, and that is a choice, not something the evidence settles. The retention guard offers a cut when the value it protects is more than the cut costs, and that value counts the acquisition cost a supplier would pay to replace the household. So a cut below cost can pass the test: losing a little on one term can cost less than winning a new customer. We still floor it, for three reasons. The loss below the floor is certain, but the save is only a belief that the household would otherwise leave. The renewal desk and the price match already hold to the floor, and one rule with a different limit for each sizing is the shape this project keeps paying for. And when the evidence is unclear, erring against our own thesis is the safe direction. Every way of sizing the offer is floored at the term's own cost (since 2026-10-14 the same floor as the renewal desk's, capital charge included: one floor for the premium, the save and the renewal cut), and the check runs on the rate the household is actually offered. Measured in the first window of the standing policy, 19 of 20 risk-tier cuts would have gone below that floor. Electricity re-fixes sit at the floor itself, so they now get no retention offer. GAP: whether a retention offer below cost ever pays for itself has not been measured. The retention holdout is the instrument that could show it, and until it does, the floor stays.

A retention offer sized as a price match needs the published default tariff to match against, and before the cap there was no such figure a supplier could read per fuel. Ofgem published the large suppliers' average standard variable tariff every month from 2012, but only as a dual-fuel annual bill (including VAT, direct debit, typical consumption). It never published electricity and gas separately, or a unit rate apart from the standing charge. Splitting that bill into two unit rates would mean choosing how to divide it, and nothing published says how. So the price match makes no offer from 2016 to 2018 (GAP, recorded in docs/market_research/svt_rates_active_passive_2016_2025.md section 1a), and whether matching the market creates value at renewal is graded from 2019 only.

WHAT THE 8 PER CENT COUNTED, AND WHAT THE PREMIUM NOW COMPARES (2026-10-14). The portfolio learning premium compares each completed term's realised margin over its revenue with a target, and closes half the gap on the next renewal, within -5 to +15 per cent. The target was PORTFOLIO_TARGET_MARGIN_RATE, 8 per cent, a literal with no cited source. Read against what it was compared with, it was not a margin. Revenue included the standing charge, and so did the margin, in full, with no cost against it: not the fixed network share it exists to recover, and not operating costs, which the term's P&L does not carry at all. By the cap's construction the standing charge IS the nil-consumption allowance, the per-customer share of network, operating costs and the other allowances (Ofgem's Default Tariff Cap level model, as read into the commons). So the ratio counted a fixed-cost recovery as profit and read 18 to 20 per cent on a book whose rates sat at cost, and the premium took the full 5 per cent off almost every renewal. For scale: the regulator's normal return for an efficient supplier was 1.9 per cent EBIT on the cap's cost allowances (not on the bill) to September 2023, and about 44 pounds per dual-fuel customer a year after it. That is a comparator, never an aim (R12), and an 8 per cent net margin on revenue is about four times it.

THE CHOICE THE DESIGN MAKES. The premium now reads the UNIT-RATE margin: each term's revenue and margin with its standing-charge revenue taken out of both, so a fixed-cost recovery is never read as profit. It compares that with the margin the term's own strike priced for, this supplier's 2 pounds per megawatt-hour over the rate the term was billed at, so the measurement and the target share one basis and one source, the company's own pricing rule. The premium then closes the gap between what the book was priced to earn and what it earned; it is a consistency check, not a margin target, because no published source sets what margin a supplier should aim for. The save takes the same cost floor the premium stops at (forward, capital, the two locked costs), so the supplier has one floor. GAP: what the standing charge itself costs to serve (operating costs, and the fixed network share once the world charges it per day rather than per kWh) is not in the term's P&L, so whether the standing charge earns or loses on its own is not measured.

expected_shape.heading: What the data should look like
expected_shape.body:
A supplier's acquisition spend should be lumpy and front-loaded against a customer book that pays back slowly: cash out at signup, margin in over something like six years. Growth should therefore look expensive in the year it happens and cheap in retrospect, which is exactly why the CMA amortised it.

The cost per domestic customer acquired through a comparison site should sit in tens of pounds, not hundreds — around £25 to £30 per fuel, so roughly £50 to £60 for a dual-fuel household. A figure in the low hundreds would imply a channel other than a comparison site, most likely direct brand marketing, for which no GB-energy-specific published benchmark appears to exist.

Business acquisition should not appear as a one-off cost line at all. It should appear as a per-kWh deduction running the length of the contract, which means a large business customer costs far more to have acquired than a small one, and the cost keeps arriving after the sale.

A retention offer should appear as reduced revenue on the retained account, concentrated at the renewal point and persisting for the term — never as a cost line. Two suppliers charging the same headline rate, one of which retained half its book with 5% discounts, should differ in revenue and not in operating costs.

And acquisition spend should show up in the balance sheet, not just the P&L. The CMA recorded the mechanism plainly: 'by growing rapidly a firm incurred significant customer acquisition costs up-front, which it expected to recover over the lifetime of the customers. However, such costs weakened a firm's balance sheet ... increasing the perceived riskiness of the supplier and, therefore, the quantity of collateral that trading counterparties required from the firm.'

live_evidence.heading: Live evidence
live_evidence.body:
The published anchors this page rests on, with what each one does and does not support.

WHAT IS SOURCED. The composition of acquisition cost and its accounting treatment (CMA Appendix 9.10 §64). The six-year amortisation base case, drawn from a reported spread of four to ten years (§74), and Ofgem's later adoption of the same figure. The existence, start date and current extent of SLC 22B, and the Market-wide Derogation that permits retention-only deals at end of fixed term. Comparison-site commission of roughly £25 to £30 per fuel switched. Broker commission bands of 0.2 to 2.0 pence per kWh by size band.

WHAT IS NOT KNOWABLE FROM THE PUBLIC RECORD. The actual per-customer acquisition costs the six large suppliers reported to the CMA are redacted in the published appendix. Every per-customer figure in that section that would settle the question is shown as an empty bracket. A supplier-specific GB acquisition cost is therefore not available at all, and any single number presented as one is an estimate wearing a citation.

ONE NEAR MISS, RECORDED BECAUSE IT IS THE FAILURE THIS PAGE EXISTS TO PREVENT. A search summary offered '£90 per customer' as an Ofgem acquisition-cost benchmark. Reading the source shows paragraph 4.24 is calculating depreciation and amortisation of FIXED ASSETS, and the £90 is that; what paragraph 4.25 shares with the CMA is only the six-year lifetime. Publishing £90 as an acquisition benchmark would have produced an invented number with a real citation attached, which is worse than an invented number, because the citation stops anyone checking.

THE SWITCHING PROCESS'S OWN OUTCOMES (added 2026-10-08). A save or win-back sits inside a family of ways a started switch does not end as a plain switch, and Ofgem measured most of that family before the July 2022 switching reform, from a January 2017 request to suppliers (impact assessment assumptions log, September 2017). Per domestic meter-point switch in 2016, out of 7.76 million: objections about 6% electricity and 5% gas, over 90% of them for debt; Customer Requested Objections, where the household asks the losing supplier to block the switch, 1.28%; withdrawals by the gaining supplier, which include cooling-off cancellations, 3.2%; switches abandoned over address data, about 1.8%; registrations rejected by the central systems, 385,000 gas and 58,000 electricity; erroneous transfers 0.96%. ElectraLink counted 7.55 million electricity switches started in 2020 against 6.2 million completed, about 18% that never finished. One correction: the 2014 consultation's '14% of electricity transfers' blocked covers domestic and non-domestic together, not households alone.

WHAT THAT BOUNDS. Stops a household makes through the losing supplier, after its 'sorry to see you go' contact, ran at 0.4% to 1.3% of domestic switches (two Ofgem papers on the same data disagree). Adding cooling-off withdrawals gives about 4%. A save is somewhere inside that, from close to zero (Ofgem counts every such stop as a prevented erroneous transfer) up to all of it. Repeat switching caps win-back: about 10% of switching electricity meter points switched twice or more in 2020, and about 6% in 2023. These are ESTIMATES that set ranges, not measured save or win-back rates.

residuals.heading: Where our picture is still weak
residuals.body:
No GB-energy-specific figure for direct or brand-marketing acquisition could be found in any public source searched. A cross-industry cost-per-lead multiplied by an assumed conversion rate gives something in the low hundreds of pounds per customer, but that is two estimates stacked on each other and should not be treated as an anchor.

No published source breaks acquisition cost out at the residential/SME boundary. Small businesses plausibly arrive through both comparison-style and broker channels, and the split between them is not published.

The comparison-site rate is cited from secondary commentary on a CMA-era figure rather than from a rate card, and no supplier publishes what it actually pays. Commission rates are commercially negotiated and are very unlikely to be uniform.

The practical effect of the BAT on what suppliers actually offer at renewal is not quantified here. The derogation permits retention deals; how deep they are, and whether they cluster at particular discount levels, is not something the licence condition tells us.

No outcome rate from after the switching reform (18 July 2022) was found: ElectraLink says it 'is no longer able to provide data on CoS started', the central service's performance reports are not public, and the Energy Switch Guarantee publishes speed only. Also not published: the share of Customer Requested Objections that are saves, where a second switch goes (back to the old supplier, or on to another one), and what a save costs.

No GB source was found that says how far a supplier's own repricing of its book (a learned premium or discount across all renewals, as opposed to a save offered to one household) may or should go, or whether suppliers in practice discount renewals when their realised book margin runs above target. This project's supplier does. It steered towards an 8 per cent net margin on revenue that counted the standing charge as profit, and read above it on a book priced at cost; since 2026-10-14 it steers towards the margin its own strike priced for, on the unit rate (How it works). Whether real suppliers reprice a book that way is not published.

scope_delta.heading: What this page does not yet establish
scope_delta.body:
It does not establish a single number to use for acquisition cost, and that is deliberate. The honest output of this research is a SHAPE — a per-switch commission for domestic, a per-kWh trail for business, a foregone margin for retention, and a six-year horizon over which any of it pays back — together with an explicit statement that the per-customer magnitude the six large suppliers actually reported is redacted from the public record.

It does not establish what our own supplier should spend. That is a company decision the simulation should be free to get wrong, not a constant to be calibrated until the answer looks right.

It does not cover customer-service cost to serve, bad debt, or the cost of losing a customer, all of which sit in the same P&L neighbourhood and none of which this page researched.

And it does not, by itself, change any code. What it does is make a specific class of future mistake visible: any acquisition or retention figure that appears in this repository without a source can now be held against a page that says what the published evidence actually supports, and what it does not.

It does not establish how a GB supplier sizes a save offer to a household that has told it, or that it has learned, it is leaving. No GB source, energy or analogous, was found that prescribes matching a competitor's price; the telecoms best-tariff remedy and consumer haggling guidance could not be retrieved when this was written, so that is not found rather than not published.

meta.title: How a GB household chooses an energy deal, and why most of them don't
meta.subtitle: Almost nobody deliberately chooses a standard variable tariff, and most of the country is on one. Both of those are true at once, and the reason is that choosing and paying are separated by years.
meta.wall_placement: Public-reality commons only. Every figure here is from a published source — Ofgem's retail market reporting, its consumer surveys, or the CMA's Energy Market Investigation. No figure produced by this project's simulation appears on this page, and no number on this page was chosen because a number was needed.
meta.no_current_level: Every number here is a published survey or regulatory statistic with its base and fieldwork date stated. None of it is a reading from this project's simulation, and none of it is a rate this project uses as an input.

The rest of the body is unchanged and keeps its 2026-08-30 dates.
