Held in the repo at docs/market_research/floor_area_anchor_need_2026_hmrc_bands.md, docs/market_research/mains_gas_is_a_meter_fact_not_a_grid_fact_need_2026.md, docs/market_research/independence_invents_one_house_in_five_that_does_not_exist.md, docs/market_research/the_tilt_table_had_a_direction_wrong_and_only_a_direction_was_claimed.md, docs/market_research/area_deprivation_adds_little_once_the_house_is_known.md, docs/market_research/gas_demand_what_drives_it_and_the_term_the_model_is_missing.md, docs/market_research/pv_yield_cannot_be_keyed_on_latitude.md; this project's measurements at docs/market_research/the_sample_is_233_houses_and_one_tail_in_five_does_not_close.md, docs/market_research/thirteen_cases_cover_demand_and_that_is_only_half_an_answer.md, docs/market_research/housing_joint_phase1_what_the_draw_already_carries.md, docs/market_research/adding_a_driver_is_not_adding_an_axis.md, docs/design/visited_corner_ledger.json.
claim_freshness.note: Every claim carries a class. FACT is a published figure with its source. CHOICE is a modelling decision this project made, with who made it and when; CHOICE claims are versioned and can be superseded. WIRING is how this project's code currently uses a fact or choice; it is a description of the code today, not a claim about the world. Where the commission asked for a figure that has not been measured, the page says so instead of supplying one.

headline.heading: The claim, in one sentence
headline.body:
What a home uses is set mostly by how big it is and how fast its fabric leaks heat, then by whether it has a gas supply at all, and much less by where it is — and because those properties come in bundles rather than independently, the homes where the potential to save is largest are a thin, specific minority that an average-home model never sees.

FACT (DESNZ NEED 2026, docs/market_research/floor_area_anchor_need_2026_hmrc_bands.md): median weather-corrected gas use in 2024 runs from 9,000 kWh in homes of 51–100 m² to 23,000 kWh in homes over 200 m², a ratio of 2.56, and the true spread is wider because the source blanks the readings at both extremes.

THIS PROJECT'S MEASUREMENT (docs/market_research/the_sample_is_233_houses_and_one_tail_in_five_does_not_close.md): 233 deliberately chosen houses reproduce 99% of the household-weighted variation across five measured outputs of Britain's housing. Four of the five tails are fully covered at 610 houses. The fifth — homes where the sun already does an unusually large share of the heating — is covered to 70% at 2,584 houses and is still climbing.

plain.heading: In plain terms
plain.body:
A house is a box that loses heat. How much heat it loses depends on how big the box is, how well its walls, roof and windows hold heat in, and how cold it is outside. The boiler, or whatever heats the house, has to put back what the box loses. That is most of a gas bill.

So the first two questions about any home are how big it is and how leaky it is. Where it is matters too, because Aberdeen is colder than Plymouth, but less than people expect: the difference between a small flat and a large old detached house is far bigger than the difference between a cold town and a mild one.

The third question is what fuel the house can use at all. About one home in five in England and Wales has no gas meter of its own. Some are rural homes on oil or bottled gas; many more are flats heated by electricity or by a shared system metered for the whole building.

These facts are not independent. Small homes are mostly flats. Old homes mostly have solid walls that leak. Rural homes are mostly detached, have a drive, and are off the gas. If you build a picture of Britain's homes by picking each feature separately, you get houses that do not exist — detached houses smaller than a one-bedroom flat — and you get far too few of the large detached homes that use the most energy.

The potential to save is about the same houses from the other side. A house that has already had its loft and cavity walls insulated has had the cheap improvements; one that has not still has them available. A house with a big south-facing roof can make more of its own electricity than one with a small north-facing roof. So where the savings are depends on what each particular house is and what has already been done to it, not on the average.

That is why this project describes Britain's housing with a few hundred houses chosen to be as DIFFERENT from each other as possible, rather than a scale model. The ordinary semi is easy; the unusual homes at the edges are where both the money and the risk sit.

theory.heading: How it works
theory.body:
HEAT LOSS IS SIZE TIMES LEAKINESS TIMES COLD. A home's space-heating demand is, to a good approximation, its heat-loss coefficient (how many watts it loses per degree of difference between inside and outside) multiplied by how cold it has been over the season, less the heat the sun and the occupants supply for free. The heat-loss coefficient grows with the area of wall, roof and floor exposed to the outside and with how poorly each one insulates. Floor area is the single best handle on the first; age and construction are the best handles on the second.

WIRING: this project's model computes a heat-loss coefficient and a thermal time constant for every home it draws, from its property type, size, age and insulation, and runs a half-hourly two-node thermal model of the building against local weather (simulation/fabric_physics.py). The sample on this page uses a closed-form annual version of the same physics, which agrees with the half-hourly model at r² = 0.9978 over 72 house-and-weather pairs (docs/market_research/thirteen_cases_cover_demand_and_that_is_only_half_an_answer.md).

FACT, AND IT CUTS AGAINST THE OBVIOUS STORY (Energy Follow-Up Survey 2017, docs/market_research/gas_demand_what_drives_it_and_the_term_the_model_is_missing.md): leaky homes are not heated to the same temperature as tight ones. Mean living-room temperature over the heating season is 17.7°C in pre-1919 dwellings against 19.1°C in post-1990 ones, 17.2°C in EPC F/G homes, and 17.5°C in homes with no insulation measures against 18.8–19.0°C with two or more. Worse-insulated homes are colder, not only more expensive, which partly cancels the fabric effect and means the saving from insulating them shows up partly as warmth rather than as lower bills.

THE FUEL IS A FACT ABOUT A METER, NOT ABOUT THE GAS GRID. FACT (DESNZ NEED 2026 metadata, docs/market_research/mains_gas_is_a_meter_fact_not_a_grid_fact_need_2026.md): NEED counts a home as gas-heated only if it has a gas meter matched to it that used at least 1,000 kWh in one of the latest three years. On that definition 19.1% of homes are not gas-heated — but 50.3% of flats, against 15.5% of detached homes and 15.0% of bungalows. Half of all flats cannot be off the gas grid; they are electrically heated or on a communal system metered at the building. The genuinely off-grid stock is the rural detached and bungalow share. CHOICE (delivery seat, 2026-09-06): the attribute this project draws is therefore 'has a mains gas supply at this meter point', the fact a supplier actually holds, and not 'off grid', which is a different and unmeasured quantity.

THE PROPERTIES COME IN BUNDLES. FACT, computed on published NEED rows (docs/market_research/independence_invents_one_house_in_five_that_does_not_exist.md): every pair of housing attributes is associated. The strongest are property type with floor area (Cramér's V 0.474), property type with mains gas (0.453) and floor area with mains gas (0.383). Age and energy rating travel together strongly too: a home built before 1930 is 2.78 times as likely as average to be rated F or G, and a home built since 2000 is 3.85 times as likely to be rated A or B (docs/market_research/the_tilt_table_had_a_direction_wrong_and_only_a_direction_was_claimed.md). Detached homes are over-represented at both ends of the rating scale — 1.21 times at A/B and 1.81 times at F/G — because old rectories and new executive homes share one label.

PLACE MATTERS LESS THAN IT LOOKS, BECAUSE PLACE IS MOSTLY HOUSE. Computed on published NEED rows (docs/market_research/area_deprivation_adds_little_once_the_house_is_known.md): median gas rises 1.38 times from the most to the least deprived fifth of English neighbourhoods. Within a single floor-area band most of that disappears — 1.09 times among 51–100 m² homes, 1.20 times among 101–150 m² homes. Less deprived areas hold bigger houses. And this project's own measurement at one fixed climate (docs/market_research/thirteen_cases_cover_demand_and_that_is_only_half_an_answer.md) puts London's housing stock lowest of the English and Welsh regions at 6,405 kWh and Wales's highest at 9,503: the warmest region has the least demanding homes, and a mild region has the most, because what is built there matters more than how cold it is.

THE POTENTIAL IS WHAT IS LEFT TO DO. A ceiling on a saving is a property of a particular house in its current state. CHOICE (director, 2026-09-05, docs/staging/done/DIRECTOR_RULING_HOUSING_VALUE_CEILING_AND_SAMPLE_PHASE1_2026-09-05.md): every ceiling is stated first in physical units — kWh generated, saved or shifted, tonnes of carbon, and the effort it asks of the household — and turned into money only on top, because prices and policy move. Where a ceiling needs something about the people rather than the house (how far a car is driven, whether the household would act), it is left as a named empty slot. Heat pumps are outside this work by the same ruling.

expected_shape.heading: What you should expect to see
expected_shape.body:
Each of these is stated so that data could contradict it. Where the commission asked for a figure that has not been measured, it says so.

1. SIZE DOMINATES PLACE. Median metered gas should rise steeply across floor-area bands — at least 2.56 times from 51–100 m² to over 200 m² — and the spread across neighbourhood deprivation should collapse to 1.2 times or less once floor area is held fixed. Measured and holding (docs/market_research/floor_area_anchor_need_2026_hmrc_bands.md, docs/market_research/area_deprivation_adds_little_once_the_house_is_known.md). If a source with different lineage showed deprivation or region still moving gas by more than 20% within a size band, this page's ordering would be wrong.

2. THE SHARE OF VARIATION SIZE AND FABRIC EXPLAIN. NOT YET MEASURED. The commission asks for the share of household-weighted gas variance that floor area and fabric heat loss explain. No regression or variance decomposition of metered gas on those two quantities exists in this project. The nearest measurements are a different question: 13 house descriptions, with weather held out, are enough to cover 99% of the variation in modelled demand (docs/market_research/thirteen_cases_cover_demand_and_that_is_only_half_an_answer.md), and modelled gas sits at 0.992 times metered gas in total for the same households (docs/market_research/adding_a_driver_is_not_adding_an_axis.md). Neither is the explained-variance figure, and neither should be read as it.

3. GAS SUPPLY IS A MINORITY FACT THAT CONCENTRATES IN FLATS AND RURAL HOMES. About one home in five should have no gas meter of its own, half of flats and about one in six detached homes and bungalows. Measured: 19.1% overall, 50.3% of flats, 15.5% detached, 15.0% bungalow (docs/market_research/mains_gas_is_a_meter_fact_not_a_grid_fact_need_2026.md). The true off-grid share is a different number and is not established.

4. AN INDEPENDENT DRAW SHOULD INVENT HOUSES. Picking type, size, age and fuel separately should put a substantial share of homes in combinations the stock does not contain and should under-produce large detached homes. Measured: 19.6% of an independent draw lands in cells the stock effectively lacks; it produces 1,303 detached homes under 50 m² per 50,000 where the stock has none, and large detached homes over 200 m² at one fifth of their real frequency (docs/market_research/independence_invents_one_house_in_five_that_does_not_exist.md).

5. BRITAIN'S HOUSING OUTPUTS SHOULD FILL A THIN SURFACE, NOT A BOX. Of the 40 possible two-way extremes across five outputs (top or bottom 5% on two at once), only some should be occupied. THIS PROJECT'S MEASUREMENT: 23 of 40 are occupied and 17 are empty, because the outputs are all driven by the same fabric (docs/market_research/the_sample_is_233_houses_and_one_tail_in_five_does_not_close.md).

6. A SAMPLE CHOSEN FOR DIFFERENCE SHOULD COST MORE HOUSES THAN ONE PLACED AT THE MASS, AND COVER THE EDGES BETTER. THIS PROJECT'S MEASUREMENT: 233 chosen houses reach 99% of the variation, where an optimal partition reaches it at 55, a factor of 4.2. Drawn on what houses ARE rather than what they DO, the same 233 cover the same 99% but leave a gap 4.4 times wider at the worst-covered point, miss 3 of the 23 corners, and miss 40% of the top-consumption tail (docs/market_research/the_sample_is_233_houses_and_one_tail_in_five_does_not_close.md).

7. THE SOLAR POTENTIAL CEILING. NOT YET MEASURED. The commission asks for the share of houses whose technical PV ceiling exceeds a given annual output. It cannot be computed: no source this project holds gives roof area or pitch, and the model currently gives every non-flat home the same east–west roof. What IS measured is the yield per kilowatt installed: 835 kWh per kWp in the dullest fifth of Britain's sunshine and 947 in the sunniest, around the MCS 2025 fleet average of 882 (docs/market_research/pv_yield_cannot_be_keyed_on_latitude.md). The sunniest and dullest bands overlap across four degrees of latitude, so sunshine is coastal and eastern as much as southern.

8. THE BATTERY, CAR-CHARGING AND HEATING-SETTINGS CEILINGS. NOT YET MEASURED. Battery potential depends on solar, which is not stated; car-charging potential needs off-street parking, which the model currently assigns by property type rather than from a published source; and the flow-temperature turn-down ceiling is deliberately unstated, because current boiler settings are not modelled (see the next sections).

9. THE INSULATION AND THERMOSTAT TURN-DOWN CEILINGS. Computed per house as two of the five sample outputs, but NO DISTRIBUTION OF THEIR SIZE IS PUBLISHED HERE YET: the sample measured how well it covers them, not how large they are across Britain.

live_evidence.heading: The evidence, measured
live_evidence.body:
FLOOR AREA AGAINST METERED USE. FACT (DESNZ NEED anonymised 2026 sample, 50,000 dwellings, floor area banded by HMRC valuation data; docs/market_research/floor_area_anchor_need_2026_hmrc_bands.md). Median 2024 weather-corrected gas by band: under 50 m², 5,700 kWh; 51–100, 9,000; 101–150, 12,100; 151–200, 16,200; over 200, 23,000. Median electricity: 2,000; 2,400; 2,900; 3,700; 5,300. NEED blanks gas readings under 1,000 or over 50,000 kWh, and this lands at the ends: 54% of the smallest band's gas readings are blanked (mostly the low cut, so its median is overstated) and 42% of the largest band's (mostly the high cut, so its median is understated). The true spread is wider than 2.56 times and this source cannot say by how much.

BUNGALOWS ARE THEIR OWN KIND OF HOME. FACT (same source): bungalows are 7.9% of the sample and concentrate in 51–100 m², where detached homes concentrate in 101–150 m². WIRING: this project's model still folds bungalows into detached when it draws a home; the published share is held, the separate type is not yet drawn.

FUEL BY PROPERTY TYPE. FACT (DESNZ NEED 2026, docs/market_research/mains_gas_is_a_meter_fact_not_a_grid_fact_need_2026.md): share not gas-heated on NEED's meter-based definition — flat 50.3% (n = 11,910), detached 15.5%, bungalow 15.0%, end terrace 7.2%, semi-detached 6.6%, mid terrace 6.5%; all homes 19.1%. NEED's own reason flag is blank for 90.6% of these, so the source cannot separate 'no gas supply' from 'no meter matched to this flat'.

GAS BY ENERGY RATING. FACT (Energy Follow-Up Survey 2017, docs/market_research/gas_demand_what_drives_it_and_the_term_the_model_is_missing.md): median annual gas 9,600 kWh for EPC A–C, 13,000 for D, 14,500 for E.

HOW THE PROPERTIES TRAVEL TOGETHER. Computed by this project on published NEED rows (docs/market_research/independence_invents_one_house_in_five_that_does_not_exist.md, docs/market_research/the_tilt_table_had_a_direction_wrong_and_only_a_direction_was_claimed.md): the association table and the lifts quoted above, over 50,000 dwellings and the 34,914 that carry an energy rating. WIRING: the homes this project draws for its market are now drawn as whole rows of this measured joint, adjusted to published national shares, rather than attribute by attribute (simulation/premise_population.py, draw_premise_from_joint). The joint carries floor area, loft and cavity insulation, existing solar and gas supply together.

THE SAMPLE. THIS PROJECT'S MEASUREMENT, 2026-09-07 (docs/market_research/the_sample_is_233_houses_and_one_tail_in_five_does_not_close.md). The population is 24,662,309 England-and-Wales households in 143,511 occupied 1 km weather cells, crossed with the 274 distinct house types NEED resolves: 39.3 million house-and-place pairs, sampled to 200,000 with household weight. Five outputs are measured for each: annual heat demand, kWh per degree-day (how strongly demand follows the weather), the share of heat loss the sun already offsets, the saving if the fabric were insulated to full, and the saving from one degree off the thermostat. Variation covered by the chosen sample: 8 houses 72.9%; 21 houses 90.8%; 55 houses 96.7%; 144 houses 98.7%; 233 houses 99.25%; 377 houses 99.6%. At 233 houses no household is more than 0.37 standardised units of behaviour from a house in the sample.

THE TAILS. Same measurement. Share of each output's top 1% that a chosen house sits in, at 233 houses: demand 100%, weather gradient 80%, solar offset 30%, insulation ceiling 100%, turn-down 80%. At 610 houses all are 100% except solar offset, at 40%; at 2,584 houses solar offset reaches 70%. That tail is a thin, structured group — small, well-insulated homes in the sunniest places — which a draw spreading houses across five dimensions has no reason to visit, however large.

THE CORNERS. Same measurement and docs/design/visited_corner_ledger.json: 23 of 40 two-way extremes are occupied. The largest: low weather gradient with a low insulation ceiling (6.9% of households); low gradient with low turn-down (5.3%); high gradient with high turn-down (5.0%); high solar offset with a low insulation ceiling (4.9%); high demand with a high insulation ceiling (4.2%). The 233-house draw visits all 23; one run has been recorded so far.

WHERE THE SUN IS. FACT and derivation (docs/market_research/pv_yield_cannot_be_keyed_on_latitude.md): yield bands keyed on HadUK-Grid annual sunshine, levelled to the MCS 2025 fleet average of 882 kWh/kWp — under 1,401 hours, 835 kWh/kWp (16.2% of households); 1,401–1,513 h, 866 (24.7%); 1,513–1,603 h, 888 (29.8%); 1,603–1,727 h, 909 (23.9%); over 1,727 h, 947 (5.4%). The level is published; the shape across bands is this project's derivation by the Angström–Prescott method.

residuals.heading: Where our picture is still weak
residuals.body:
THE ROOF IS MISSING, SO THE SOLAR CEILING IS MISSING. No source this project holds gives roof area, pitch or flat-versus-pitched; the commission anticipated this. WIRING: the model gives every non-flat home the same east–west roof and every flat none. Until a published roof source is found, the per-house solar ceiling cannot be stated in kWh, only bounded by sunshine and orientation — and with it the battery ceiling, which depends on solar.

CURRENT HEATING SETTINGS ARE DELIBERATELY ABSENT. CHOICE (director, 2026-09-05, recorded in docs/market_research/floor_area_anchor_need_2026_hmrc_bands.md): 'The lever only means something once there's a product that could turn it down, and that isn't built. Don't invent hidden state for a ceiling nothing can act on.' The consequence is stated so it is not mistaken for an oversight: the ceiling on turning down a boiler's flow temperature is unstateable, not merely uncomputed.

THE MODEL HEATS EVERY HOME TO THE SAME TEMPERATURE IN THE SAMPLE MEASUREMENT. WIRING (docs/market_research/gas_demand_what_drives_it_and_the_term_the_model_is_missing.md): the closed form behind the sample holds the thermostat at 20°C for every household, while published measurement shows leaky homes sitting 1.4–2.1°C colder. So the model overstates demand, and therefore overstates the insulation saving, in exactly the homes a supplier would target for insulation. The full building model does draw a per-home set-point, but at a mean (20.5°C) and spread that are not anchored and sit above the published median of 20°C.

RATED SAVINGS AGAINST WHAT METERS SHOW. The commission requires every ceiling to carry the in-use figure with the rated one beside it. That gap is not yet represented. Two published figures are held. A general one for energy certificates: modelled consumption 50–100% above metered billing consumption (docs/market_research/epc_open_data.md, citing a 2023 study). And the regulator's own measure-specific discounts, ECO1's in-use factors, which cut a measure's modelled saving by 35% for cavity wall and loft insulation, 33% for solid brick walls built before 1967 (1965 in Scotland), 25% for later or non-brick solid walls and room-in-roof, 15% for flat roofs, floors, cylinder jackets, pipework, draught-proofing, glazing and doors, and 10% for district heating (Ofgem ECO Measures Table v1.6, Dec 2014). ECO1 gave none for boilers, storage heaters, controls, heat pumps or solar, and ECO3 and ECO4 replaced in-use factors with deemed scores, so there is no current equivalent.

PARKING IS ASSUMED, NOT SOURCED. WIRING: off-street parking is currently given to every detached and semi-detached home and no other, which is a rule of thumb rather than a published figure; it is what the car-charging ceiling would rest on.

FLOOR AREA IS BANDED. Five bands with an open top above 200 m². Any continuous size within a band is an interpolation choice; the model currently uses band midpoints.

ENGLAND AND WALES ONLY FOR THE HOUSES. NEED carries no Scottish dwellings, so the sample and every cross-tabulation here exclude Scotland's homes — the coldest 8% of Britain's households.

ONE TAIL DOES NOT CLOSE. The solar-offset tail needs a sample built to draw into it on purpose; that is not built, so at the reported size it is covered to 30%.

THE SAMPLE IS MEASURED, NOT YET USED. The 233-house design describes the method. The homes this project's market actually draws come from the fitted joint above, in proportion; the chosen-for-difference draw is not yet what a run uses.

GENERATION AND VALIDATION SHARE A SOURCE. The size, fuel and association figures all come from NEED, and NEED also anchors this project's high-end gas figure. Checking the model's gas against NEED after fitting the housing to NEED would be circular; validation needs a source with different lineage and none is in use yet.

scope_delta.heading: What this page does not yet establish
scope_delta.body:
WHAT IS GENERAL AND WHAT IS OURS. The physics — heat loss as size times leakiness times cold, the free heat from the sun and occupants — is standard building science. The published facts are the government's. The method — choose houses for how differently they behave, weight them back to the population, measure coverage on outputs not labels — is general statistics. The sample size, the corners and the tail coverage are this project's measurements of its own model of Britain, and carry its assumptions.

IT DOES NOT STATE WHERE THE MONEY IS IN POUNDS. Ceilings are physical first by decision, and the per-house ceilings on solar, battery, car charging and heating settings are not stated at all. The page explains what drives potential and where in Britain's housing it concentrates; it does not yet price it.

IT DOES NOT SAY WHAT A SUPPLIER CAN SEE. Everything here is about what a house actually is. What a supplier can learn of it — an energy certificate where one exists, an address, a meter — is a separate question with its own page, not yet written.

IT DOES NOT SAY HOW HOUSES CHANGE. Boilers are replaced, solar panels and cars arrive, homes are extended. That is a separate page, not yet written.

IT LEAVES PEOPLE OUT ON PURPOSE. How many people live in a home, how they use it, whether they would act on advice and what they can afford are a separate programme. Where a house's potential needs a people-side input to become real, the slot is named and left empty.

CHOICES ON THIS PAGE, VERSIONED. Sample design: drawn for difference, similarity judged on five outputs, N reported from two coverage curves rather than chosen (director's ruling 2026-09-05; measured 2026-09-07, version 1). N = 233 for 99% of household-weighted variation; 610 for four of five tails; the fifth unreached. Fuel attribute defined as gas supply at the meter (2026-09-06). Current heating settings excluded (director, 2026-09-05). Ceilings physical first, heat pumps excluded (director, 2026-09-05). Each of these can be superseded; a superseded figure will be struck through beside its replacement, not removed.

meta.title: Who lives where: an address explains a tenth of who is inside, and the way a household pays marks where the risk is
meta.subtitle: A supplier knows a customer's address before it knows anything else. For the number of people inside, that address is worth surprisingly little. For money, the payment method a household chooses tells you more, and the reason it does is not the reason it looks like.
meta.wall_placement: Two kinds of figure, kept apart and labelled on every line. PUBLISHED FACTS: Census 2021 household size by output area (TS017), the English Housing Survey, DESNZ fuel poverty statistics for England (2024 data), DESNZ Quarterly Energy Prices, the DESNZ National Energy Efficiency Data-Framework (NEED) and Energy Follow-Up Survey, DESNZ's 2024 metered hot-water study, Ofgem's price-cap debt allowance, and one supplier's published accounts. THIS PROJECT'S OWN MEASUREMENTS, labelled as such: the nine per cent split (this project's arithmetic over the whole published census table, not a sample), and every figure about the simulated book. The page also describes how this project's simulated world draws its households, which is why it sits outside what the simulated supplier is allowed to read: the supplier may know what any real supplier could look up from an address, and nothing about how the world was built.
meta.no_current_level: There is no single current level on this page. The published figures carry their own year and are slow-moving (a census every ten years, fuel poverty annually). The figures about the simulated book were measured on 27 September 2026 and move whenever the book is redrawn.

Held in the repository at: docs/market_research/the_postcode_explains_nine_percent_of_who_lives_there.md; docs/market_research/ASSUMPTIONS.md (rows for TS017, EHS tenure and size, fuel poverty, payment-method remainder); docs/market_research/dd_attribution_confound_w2_10.md; docs/market_research/dd_failure_basis_and_live_arrears_provision_rates.md; docs/market_research/occupancy_consumption_volume_shape_w2_13.md; docs/market_research/children_within_household_size_census_2021.md and docs/institutional/knowledge_map.md (children row); docs/market_research/adding_a_driver_is_not_adding_an_axis.md; docs/staging/records/SEAT_RESULT_W2_19_LAYER_ONE_REACHES_NO_HOME_AND_AT_REAL_INPUTS_WIRING_IT_MOVES_THE_MEAN_HEADCOUNT_0_09_2026-09-25.md; docs/staging/records/PREREG_W2_19_LAYER_ONE_THE_SITED_CELL_CARRIES_ITS_OUTPUT_AREA_2026-09-27.md (results section); code: simulation/dwelling_records.py, simulation/household_physical_layer.py (LAYER_CORRELATIONS), simulation/household_segments.py, simulation/premise_trace.py, simulation/dd_attribution.py (placeholder split), simulation/willingness_classification.py (placeholder won't-pay incidence), tools/people_physical_layer.py.
claim_freshness.note: Written on the director's people ruling of 5 September 2026 (item 5), as amended the same day. An earlier record (25 September) said the address-conditioned headcount was built but reached no home. That stopped being true on 27 September (commit c08932808, an ancestor of origin/main): every England-and-Wales home in the book now draws its headcount from its own output area. This page states the current position and keeps the earlier one beside it. Two slots the ruling asked for are filled differently: the fuel-poverty multiple is published arithmetic; the share of usage variance explained by occupancy has not been measured and is stated as such rather than estimated.

headline.heading: The claim, in one sentence
headline.body: Where a household lives tells a supplier very little about how many people are inside — across every household in England and Wales an output area explains 9% of the variation in household size — so occupancy, which drives how much energy a home uses and when, has to be learned from the meter rather than looked up; while the way a household pays is strongly associated with money risk (prepayment households are in fuel poverty at 2.5 times the rate of direct-debit households), and nothing published says how much of that association the method causes and how much comes from which households choose it.

plain.heading: In plain terms
plain.body:
A supplier signing up a new customer knows the address, the meter, and soon the payment method. It does not know who lives there. So the natural question is how much the address gives away.

For the number of people, the answer is about a tenth. The census publishes how many people live in each home for every neighbourhood of roughly 130 households in England and Wales. Inside any one of those neighbourhoods you find almost the full national mix: single people, couples, families, the odd household of six. Knowing the street narrows things down only a little. The pensioner alone in the four-bedroom house and the five people in the two-bedroom flat are not rare exceptions sitting on top of a good guess. They are where most of the variation is.

That matters because the number of people is one of the main things that sets a home's usage. More people means more hot water, more cooking, more washing, and someone at home during the day. But the effect is not proportional. The second person adds a lot; the fifth adds much less, because the fridge, the lighting and the boiler's own losses are shared.

Money is different. How a household pays — direct debit, paying each bill when it arrives, or a prepayment meter — lines up strongly with how stretched it is. Prepayment households are in fuel poverty at about two and a half times the rate of direct-debit households, and the cost of bad debt built into the price cap is several times higher for customers who pay on receipt of a bill than for those on direct debit.

The trap is to read that as direct debit making people better payers. At least part of it runs the other way: households that are organised and not under pressure choose direct debit, and households under pressure end up on prepayment or paying late. Nobody has published how the gap divides between the two, so the safe reading is that the payment method marks the risk, and how much it cures is unknown.

theory.heading: How it works
theory.body:
TWO LAYERS, AND WHERE THE LINE BETWEEN THEM FALLS. Choice (director, 5 September 2026): every simulated household is drawn as the household you would EXPECT at that address, plus how this particular household DIFFERS from that expectation. The first layer is built from published small-area statistics, so a real supplier could reconstruct it from an address. The second is private and has to be discovered — from meter readings, payment records, contacts, or by asking. The value of the split is that it can be measured rather than assumed.

HOW MUCH THE ADDRESS IS WORTH, FOR HOUSEHOLD SIZE. Fact (ONS Census 2021, TS017): household size is published for all 188,880 output areas of England and Wales, covering 24,783,116 households, mean 2.359 people. This project's measurement over that whole table: the variance of household size is 1.762; 0.159 of it lies BETWEEN output areas and 1.603 WITHIN them. That is 9.0% and 91.0%, and the split is exact (between plus within equals total), not a model. An output area averages about 131 households. A finer geography could explain more, and household size is not published at a finer grain; a coarser one would explain less.

HOW PEOPLE TURN INTO ENERGY. Fact (DESNZ NEED, 2023 consumption year, England and Wales, median kWh a year by number of adults): electricity 1,993 for one adult, 2,867 for two, 4,129 for five or more — about twice. Gas 8,546, 10,624 and 14,486 — about 1.7 times. Gas responds less because most of it heats the building, and the building is the same whoever is in it. The table counts adults only; children are not in it. Fact (SAP 2012 / BREDEM): daily hot-water volume is modelled as 36 litres plus 25 litres per person, so four people use about 1.6 times the hot water of two, not twice. Fact (DESNZ, March 2024, 45,000 metered homes on gas combi boilers): median daily hot-water volume 90 litres, against the 96 that formula gives at 2.4 people.

HOW PEOPLE SET THE SHAPE OF THE DAY. Fact (DESNZ/BRE Energy Follow-Up Survey, winter 2018/19, about 1,170 households): someone is home all weekday daytime in 37% of one-person households and 67% of households of five or more; 63% where someone is over pension age against 34% where nobody is. In the evening (88%) and overnight (94%) almost every household is home whatever its make-up. So composition changes the daytime part of the load curve and barely touches the rest.

HOW PAYMENT METHOD LINES UP WITH MONEY. Fact (DESNZ fuel poverty statistics, England, 2024): 11.0% of households are in fuel poverty; by electricity payment method the rate is 22.3% for prepayment, 18.5% for standard credit and 8.8% for direct debit. Fact (Ofgem, price cap October–December 2024): the allowance for debt-related costs is £25 per dual-fuel customer on direct debit (1.4% of that cap), £121 on standard credit (6.5%) and £10 on prepayment (0.6%). Prepayment's allowance is lowest because a prepayment customer pays before using, so little debt can build up on the account. Fact (Centrica plc accounts, 2025, UK residential): provisions held against direct-debit receivables were 2.8% of the gross balance; against pay-on-receipt balances 44.7%; against final bills from customers who have left, 84.0%.

WHY THE PAYMENT LINE IS PARTLY, AND UNMEASURABLY, SELECTION. Fact (Ofgem): the regulator sets a higher cap for standard credit because of the extra cost and risk of serving it, and has written that a general shift to direct debit “reduced the numbers of customers who fell into arrears” — which is exactly the causal reading the evidence cannot yet support. Nothing published splits that gap into the part direct debit CAUSES and the part that comes from which households choose it. Choice (this project, July 2026, a placeholder awaiting the director's figure): the simulated world needs SOME split to run, so it carries one — direct debit by itself removes 15% of a household's arrears risk, and the rest of the gap is selection. That figure is marked in the code as unmeasured and is never tuned toward a result. A real supplier cannot see the split either, which is the point.

expected_shape.heading: What you should expect to see
expected_shape.body:
Each statement below can be checked and can fail. Where the ruling asked for a figure that has not been measured, the gap is stated instead of a number.

AN ADDRESS EXPLAINS ABOUT 9% OF HOUSEHOLD SIZE. Fact-derived, this project's arithmetic over the full Census 2021 table for England and Wales. Any population drawn from output-area distributions should reproduce a between-area share near 9%, and a simulated book's EXPECTED mean household size, given the neighbourhoods it sits in, should land on the national mean of 2.359. If a book's expected mean drifts well away from that, its homes have been placed in unrepresentative neighbourhoods.

OCCUPANCY EXPLAINS X% OF THE VARIATION IN USAGE BETWEEN OTHERWISE SIMILAR HOMES. Not yet measured: no published source held here gives a variance share for usage by occupancy within a dwelling type, and the NEED tables are medians by number of adults, which show the gradient but cannot give a share of variance. What can be stated falsifiably is the SHAPE: electricity should rise about twofold from one adult to five or more, gas about 1.7-fold, with the largest step at the second adult for both fuels.

PREPAYMENT HOUSEHOLDS CARRY 2.5 TIMES THE FUEL-POVERTY RATE OF DIRECT-DEBIT HOUSEHOLDS. Fact-derived: 22.3% divided by 8.8%, both from the same DESNZ release for England in 2024 and both measured as the share of households using that payment method who are fuel poor. Standard credit sits at 2.1 times. A simulated population that uses these rates should show this ordering — prepayment above standard credit above direct debit — and not a flat rate.

BAD DEBT SHOULD SIT ON PAY-ON-RECEIPT, NOT PREPAYMENT. Fact: the cap's debt allowance is 4.6 times higher for standard credit than for direct debit, and lowest of all for prepayment. A book where prepayment customers generate the most written-off debt is modelling the wrong mechanism.

DAYTIME PRESENCE SHOULD RISE WITH HOUSEHOLD SIZE AND WITH A PENSIONER PRESENT, and evening and overnight presence should not depend on composition at all.

THE OWNER-RENTER SPLIT IS 65 / 19 / 16, and household size differs by tenure. Fact (English Housing Survey 2023-24): 65% owner-occupiers (35% outright, 30% with a mortgage), 19% private renters, 16% social renters. Mean household size is 2.7 for mortgagors, 2.3 for private renters and 1.8 for outright owners.

HOW MUCH OF TENURE AN ADDRESS EXPLAINS. Not yet measured. Tenure and dwelling type are expected to be far more clustered by neighbourhood than household size is, which would make an address worth more for those than for size; that is a prediction, not a result.

HOW TENURE AND PAYMENT METHOD COMBINE. Not yet measured: no published cross-tabulation of tenure against payment method is held here, so the association a reader might expect between social renting and prepayment is not established on this page.

live_evidence.heading: The evidence, measured
live_evidence.body:
THE FULL-POPULATION SPLIT. This project's measurement, over the Census 2021 TS017 table for all 24,783,116 households in England and Wales: between output areas 0.159, within 1.603, total 1.762, mean 2.359. Reproducible from tools/people_physical_layer.py --split.

WHAT THE SIMULATED BOOK DOES WITH IT, AND HOW THAT CHANGED. Wiring. On 25 September 2026 the address-conditioned headcount was built but reached no home: no simulated dwelling carried an output area, so all 231 dwelling entries drew from the national distribution. Since 27 September every simulated home is placed in a real one-kilometre cell and then in a real output area inside that cell, in proportion to where the census puts households, and draws its headcount from that output area's published distribution. Of the 231 entries, 218 are now conditioned on their own area. The other 13 are in Scotland, which TS017 does not cover; they carry their Scottish area code and read the national distribution, and say so.

THE NUMBERS AT REAL INPUTS. The 231 entries are 155 homes, because a dual-fuel household's gas and electricity accounts are one house. Measured per home: the realised mean household size is 2.297, against 2.419 for the same homes under the national draw. A mean over 155 homes has a standard error of about 0.09, so a single draw landing there says little. The quantity that does mean something is the EXPECTED mean given the neighbourhoods the homes sit in: 2.356, against the census figure of 2.359. The book's homes are not placed in neighbourhoods biased toward small or large households.

A PREDICTION THAT MISSED, KEPT BESIDE THE RESULT. Before building, the expected realised mean was written down as 2.336 plus or minus 0.03. It came out at 2.277 across the 231 entries. The band was too narrow: it was estimated from the homes that changed rather than from the whole draw.

WHAT OCCUPANCY DOES TO THE MODELLED DEMAND. Wiring. Adding the people-driven hot-water term moved the modelled gas total from 0.883 times the metered gas of the same households to 0.992 times. It left the number of synthetic households needed to represent Britain where it was — 6,813 before and 6,816 after, the same step of the ladder of sizes tried, so the three is rounding — because occupancy changes how much a home uses without adding anything new that the sample has to cover.

WHAT THE WORLD DRAWS INDEPENDENTLY, AND SAYS SO. Wiring, measured 30 September 2026. Household size and income stress are drawn independently because no published table of household size against income was found; a test of independence on two draws gave chi-squared values of 5.6 and 6.9 on 6 degrees of freedom, as expected for independent draws. Tenure is drawn from the national 65 / 19 / 16 shares and is not yet conditioned on the neighbourhood. Payment method is drawn per household — direct debit at the published 72% for electricity and 75% for gas, with the rest split evenly between prepayment and standard credit, after Ofgem's roughly 74 / 13 / 13 — and is not conditioned on tenure or area. One association nobody intended was found by measuring: retirement is triggered by the age of the building rather than of the people, which links building age to income stress (Cramér's V 0.14). It is declared in the code rather than hidden.

THE FUEL-POVERTY ORDERING IN THE WORLD IS ARITHMETIC, NOT EVIDENCE. Wiring. The world draws fuel poverty conditional on payment method at exactly the DESNZ rates of 22.3%, 18.5% and 8.8%. So a simulated book showing prepayment at 2.5 times direct debit is reproducing its input, and is not presented here as confirmation.

residuals.heading: Where our picture is still weak
residuals.body:
THE FIRST LAYER IS CONDITIONED ON THE ADDRESS BUT NOT ON THE HOUSE. The ruling asks for the household you would expect given the postcode AND the house. Headcount is drawn from the output area alone; a one-bedroom flat and a four-bedroom house in the same area draw from the same distribution. The census occupancy rating — people against bedrooms, by area — is the published source for that, and it has not been pulled.

THE SECOND LAYER IS NOT YET ANCHORED. How far a household departs from the expectation for its house is what the ruling says must be anchored in the published spread of usage within similar homes. That spread has not been measured here, which is why the occupancy share of usage variance above is a gap rather than a figure.

SCOTLAND READS THE NATIONAL DISTRIBUTION. The census table used here covers England and Wales. Scottish homes in the book carry their area and fall back to the national mix, visibly.

THE NINE PER CENT IS FOR HOUSEHOLD SIZE ONLY. Presence patterns, heating schedules and appliance ownership have their own between-area shares and none has been measured.

CHILDREN ARE HALF-ANSWERED. How many children a household of a given size has is now drawn from a census-derived joint (71.5% of households have no dependent children). What a child adds to usage compared with an adult is not published — the NEED tables count adults only — so it is sampled across a range rather than stated.

INCOME AND OCCUPANCY ARE DRAWN INDEPENDENTLY because nothing published was found to couple them. The independence is measured and declared, not claimed as true of the world.

THE PAYMENT GAP HAS NO PUBLISHED DECOMPOSITION. How much of direct debit's better record is caused by direct debit, and how much by who chooses it, is unpublished. So is the split between households that cannot pay and households that will not. Both are values for the director to set. The world currently runs on placeholders for both, marked as placeholders in the code: direct debit's own effect at 15% fewer arrears, and households that could pay but will not at 10%. Neither is evidence and neither is presented here as a finding.

THE NON-DIRECT-DEBIT SPLIT IS THIN. The 50/50 split between prepayment and standard credit rests on one Ofgem figure of roughly 13% each; DESNZ's own quarterly series publishes the direct-debit share only.

NOT ON THIS PAGE YET, AND IN SCOPE FOR THE SAME PHASE OF WORK. How households respond to collections — a payment plan, a resized direct debit, a prepayment proposal — vulnerability and when it is disclosed, and moving house and change of tenancy. Those were brought forward into this phase on 5 September and are not established here.

scope_delta.heading: What this page does not yet establish
scope_delta.body:
WHAT IS GENERAL AND WHAT IS OURS. The census split, the consumption gradients, the presence rates, the fuel-poverty rates and the debt allowances are published facts about Great Britain and transfer to any model. The two-layer structure is this project's choice, made by the director on 5 September 2026. The figures about the simulated book are measurements of this project's world and describe nothing else.

IT DOES NOT SHOW A SUPPLIER CAN INFER OCCUPANCY FROM AN ADDRESS. At 9% it largely cannot, which means any product that assumed it could was assuming a number nobody had measured. Occupancy has to be inferred from the meter, and how well a supplier can do that is a separate question this page does not answer.

IT DOES NOT SAY DIRECT DEBIT MAKES HOUSEHOLDS PAY. It says payment method marks risk. A business case that credits direct debit with the whole difference in outcomes is crediting it with selection.

WHERE EACH FIGURE LIVES. The census split: docs/market_research/the_postcode_explains_nine_percent_of_who_lives_there.md and tools/people_physical_layer.py. The book's headcounts: docs/staging/records/PREREG_W2_19_LAYER_ONE_THE_SITED_CELL_CARRIES_ITS_OUTPUT_AREA_2026-09-27.md and simulation/dwelling_records.py. Consumption by adults and daytime presence: docs/market_research/occupancy_consumption_volume_shape_w2_13.md. Hot water: simulation/premise_trace.py. Tenure, household size by tenure and fuel poverty: docs/market_research/ASSUMPTIONS.md. Payment mix and the selection argument: docs/market_research/dd_attribution_confound_w2_10.md and simulation/household_segments.py. Debt allowances and provisions: docs/market_research/dd_failure_basis_and_live_arrears_provision_rates.md. Declared independences: simulation/household_physical_layer.py.

NEXT IN THIS SERIES. How households behave toward a supplier, and the residual and the change, are written as stubs: their scope is decided and their work is not yet authorised.

meta.title: The first-year blind spot: how a shock count that could not see year one invented a loyalty pattern
meta.subtitle: In this project's simulated world, new customers looked more loyal than long-standing ones. Real GB evidence points the other way. All of the difference came from one measure that needed a year of history, and so read zero in every household's first year.
meta.wall_placement: Method, illustrated with this project's own simulation. THE TENURE GRADIENT, ITS CAUSE AND EVERY RETENTION FIGURE ON THIS PAGE ARE MEASUREMENTS OF THIS PROJECT'S SIMULATED WORLD, not of real GB households, and they are labelled as such where they appear. Three things on the page are published record and are cited to the files that hold them: what bill shock is for each payment population, the direction of the real tenure effect, and the published bound on how switching relates to bill size. One part of the lesson is general and holds well beyond this project. A measure that compares this year with last year does not exist in a customer's first year. If that gap is stored as zero rather than as unknown, it produces a tenure effect that nobody's behaviour caused.
meta.no_current_level: This page reports a defect that was found and the repairs made since, not a calibrated rate. No figure here is a real-world switching or retention rate, and none is used as an input. The real-world size of first-year switching is NOT established in this repository: docs/market_research/first_renewal_departure_rate_small_gb_supplier.md researched it on 2026-10-01 and found no published figure, so the code carries it as None.

claim_freshness.source: Finding: docs/staging/WORKER_FINDING_THE_WORLDS_BILL_SHOCK_COUNT_IS_BLIND_IN_A_HOUSEHOLDS_FIRST_YEAR_AND_CARRIES_THE_WHOLE_TENURE_GRADIENT_2026-10-01.md. Per-term table and pre-registered predictions: docs/staging/records/SEAT_PREREG_THE_NEXT_AB_ON_THE_SINGLE_ROLL_WORLD_WHAT_A_SEED_VARIES_2026-09-30.md (section 'What drives the world', predictions committed first as 33e9c1ba3, graded in 8dd7794bd). Definitions: docs/market_research/what_bill_shock_is.md and docs/market_research/satisfaction_drivers_and_the_three_bill_shocks.md. Published tenure direction: docs/market_research/svt_rates_active_passive_2016_2025.md. Bill-size bound: docs/market_research/is_there_a_bill_level_at_which_switching_rises.md. Read error: docs/market_research/how_far_a_settled_eac_sits_from_next_years_use.md.
claim_freshness.note: Commissioned by the director on 2026-10-02 (docs/staging/console/DIRECTOR_CONSOLE_2026-10-02.md), who asked for a page on 'the loyalty finding'. Read the direction carefully. In this world the artefact made loyalty look as if it FELL with tenure, because first-year households looked unusually calm. The general trap works in either direction, depending on which year the blind measure undercounts.

headline.heading: The claim, in one sentence
headline.body:
A table of churn by tenure is only as honest as the measures behind it in each year. In this project's simulated world, ONE measure that could not see a household's first year produced the WHOLE of the apparent link between tenure and loyalty.

The measure was the world's count of bill shocks. It compared each month's bill with the same month a year earlier. In a household's first year there is no year earlier, so the count was zero for every one of the 156 households decided at their first anniversary. Households first decided at a later anniversary averaged 6.86 shocked months out of 12. The simulated world kept 0.775 of the first group and 0.651 of the second, so long-standing customers looked LESS loyal. The published GB record points the other way.

Hold that one term at its average and the gradient against years on supply moves from −0.346 to −0.009. Nothing else in the model was carrying it. (Simulation measurements, docs/staging/WORKER_FINDING_THE_WORLDS_BILL_SHOCK_COUNT_IS_BLIND_IN_A_HOUSEHOLDS_FIRST_YEAR_AND_CARRIES_THE_WHOLE_TENURE_GRADIENT_2026-10-01.md.)

plain.heading: In plain terms
plain.body:
A TENURE GRADIENT is the pattern you see when you sort customers by how long they have been with you and ask how many leave. The usual expectation in energy, and in most subscription businesses, is that the longer someone stays, the less likely they are to go. People settle in, stop shopping around, or never started.

Now suppose that one of the things that makes a customer leave is a nasty surprise on their bill, and you count surprises by comparing this January's bill with last January's. That works well for anyone who has been with you for two years or more. For someone in their first year there is no last January. The comparison cannot be made.

The trap is what happens next. If 'cannot be made' is stored as 'no surprise', every first-year customer looks calm on paper. Any model or analysis that reads that number will conclude that first-year customers are safe and that surprises pile up later, so customers seem to sour with tenure. In fact nobody behaved differently. The ruler simply had no markings for year one.

This is what happened in this project's simulated world. The fix is not to stretch the ruler. It is to ask what a surprise actually is in a customer's first year, and to measure that.

theory.heading: Why the first year needs its own measure
theory.body:
THE FIRST YEAR HAS A DIFFERENT REFERENCE POINT. After year one, a household can judge its bills against last year's. In year one the only reference is what it was told at sign-up: the quote, and for most households the first monthly direct debit. So a shock in year one is a gap between expectation and reality, and that is a different quantity from a change between one year and the next. A measure built only on year-on-year change cannot see it. That is a fact about the arithmetic, not about energy. It applies equally to any comparison with the prior year, any trailing-twelve-month change, and any 'versus the same period last year' signal used in a churn model.

WHAT A SHOCK IS DEPENDS ON HOW THE HOUSEHOLD PAYS. Fact, from docs/market_research/what_bill_shock_is.md (Ofgem sources, fetched 2026-09-01). About 74% of GB domestic households pay by direct debit. For those paying a level amount, the bill shocks nobody. The shock is a material change to the monthly payment, or a credit or debit balance they do not understand. About 13% pay on standard credit, and for them the bill itself is the shock, triggered by cold weather, a change in usage, or an actual meter read replacing a run of estimates. About 13% are on prepayment, which is outside 'bill shock' altogether. That page also records that the fixed-versus-variable split within direct debit is not published.

SO THE OLD MEASURE WAS WRONG TWICE. Wiring: the world's count (saas.customer_reaction.score_experience_signals in yoy mode, called by saas.churn_model.build_churn_risk) compared two bills. Every household in the measured population paid by direct debit, so this was the full-payment definition applied to households who do not pay the bill (docs/staging/WORKER_FINDING_THE_WORLDS_BILL_SHOCK_COUNT_IS_BLIND_IN_A_HOUSEHOLDS_FIRST_YEAR_AND_CARRIES_THE_WHOLE_TENURE_GRADIENT_2026-10-01.md). It also used an absolute difference, so a bill that FELL by 15% counted as a shock. The year-one blind spot was the third defect, and it was the one that carried the gradient.

WHY THE FIRST YEAR IS WHERE IT MATTERS MOST. For a household on a one-year fixed deal, the price does not move during the first year. So the first renewal's shock is the gap between the sign-up quote and the year's actual bills, and that gap is entirely the supplier's estimate of consumption being wrong. This is the reasoning in docs/staging/SEAT_FINDING_A_FABRIC_PREMISES_REGISTRY_EAC_IS_NOW_ITS_OWN_READS_AND_YEAR_ONE_SHOCK_IS_SET_BY_AN_UNSIZED_READ_ERROR_2026-10-01.md. The first year is the only year whose shock depends on the supplier's own estimate and nothing else, and it was the one year the count left out.

expected_shape.heading: What you should expect to see
expected_shape.body:
WHAT THE PUBLISHED RECORD SAYS ABOUT DIRECTION. Fact, at stated confidence. docs/market_research/svt_rates_active_passive_2016_2025.md §4 puts annual switching at about 5–10% for households on a standard variable tariff for three years or more, against about 15–20% for those on one for under three years. It cites Ofgem engagement surveys and marks the figures as medium-confidence structural inference rather than direct quotation. The same file records the CMA's 2016 finding that 70%+ of Big Six customers were on a standard variable tariff and had never switched or had rolled back. So the real-world direction is that longer-tenure households switch LESS.

WHAT IT DOES NOT SAY. How many customers of a small supplier leave at their FIRST renewal is not established here. docs/market_research/first_renewal_departure_rate_small_gb_supplier.md searched for it on 2026-10-01. The nearest published figure is a 2019 Ofgem trial at one large supplier: 6% external switching within six weeks of a one-year fix ending, in a book with a mean tenure of 17 years. That file judges it a floor for an inert incumbent book, not a figure that transfers. The code therefore carries the prior as None. This page does not claim a real-world size for first-year switching.

WHAT A BLIND FIRST YEAR PREDICTS. If a shock measure reads zero in year one and the model turns shocks into departures, three things should follow. First-year customers will look calmer than they are. The tenure gradient will lean towards 'loyalty falls with time', against the published direction. And holding the shock term fixed should make the gradient disappear. These were filed as predictions before any term was computed (docs/staging/records/SEAT_PREREG_THE_NEXT_AB_ON_THE_SINGLE_ROLL_WORLD_WHAT_A_SEED_VARIES_2026-09-30.md, committed as 33e9c1ba3). W1 said the count would be zero on at least 80% of tenure-1 rows, at 70% confidence. W2 said holding the shock hazard would take the tenure gradient above −0.10, at 55% confidence. Both held. The section below gives the details.

live_evidence.heading: The evidence, measured (this project's simulation)
live_evidence.body:
EVERY FIGURE IN THIS SECTION IS A MEASUREMENT OF THIS PROJECT'S SIMULATED WORLD. None of them is a fact about real households.

THE POPULATION. The population was 317 first decided renewals of direct-debit households (53 accounts) from one logged run, pinned at a322166cc. No new simulation was run. Each hazard term was recomputed with the world's own functions. Before any term was graded, the rebuild had to reproduce the world's logged retention probability. It did, with a median error of 0.0169 against a pre-registered bar of 0.02. One caveat: 'first decided renewal' is not always the first anniversary. The world decides at one anniversary in five, so years on supply at that decision ranged from 1 to 8. Source: docs/staging/records/SEAT_PREREG_THE_NEXT_AB_ON_THE_SINGLE_ROLL_WORLD_WHAT_A_SEED_VARIES_2026-09-30.md.

THE BLIND SPOT. At 1 year on supply (n = 156), 100% of rows had zero shocked months, the bill-shock base averaged 0.0225, and the world retained 0.775. At 2 to 8 years (n = 161), 6.8% had zero, the mean was 6.86 shocked months of 12, the base averaged 0.1154, and the world retained 0.651.

ONE TERM CARRIED IT. Within each (seed, year) cell, the world's retention correlated −0.346 with years on supply and −0.272 with bill size. Each term was then held at its book average:
- Bill-shock hazard: the tenure gradient went to −0.009 and the bill-size gradient to +0.003.
- Price-position hazard: −0.356.
- Dissatisfaction hazard: −0.358.
- The satisfaction tenure bonus: −0.349.
- Income stress and housing tenure together: −0.399. This moved the bill-size gradient by 0.071, the one confound large enough to note.
No other term came close.

IT ALSO MISLED THE COMPANY'S OWN JUDGEMENT. The simulated company's retention estimate had appeared to rank customers backwards against the world, with a correlation of −0.336. Scored against the world with only the bill-shock artefact held, that became +0.197. Most of the apparent failure was the world's blind spot, not the company's model (docs/staging/WORKER_FINDING_THE_WORLDS_BILL_SHOCK_COUNT_IS_BLIND_IN_A_HOUSEHOLDS_FIRST_YEAR_AND_CARRIES_THE_WHOLE_TENURE_GRADIENT_2026-10-01.md).

AGAINST THE PUBLISHED RECORD. Fact. Ofgem/BMG 2024 bounds the correlation between spend and switching at −0.07 to +0.05 (docs/market_research/is_there_a_bill_level_at_which_switching_rises.md). The world's −0.272 was outside that band. Its tenure direction was the reverse of the Ofgem surveys and the CMA finding cited above.

WHAT WAS CHANGED, IN ORDER (Choice and Wiring, each with its commit):
1. a0ccd009b built a shock measure by the published definition, one event a year. For direct-debit households it compares the reviewed payment with the payment in force, and in year one that is the amount quoted at sign-up. For standard-credit households it compares the year's bills with the quote, or with the prior year. Prepayment returns None with a reason, and a fall is not counted as a shock. Where no quote exists (sign-ups before 2019), the measure returns None rather than 0.
2. 8efcafc82 tried it on one world. Later renewals worked. Year one was defined on only 4 of 36 rows, because the quote was priced at a price cap that the repository does not hold before 2019.
3. d3009f5a9 priced the quote at the rate actually sold. Year one became defined on 31 of 31 in-scope rows, with 9 shocked (0.290) against 0.323 at later renewals.
4. 7c872f2d0 put the quote and the review on one basis: VAT-inclusive, at the standing charge sold. Year one then read 17 of 31 shocked, and 7 rose by more than 100%. Those 7 were electrically heated homes whose registered annual consumption was a fraction of their real use.
5. 3bf64c4e7 set each such home's registered consumption from its own trailing year of meter reads. Year one fell to 3 of 31 shocked (0.097). Later renewals stayed at 21 of 63 (0.333), with no row changed.
6. c3939e7b1 made the experienced shock, one event a year, drive the departure hazard, and refitted the departure level against the published band (5 of 6 fitted years in band). On the capture behind that refit, 2 of 31 first renewals were shocked against 20 of 60 later ones.

THE GUARD THAT NOW STANDS. Wiring: tests/simulation/test_experienced_bill_shock.py builds two first-year households, one shocked and one not, and asserts that their departure bases now differ. It asserts that both cases can be reached before it reads the ratio. Under the old count, the two read identically.

CHOICE, RECORDED SO THAT IT IS NOT UNDONE BY ACCIDENT. The finding instructs that the company-side learning atom (B8) must NOT fit the world's old tenure or bill-size gradient. Learning from a defect in the world would teach the company an advantage that does not exist.

residuals.heading: What this page does not settle
residuals.body:
THE NEW YEAR-ONE LEVEL IS SET BY AN ASSUMPTION, NOT A MEASUREMENT. A first renewal's shock is the supplier's consumption estimate being wrong. The simulated world currently gives that estimate ZERO error, because no published figure splits it by meter type. The published spread is wide. docs/market_research/how_far_a_settled_eac_sits_from_next_years_use.md, from 330,884 NEED year pairs, finds no bias (median ratio 1.000) but a median absolute change of 0.147 and a 90th percentile of 0.58. That spread bundles real changes in use, changes of occupier, and corrections from estimated to actual reads, so it is not a target as it stands. The consequence: the world's year one now reads about 0.10 shocked against about 0.33 later, a gradient leaning the other way, and its year-one level is a direct function of that one unsized gap. It would be a repeat of the original mistake to read it as a finding about real first-year households.

THE TENURE GRADIENT HAS NOT BEEN RE-MEASURED ON THE REPAIRED WORLD. The finding defines done as re-running its own analysis against the new world, at which point the sign and size come from whatever term remains. No re-run is recorded in the repository as of this writing. One aggregate comparison exists: the mean shock base at later decisions over the first decision in a capture moved from 1.46 to 1.02. That capture had no tenure field, though, so its 'first' was not the first renewal and its own grading says it cannot be read as a tenure gradient (docs/staging/done/SEAT_PREREGISTRATION_WHAT_THE_PB4_BILL_SHOCK_SWAP_MUST_MOVE_2026-10-01.md).

THE SAMPLES ARE SMALL. The finding rests on 317 rows from 53 accounts. The year-one repairs rest on 31 first renewals. Every correlation here has wide room. For example, the related belief correlation of −0.379 at account level has a 95% interval of −0.58 to −0.13 on 57 accounts (docs/staging/records/SEAT_PREREG_THE_NEXT_AB_ON_THE_SINGLE_ROLL_WORLD_WHAT_A_SEED_VARIES_2026-09-30.md).

HOW OFTEN THE OLD COUNT SCORED A FALL AS A SHOCK WAS NOT MEASURED. The logged run did not carry bills per period. One later one-world reading found 16 falls that the old count had scored (commit 8efcafc82).

THE PUBLISHED RECORD HAS TWO GAPS THAT BEAR ON THIS. The split between fixed and variable direct debit is not published, so the boundary between 'the payment is the shock' and 'the bill is the shock' cannot be drawn from public data (docs/market_research/what_bill_shock_is.md). And how many of a small supplier's customers leave at their first renewal is not published. It is None in the code and is put to the director as trade knowledge (docs/market_research/first_renewal_departure_rate_small_gb_supplier.md).

scope_delta.heading: Scope and honesty
scope_delta.body:
WHAT IS GENERAL. Any measure defined as change from a prior period does not exist for a customer's first period. 'Does not exist' and 'zero' are different answers. Store the first as the second and any analysis by tenure inherits a gradient made by the instrument. The direction of the false gradient depends on which side of the gap the measure undercounts. Here it made new customers look safe. A measure that defaulted the other way would make them look fragile. The remedy is also general: define what the experience is in year one, against the reference the customer actually had (the quote, the first payment), and record 'cannot tell' as unknown, never as a value. Before reading any churn-by-tenure table, ask of each driver whether it is defined in year one.

WHAT IS OURS. The gradient (−0.346), its collapse (−0.009), the retention figures (0.775 against 0.651), the counts of shocked first renewals and every repair are this project's simulation measurements and code decisions. They show that the trap is real and how large it can be. They say nothing about how large the effect is in any real supplier's book.

WHAT IS PUBLISHED. The definitions of bill shock for each population, the direction of the real tenure effect, and the bound on spend against switching are published record, cited to the files that hold them. The real-world size of first-year switching is not established here, and this page does not supply one.

HOW IT WAS CAUGHT. It was not caught by looking at the gradient, which looked like a plausible behaviour. It was caught by asking which term of the model read years on supply, and then holding each term in turn. The predictions were filed before the answer was known, so the result could have refuted them.

headline.heading: The claim, in one sentence
headline.body: A supplier never sees a house; it sees an address, a meter, and sometimes an energy certificate, and every decision about which households it can help has to be built from those. NOT YET WRITTEN IN FULL: the work behind this page is decided and has not started.

plain.heading: In plain terms
plain.body: The companion page explains what a house's size, fabric and fuel do to its energy use. A supplier cannot measure any of that directly. It knows where you live, what your meter reads, and — for some homes — what an assessor wrote on an energy certificate, possibly years ago and before the loft was insulated. This page will explain what each of those signals can and cannot tell a supplier, and why a missing certificate is itself information rather than a gap to fill with an average.

theory.heading: How it works
theory.body: To be written. It will treat the three signals separately because they fail differently. FACT (docs/market_research/epc_open_data.md): the energy certificate is MODELLED (certificate estimates of consumption run 50–100% above metered use), DATED (certificates last ten years and describe the house as it was when assessed), and PARTIAL (about 60% of English homes have one, biased toward homes recently sold or let). The postcode and address are free and say something about the house and little about the household. The meter reveals use over time, and how much that shows depends on how often it is read.

expected_shape.heading: What you should expect to see
expected_shape.body: Not yet stated. When written it will state falsifiably how much of a home's metered use a supplier can predict from certificate, address and meter alone, and how that changes for homes with no certificate. NOT YET MEASURED.

live_evidence.heading: Live evidence
live_evidence.body: None yet. The published facts above are the only evidence held. WIRING: this project's model of Britain's homes already records which homes have a certificate and when it was lodged, but lodgement dates are drawn evenly over ten years where the real ones cluster at recent sales (simulation/premise_population.py).

residuals.heading: Where our picture is still weak
residuals.body: WHAT BLOCKS IT: this page describes a partial view OF something, and that something — the full physical model of each house — is still being completed (see what-a-house-does-to-its-energy). Until it lands there is nothing for the supplier's view to be a partial, dated, modelled view of. The work is decided and registered but not authorised to start.

scope_delta.heading: What this page does not yet establish
scope_delta.body: Everything beyond the question. It will answer: what a supplier can know about a house from an energy certificate, an address and a meter; how wrong each signal is and in which direction; and how much of the potential described on the housing page a supplier could actually find. It will not cover how houses change over time, which has its own page.

meta.subtitle: Boilers die and are replaced, solar panels and cars arrive, homes are extended — mostly without a supplier hearing about it.
meta.one_line: This page is a placeholder. It will explain how British homes change without anyone selling them anything: boilers replaced at end of life, solar and electric cars arriving on their own adoption curves, extensions, and the energy certificate falling further behind the house it describes. That background change is what lets a supplier tell a saving it caused from one that would have happened anyway. The work behind it has been decided and is not yet started.

headline.heading: The claim, in one sentence
headline.body: Houses improve and degrade on their own timetable, and a supplier that cannot tell that background change from what it caused cannot honestly claim to have saved anyone anything. NOT YET WRITTEN IN FULL: the work behind this page is decided and has not started.

plain.heading: In plain terms
plain.body: If every improvement to a home in a model happened because the supplier sold it, every saving would be credited to the supplier by construction. Real homes are not like that. A boiler breaks in February and whoever can come on Tuesday fits a new one; a neighbour gets solar panels and so do you; a family builds an extension. This page will describe how often each of those happens, and what it does to the house's energy use and to the certificate that is supposed to describe it.

theory.heading: How it works
theory.body: To be written. It will cover end-of-life boiler replacement (a new condensing boiler cutting heating gas), solar and electric-car adoption curves, extensions, and how each moves the house's physics and its potential. CHOICE (director, 2026-09-05): heat pumps are excluded from the savings this work may model; whether that also removes them from the background change is recorded as an open reading in docs/design/W2_24_HOUSING_PHASE3_FRAME.md.

expected_shape.heading: What you should expect to see
expected_shape.body: Not yet stated. When written it will state falsifiably the share of homes whose boiler, solar, car or size changes in a year, from published sources, and how far certificates fall behind. NOT YET MEASURED: no published adoption or replacement rate has been checked for this page.

live_evidence.heading: Live evidence
live_evidence.body: None published yet. THIS PROJECT'S MEASUREMENT of its own model (docs/design/W2_24_HOUSING_PHASE3_FRAME.md), on 3,000 homes over 2016–2025: the energy certificate already falls behind — 10.6% of homes have changed insulation without their recorded rating changing — but nothing yet measures or uses that. And a defect: gas-heated homes eligible for a heat pump never reach the boiler-replacement step, so 71% of all homes in the model have a boiler that can never be replaced. That defect is found and not yet repaired.

residuals.heading: Where our picture is still weak
residuals.body: WHAT BLOCKS IT: a timeline needs a house to change and a supplier's view to fall behind. The full house model and the supplier's-view page both have to land first. Separately, the model has no way to make a home bigger: floor area is fixed when a home is drawn and nothing changes it, so extensions need new structure, not a new rate. No published extension rate has been established.

scope_delta.heading: What this page does not yet establish
scope_delta.body: Everything beyond the question. It will answer: how often each kind of unprompted change happens to British homes, what each does to energy use and potential, and how quickly what a supplier knows goes out of date. It will not cover changes in who lives in a home, which belong to a separate programme.

headline.heading: The claim, in one sentence
headline.body: Not yet written. The topic is how a household behaves toward whoever supplies it — how much price moves it, how it gets in touch, whether it prefers a stable bill or a time-of-use one, when it is at home, whether it will let a supplier control a battery or an electric car, and how far it trusts that supplier — and the claim this page will make has not been established.

plain.heading: In plain terms
plain.body: Two households in identical homes, with identical families, can be worth very different amounts to a supplier. One compares prices every year and leaves for a few pounds; the other has not looked in a decade. One phones about every bill; the other never calls. One has a battery and will happily let it be charged overnight when power is cheap; the other has the same battery and will not let anyone else decide when it runs — so for any product that depends on that control, it is worth nothing. This page will describe those differences once they are researched.

theory.heading: How it works
theory.body: Not yet written. What is decided is the list of things this page will cover: how strongly price moves a household and whether it prefers stability or time-of-use pricing; how likely it is to contact the supplier and through which channel; the patterns of presence that make its load shape (working hours, holidays, shift work, working from home); consent to control; and its stance on carbon and its trust in the supplier.

expected_shape.heading: What you should expect to see
expected_shape.body:
One published row is already held and can be stated falsifiably. Fact (Ofgem Consumer Impacts of Market Conditions survey, wave 6): over six months, 5.3% of households reported switching supplier. Cut by payment method, 5.6% of direct-debit households, 5.7% of standard-credit households and 3.1% of prepayment households did so, and 1.7% of households on a traditional prepayment meter. Households on a fixed tariff reported switching at 7.0% against 2.5% on a variable one. A simulated population should show prepayment households shopping markedly less than credit households, and the credit methods close to each other.

Everything else on this page: not yet measured.

live_evidence.heading: Live evidence
live_evidence.body:
What already exists in this project's simulated world, as an inventory rather than evidence (Wiring). How strongly price moves each household is drawn and used. How likely a household is to contact the supplier is drawn and used. A household's stance on carbon and its preferred contact channel are drawn and used by nothing. A trust score exists in one place, inside the model of how a household responds to a conversation, with no published anchor. Consent to control does not exist.

Two settings this page will have to examine. Choice (this project, July 2026, not independently sourced): private renters are modelled as 20% less likely and social renters 25% less likely to switch than owners. Households under high income stress are modelled as 35% less likely to switch and households under none as 10% more likely; the code cites no published source for those figures.

residuals.heading: Where our picture is still weak
residuals.body: Almost everywhere, which is why this is a stub. The level of household-level switching response is a value the director sets and has not yet set, so the spread of price sensitivity has nothing to be spread around. The preferred contact channel the world draws is not the one its contact model uses. Trust exists once, without an anchor, and must not be built a second time. No published source has been found for consent to control. A supplier's own added contact wakes about one in nine of the households that would otherwise have let a fixed term lapse onto the default (Ofgem's End of Fixed Term trial). Most of the woken re-fix with the same supplier, so the advice creates value for the household as well as the supplier. The company's per-household tariff advice (C34) cannot reach those households yet: the simulated world decides which households will let their fix lapse before the renewal notice exists, so the advice goes only to households already choosing, and on the published evidence a letter does not change those. Full treatment: docs/market_research/how_households_respond_to_supplier_contact.md, section 7.
