headline.heading: The claim, in one sentence
headline.body: Not yet written. The topic is how a household changes over time — income shocks, children arriving and leaving, kit bought unprompted — and the difference between a household willing to BUY something from its supplier and one that merely appreciates being saved money and carbon.

plain.heading: In plain terms
plain.body:
A household is not fixed. Someone loses a job and the bills become hard to pay. A baby arrives and the washing machine never stops. The children leave and a four-bedroom house holds two people. Someone buys an electric car because the neighbour did. A supplier that treats each customer as the household it signed up will be wrong about more of its book every year.

The second idea here is easy to blur. A customer can be warmly grateful for advice that cut their bill, recommend you to a neighbour, and never buy anything. That is a different thing from being willing to buy a heat pump or a battery, and counting both as “engaged” hides the difference.

theory.heading: How it works
theory.body: Not yet written. Two definitions come first and must be fixed before anything is measured: willingness to buy kit or services, and willingness to appreciate being saved money and carbon. They are related and they are not the same quantity.

expected_shape.heading: What you should expect to see
expected_shape.body: Not yet stated. The published rates already in use are listed under live evidence, but none of them yet carries a falsifiable statement about a simulated book.

live_evidence.heading: Live evidence
live_evidence.body:
What this project's simulated world already does (Wiring). Income shocks are drawn: job loss at 2.2% of households a year, citing ONS labour market statistics, alongside recovery, illness and retirement. Kit arrives with no supplier involvement: solar panels follow DESNZ's register of domestic installations, from 3.0% of 28.4 million households in 2016 to 5.7% in 2025; electric cars follow a stock curve from 0.3% to 7% over the same years; heat pumps, batteries, smart meters, insulation and boiler replacements are events too.

A new baby is drawn at 1.1% of households a year, citing the ONS birth summary tables. In the world it raises the household's financial stress and adds nobody to the household. No event removes a child.

residuals.heading: Where our picture is still weak
residuals.body:
CHILDREN ARRIVING AND LEAVING DO NOT EXIST AS CHANGES TO WHO LIVES THERE. The event called a new baby changes only money, so it cannot change hot-water use or daytime presence.

TWO RATES ARE APPLIED TO A DIFFERENT UNIT FROM THE ONE THEY ARE PUBLISHED IN. The birth rate the code cites is about 10.7 per 1,000 people; it is applied as 1.1% per household, which is a rate per person used as a rate per household. The job-loss rate is a share of working-age employed people, applied per household. Neither has yet been converted, and both will be checked before this page states any shape.

THE VALUE-ADD TERM DOES NOT EXIST, AND ITS NAME IS TAKEN. The word “willingness” already names whether an indebted household will pay, so the two new quantities need their own names before they are defined.

scope_delta.body: Anything. The scope is decided and the work is not yet authorised; it opens after the first two pages in this series are complete, because a residual is only definable once there is something for it to be residual to.

meta.title: Energy that was used but never correctly billed
meta.subtitle: Every supplier pays for more energy than it bills. Some of the gap is just timing and closes by itself. Some of it is energy nobody will ever pay for. These are different things, and a supplier can only see some of them.
meta.wall_placement: Public-reality commons only. Every figure here comes from a published source: Ofgem licence decisions and impact assessments, the gas industry's Unidentified Gas statement, the Retail Energy Code Company, the Energy Ombudsman, and one supplier's audited accounts (Centrica 2024). No figure produced by this project's simulation appears as evidence on this page, and nothing here was chosen because a number was needed.

claim_freshness.source: Ofgem, Decision on backbilling (SLC 21BA), 5 March 2018; Centrica plc Annual Report and Accounts 2024, notes 3 and 17; AUGE Final Allocation of Unidentified Gas Statement for Gas Year 2024-2025 (31 March 2024); Ofgem, Tackling Electricity Theft impact assessment, March 2014; RECCo theft estimation (Capgemini, published January 2023); Energy Ombudsman annual data 2025; DESNZ Smart Meter Statistics Q4 2024; Elexon settlement timetable; Ofgem, overview of questionnaire responses on theft of energy (26 March 2012); Ofgem, open letter on low and zero consumers of gas (20 June 2014); Elexon P245 Long Term Vacant site timescales (2009).; DCUSA Schedule 23, Revenue Protection Code of Practice, version 5.11. Full citations in docs/market_research/unbilled_energy_and_revenue_assurance.md; Ofgem, Standard conditions of electricity supply licence, SLC 27.17 (final bills); Elexon, BSCP504 s.4.4.1 (change of supplier readings); HMRC, VAT Notice 701/19 (fuel and power), s.3.1, 3.2.1, 3.5, 5.2; gov.scot, Council tax (Scottish Assessors)
claim_freshness.note: Written for step 1 of the director's priority order of 5 October 2026, to feed step 2 (unbilled energy and billing accuracy). Writing it showed that the simulation settles and bills every premise to the same true consumption, so the company has nothing real to find. The page sets out what that leakage looks like, so the gap has something to be measured against.

headline.heading: The claim, in one sentence
headline.body: A GB energy supplier always pays for more energy than it bills: some of the gap is timing that closes when a meter is read; some is lost to a 12-month legal limit on catching up; and some is energy no customer is ever billed for (in gas, about 2.5% of everything put through the network; theft across both fuels is estimated at up to £1.4bn a year, and the two figures overlap), which the industry spreads across suppliers in a way no single supplier can trace to a home.

plain.heading: In plain terms
plain.body:
Three different parties count the same energy. The meter, if anyone reads it, says what a home used. The industry settlement system (Elexon for electricity, Xoserve for gas) says what the supplier must pay for, and it keeps revising that figure for 14 months or more. The supplier's own bills say what customers were charged. Unbilled energy is the gap between these three counts.

Most of the gap is innocent timing. At any month end, every customer has used some energy since their last bill. Many bills are based on an estimate, because nobody read the meter, and are corrected later. That gap closes on its own.

Some of it never closes. If a supplier leaves a customer unbilled or under-billed for more than a year through its own fault, the law stops it charging for the older energy, and it writes that off. And some energy is never attached to any customer at all: stolen through a bypassed meter, used at a site no supplier has registered, or simply lost in the arithmetic. The industry still has to charge someone for that energy, so it shares the cost out between suppliers by formula. A supplier pays its share and has no way to bill it on.

theory.heading: How it works
theory.body:
There are seven distinct kinds, and each one arises and is found in a different way.

ACCRUAL. Revenue for energy used since the last meter reading, estimated at the period end. Centrica estimates it 'through the billing systems, using historical consumption patterns, on a customer-by-customer basis, taking into account weather patterns, load forecasts and the differences between actual meter readings being returned and system estimates'. It is an accounting estimate, not an error.

ESTIMATED BILLS. When no actual read arrives, the bill uses an estimate, and the next real read corrects it up or down. That correction is the catch-up.

BACK-BILLING. A catch-up for energy that was never properly billed. Since May 2018, Standard Licence Condition 21BA stops suppliers billing domestic customers (and later microbusinesses) for energy used more than 12 months before the bill. It applies to every meter type and payment method. The exceptions are a bill sent before the rule began, chasing charges that were already properly billed, and a customer who behaved 'obstructively or manifestly unreasonably'. Energy UK adds that it also bars recovery where the customer's direct debit was set too low.

UNKNOWN CONSUMPTION. Theft, unregistered meters, and gas sites with no shipper. A supplier finds some theft through investigations and the industry's Theft Risk Assessment Service. The rest shows up only as an industry-wide gap.

METER FAULTS AND CROSSED METERS. A meter that records wrongly, or two homes' meters swapped on the records, so each is billed for the other.

SETTLEMENT AGAINST BILLING. Electricity settlement runs at 1 week, then 1, 2, 4, 7 and finally 14 months after each day, moving from estimated to actual data as it goes. Gas settlement allocates Unidentified Gas (UIG) to suppliers every day by formula and reconciles it later. In both fuels, a supplier's settlement bill includes a share of energy that other people's homes used or stole.

SMART METER READ FAILURES. A smart meter that has lost its connection, or has not been taken on by a new supplier, falls back to 'traditional mode' and needs reading by hand, like an old meter.

A HELD BILL ON AN ACCOUNT THAT HAS CLOSED. A bill held because it looks too big for a home waits for an actual meter reading. Once the customer has left, no later reading comes to this supplier: the meter's next reading belongs to the new supplier. The licence asks for a final bill within six weeks (SLC 27.17), running to the closing reading. That reading, even an estimated one, is the one the industry settles the old supplier on, and it changes only if someone disputes it. So the held energy goes out on the final bill, provided the address is a listed dwelling. Energy used more than 12 months before the final bill cannot be charged (SLC 21BA), so it is written off instead.

A BILL HELD BECAUSE IT LOOKS TOO BIG FOR A HOME. Domestic energy takes 5% VAT, business energy 20%, and HMRC says the supplier 'must be certain that the supply is to a dwelling' (VAT Notice 701/19). So a supplier holds a bill that looks too big for a home, and checks the address against the council tax list. That list is public in England and Wales, and kept by the Scottish Assessors in Scotland. If the address is a listed dwelling, the bill goes out at 5% whatever its size, as long as an actual meter reading supports the volume. If the list cannot answer, HMRC's own tool is a declaration from the customer. If the answer is that the premises is not a dwelling, the account is business and the bill goes out at 20%. No published source says how long a supplier's queue takes over either step.

expected_shape.heading: What the data should look like
expected_shape.body:
Most kinds should be small and constant, a few should be rare and large, and one should be hard to see at all.

Accrual should be large in pounds and seasonal, and should net to nothing over time. British Gas held £670m of gross unbilled income at the end of 2024 against £12.1bn of revenue for the year. That is a balance on one day set against a year's flow, so the fair reading is about 20 days of average revenue.

Estimated bills should affect a minority of customers in any year. In 2017 the median large supplier had about 5% of customers with no bill based on a meter reading in the past year. A small group that is rarely read should account for most of them.

Back-bills should be rare per customer, but a steady source of complaints: about 10% of Ombudsman and Citizens Advice cases before the 2018 rule, and about 3,200 Ombudsman cases a year in 2024 and 2025 (roughly 3.5–4% of all cases).

Unknown consumption should be a persistent leak. Gas UIG has run at about 2.5% of throughput since 2017, and most of the part the industry can identify is put down to theft (6,362 of 7,761 GWh forecast for 2024-25). It can turn negative: from March 2022 to summer 2023 the gas allocation over-charged suppliers, because households cut their use faster than the formula assumed.

live_evidence.heading: Live evidence
live_evidence.body:
WHAT IS SOURCED, AND READ IN THE PRIMARY DOCUMENT. The 12-month back-billing rule, its exceptions, the 2017 complaint share and the 94.4–94.8% read-based billing medians (Ofgem decision, 5 March 2018). British Gas's £670m of gross unbilled income and £56m provision, the group's £968m and 6% coverage, and £2,732m of 'unread' revenue, where a 2% change in assumptions moves profit by £55m (Centrica Annual Report and Accounts 2024). The UIG breakdown by contributor and the 2.5%-of-throughput history (gas UIG statement, March 2024). The 2014 picture of electricity theft: about 275,000 domestic thefts under way at any time, about 1% of domestic meters, against 15,956 domestic detections a year (Ofgem impact assessment). RECCo's upper estimate of up to 2,837 GWh of electricity and 1,069 GWh of gas stolen a year, up to £1.4bn. Smart meters in traditional mode at the end of 2024: 4.7% of domestic electricity and 9.1% of domestic gas (DESNZ).

WHAT CAME FROM A SUMMARY RATHER THAN THE SOURCE. The Energy Ombudsman's back-billing case counts, Energy UK's list of exceptions, and Xoserve's account of negative UIG.

A NOTE ON METHOD. The tool used to summarise Ofgem's 2018 decision returned two figures, '1.9 million consumers received a backbill' and 'an average backbill of £300 to £400', that do not appear anywhere in the document. Neither is used here.

WHAT A SUPPLIER DOES WITH AN ACCOUNT ITS SCREEN FLAGS (added 17 October 2026; read in DCUSA Schedule 23, the Revenue Protection Code of Practice, version 5.11). A flag is a lead. The duty it engages is an investigation where there are reasonable grounds to suspect theft (licence condition 12A.6), read alongside the industry's TRAS risk score. The visit is unannounced, a warrant is sought only after reasonable attempts at access have failed, and safety comes first. The stolen energy is assessed from the account's own history before the change, an appliance audit, typical use for the property, monitoring, or a load test. Nothing may be charged until the supplier has evidence that the theft was the customer's intentional act or culpable negligence (12A.11(g)). The 12-month back-billing limit does not apply where the customer was at fault (21BA.2(c)), and no other licence cap replaces it. Our company's billing run now records each flag and the act it calls for, behind a switch that is off. Switched on over the published run, it flags 16 empty electricity periods. All 16 are empty homes between tenants, so none calls for an investigation and none raises a charge. The simulated world does not yet put theft into the run, so there is nothing for the screen to find.

residuals.heading: Where our picture is still weak
residuals.body:
No published source says how unevenly meter reading is spread across households: whether the same homes go unread year after year. That decides whether back-bills are rare and large or common and small, and it may be the kind of thing everyone in the trade knows and nobody writes down.

The number of back-bills, their typical size, and what suppliers write off under the 12-month rule are not published. Neither is how often crossed meters or faulty meters occur.

Only one supplier's accounts were read. British Gas's customer base is older and more gas-heavy than a typical new supplier's, so its unbilled balance should not be taken as typical.

The RECCo theft estimate is an upper bound and is not split between homes and businesses. The size of the electricity equivalent of gas UIG (the 'GSP group correction') in 2016–2025, and what UIG costs per gas customer per year, can be worked out from published data but have not been worked out yet.

scope_delta.heading: What this page does not yet establish
scope_delta.body:
It gives no single 'unbilled percentage', and that is deliberate. The seven kinds are different quantities with different owners, and adding them up would produce a number that counts nothing.

It does not say what our supplier should accrue, provide or write off. Those are the company's own measurements, made from its own books, and the simulation must leave it free to get them wrong.

It does say what our simulated world currently lacks. The world settles and bills every home to the same true consumption, so energy used, energy paid for in settlement and energy billed always agree in the end. The ledger's 'unbilled revenue' counts the whole value of bills based on estimates, which is a different quantity from energy used but not yet billed. A forced meter read after 12 estimated months means the back-billing limit can bind only at the edge. And the company has theft and gas-UIG registers that nothing in the world feeds. Until the world can make those three counts disagree in the way the record above describes, the company cannot measure unbilled energy, because there is none to measure.

meta.title: What a GB household's energy debt is, how big it has become, and how a supplier gets paid back
meta.subtitle: Energy debt is not one thing. A missed direct debit, a bill nobody opened, a prepayment meter quietly taking a few pounds a week, and an empty flat on a deemed contract all count as debt. They have different causes, different rules and very different chances of being repaid.
meta.wall_placement: Public-reality commons only. Every figure here comes from a published source: Ofgem's debt and arrears indicators and price-cap decisions, Ofgem's Debt Relief Scheme papers, the involuntary-prepayment licence rules, DWP's deductions guidance, Energy UK's February 2026 debt report, and Centrica's 2025 annual report. No figure produced by this project's simulation appears on this page. Where nothing published establishes a number, the page says so instead of supplying one.

It also records that the simulation's payment-failure rates are not sourced, and that the world generates no prepayment debt at all.

headline.heading: The claim, in one sentence
headline.body: Since 2022, GB domestic energy debt has grown mainly because each indebted household owes much more, not because many more households are in debt. Most of that money sits with standard-credit customers who have no repayment plan, or on accounts that have already closed. Those are the two places a supplier is least likely to be repaid.

plain.heading: In plain terms
plain.body:
Ofgem counts a household as 'in arrears' when a bill has been unpaid for more than 91 days with no repayment plan. It counts a household as 'in debt' when it is repaying under a plan. At the end of 2025 about 1.15 million electricity accounts were in arrears, roughly 4% of all customers, and about 830,000 were repaying a debt. Arrears and debt together came to £4.55bn, against £1.1bn in 2018. In 2016 the count of electricity accounts in arrears was about half today's. The average amount owed has more than tripled.

The money is concentrated. Standard-credit customers (those who pay each bill when it arrives) are about 16% of households. They hold about half of the indebted accounts and about three-quarters of the money owed. About three-quarters of the money is owed by people with no repayment plan at all. Between a tenth and two-fifths sits on accounts where someone moved in and never opened an account; the two published estimates disagree.

Two things are easy to get wrong. First, 'written off' is an accounting step, not forgiveness: suppliers keep chasing written-off debt. Second, disconnecting a home for debt has stopped. None has been recorded since early 2023. The levers that remain are repayment plans, prepayment meters, deductions from benefits, and getting the customer to engage.

theory.heading: How it works
theory.body:
A debt starts as a payment event: a direct debit bounces, or a bill passes its due date. A bounced direct debit is tried again up to twice. British Gas, for example, retries after 14 days and then moves the customer off direct debit. The unpaid amount then becomes a balance, and the supplier's licence (SLC 27) requires it to spot payment difficulty and offer a repayment plan the customer can afford before escalating.

The debt then follows one of several separate paths, each with its own rules:
- A repayment plan on a credit account. Plans break often: in 2015 about two in five large-supplier plans had at least one missed payment in a year, and the share rose with the size of the weekly instalment.
- A prepayment meter that takes a fixed amount from each top-up. For new installs in 2025 this averaged £6.01 a week on electricity, agreed over about seven years. A household that cannot afford this does not default; it runs out of credit and goes without energy.
- Involuntary prepayment meters. These are allowed only under the November 2023 rules: at least £200 per fuel outstanding for three months, at least ten attempts at contact, a recorded welfare visit, and none at all for over-75s without support or for households with children under two.
- Deductions from Universal Credit (Fuel Direct). These run at a flat 5% of the standard allowance.
- A final bill when the account closes. Here the supplier loses every lever except collection agencies and sale.

The loss reaches the accounts first as a provision, and only later as a write-off. Centrica's 2025 accounts provide about 3% of its live direct-debit balances, 45% of its pay-on-receipt balances, and 84% of its closed-account balances.

All customers pay for this through the price cap. Since July 2025 the cap carries a distinct debt allowance of £71 per dual-fuel customer a year, about 3.6% of the bill. It is split as £57 for direct debit, £160 for standard credit and £19 for prepayment. Before that, temporary top-ups (£9 from October 2023, £31 from April 2024) covered costs the earlier allowance had missed.

Setting the direct debit is the first defence against debt. Since 21 October 2022 (Ofgem's decision of 26 August 2022 strengthening SLC 27.15) a fixed direct debit must be set on the best and most current information in all cases, including meter reads and what the customer or a third party has said, and reassessed when new information is likely to change it materially. Ofgem declined to mandate a fixed review cadence. Refunding a credit balance on request is a duty; refunding it proactively is a service choice above that floor. Ofgem describes winter shortfalls and surplus credit as commonly spread over the following twelve months; the shape of that glide is not published.

When a customer falls behind, the October 2023 Consumer Standards decision added a duty to make contact after two missed monthly payments (SLC 27.5B) and requires repayment rates set on ability to pay, with pauses and monitoring of plans that fail (SLC 27.8A). A security deposit may be asked only where reasonable, and not of a customer who accepts a safe prepayment meter (SLC 27.3-27.4). Differences between payment methods must reflect cost (SLC 27.2A). Moving a customer to prepayment without consent runs through hard gates that no risk score can bypass (SLC 28B and the 2023 code of practice). Vulnerability overrides any risk tier rather than being one.

Since 1 April 2024 the price cap has levelised the standing charge between direct debit and prepayment, so a typical dual-fuel prepayment bill is now below the direct debit one; standard credit carries the clear premium.

The early signals arrive in a known order. A cancelled direct debit mandate reaches the supplier the working day after the bank records it, and the supplier must act within three working days: it is the only warning that comes before a collection fails. A failed collection is reported the working day after the debit. Of the twelve unpaid reasons the scheme reports, only one, refer to payer, is about the customer's money, and only that one may be presented again, within a month; the others are administration, the supplier's own errors, a death or a customer leaving.

The duty to help starts before arrears. A supplier must act when a customer is having or will have difficulty paying (SLC 27.5); a repayment plan set in breach of the rules makes the debt unrecoverable under the contract until it is put right (SLC 27.8C); Ofgem sets no minimum or maximum repayment rate. For prepayment customers a supplier must keep checking for self-disconnection and offer emergency, overnight and extra credit (SLC 27A). Moving a customer to prepayment without consent is barred for some households and gated for the rest by contact attempts, a welfare visit and an ability-to-pay assessment. A Breathing Space under the 2020 Debt Respite regulations stops collection of the old debt, including through the meter, for sixty days, while the energy used meanwhile must still be paid.

What becomes of a repayment plan is published only outside Great Britain: in Victoria's energy hardship programmes between a fifth and a third of customers left with their arrears cleared and around half were excluded for not keeping to the terms, and in GB insolvency arrangements about one in three breaks, most of them early.

expected_shape.heading: What the data should look like
expected_shape.body:
A credible world, and a credible supplier book inside it, should show these shapes:
- A stock of accounts in arrears of a few per cent per fuel, rising gently from 2016 and jumping in 2023.
- An average amount in arrears that roughly triples from 2016 to 2025, while the amount owed under plans grows much more slowly.
- A dip in arrears through late 2022 and early 2023, while government bill support was in place, followed by a sharp rebound.
- Money concentrated in standard credit and in closed accounts, with direct-debit losses small.
- Losses that grow through provisions on old, unplanned arrears faster than write-offs crystallise them.
- Prepayment customers repaying slowly over years, with going without energy, not default, as their form of failure.
- Recovery that falls sharply with the age of the debt. Energy UK's supplier data shows recovery on debt older than a year falling from 31% to 9% in three years.

A world in which most households miss a bill every few years, or in which prepayment customers never carry debt, does not match the record.

live_evidence.heading: Live evidence
live_evidence.body:
WHAT IS SOURCED.
- Ofgem's full quarterly series, 2006 to mid-2026: accounts in arrears and repaying, average balances, total value, the share repaying through prepayment, disconnections and prepayment self-disconnections. These were read as the data behind the regulator's charts.
- The price-cap debt allowance decisions and their amounts.
- The involuntary-prepayment licence rules and the debt trigger.
- The benefit deduction rates.
- The Debt Relief Scheme design. It writes off debt from April 2022 to March 2024 for engaged customers on means-tested benefits who owe £100 or more, about £0.5bn in phase one.
- From the scheme's impact assessment: average recovery takes more than 22 months, and collection costs about 3p per pound owed.
- Centrica's 2025 split of provisions by payment method and by live or closed account. Its domestic bad-debt charge was £277m, against retail bad debt of 2.6% of revenue.
- Energy UK's split of the debt stock by payment method.

WHAT IS NOT. There is no published rate at which direct debits fail. There is no published share of households who accept an offered repayment plan, and no per-payment rate at which plans are kept. There are no published roll rates from one stage of lateness to the next, and no price at which energy debt is sold. The size of deceased-customer and disputed-bill debt is not published. The two estimates of the share caused by people moving home (10-15% and 20-40%) do not agree.

residuals.heading: Where our picture is still weak
residuals.body: The regulator collects the flows that matter (plans started, plans broken, weeks to recover) and publishes only the stocks. So the dynamics this page would most like to state, such as how many late accounts recover on their own and how fast unplanned arrears turn into plans or losses, are known to suppliers and not to the public. The best evidence on which repayment terms work is a single 2015 chart. The best evidence on which contact strategies work comes from mortgage and court-fine trials, not energy. Most of the money owed belongs to households with no visible sign of hardship, so whether they cannot pay or will not pay is exactly what a supplier cannot see. These are questions for someone who has run an energy collections book, not for a further search. The simulated world therefore answers an offer of a repayment plan, a lower payment or a pause from labelled ranges, not from a GB figure: about a third to a half of households agree, a little under half to two thirds of agreed plans break, mostly in the first months, an unaffordable instalment breaks more often in proportion, and a cut too small to change a household's month changes nothing. Those ranges come from US debt-counselling and mortgage trials, Australian energy hardship programmes, UK insolvency and the FCA's Covid payment-deferral findings, and they ship switched off. A contact about a missed payment is answered the same way: it wakes some households that would not otherwise have dealt with the miss, most strongly in the first five days and hardly at all after a month, and a woken household that has the money pays while one that has not gets in touch; how many it wakes is carried as a range from credit and court-fine trials, because no energy trial exists. A household can also cancel its own direct debit with no bill shock behind it and pay by hand from then on; no source publishes how often, so the simulated world carries that as a labelled range as well, and it does not yet tie the way a household pays to its income or tenure, because the figures that would set that link were not reached. Moving a direct debit nearer pay day is treated the same way: in the simulated world it helps only stretched households whose collection currently comes before their income, about half of them on an Argentine natural experiment, and by between a tenth and a little over a third fewer failed collections, a range from US and UK credit evidence because no British figure exists.

scope_delta.heading: What this page does not yet establish
scope_delta.body:
It does not give a probability that any particular household will fall behind, recover, or be written off, and it deliberately supplies none. It does not establish how long suppliers wait before writing off a closed account, or the order in which they use collection agencies, write-offs and debt sale, because that is each supplier's own policy. It does not say whether the 2023 rules have changed how many prepayment meters are fitted for debt; that count was not found. And it does not yet describe this project's simulation against these shapes. The companion research notes record that the simulated world's lowest-stress payment-failure rate is an estimate from one supplier's published figures, that how failure rises with financial stress is not sourced, and that the simulated world creates no prepayment debt; they propose grading the world against Ofgem's series before any debt forecasting is built on it.

It does not establish whether a credit-risk tier, on its own, may be the stated basis for a higher direct debit under SLC 27.15; how much a large or frequent change in a direct debit raises failed payments, complaints, churn or debt; the take-up of seasonal, flexible or buffered payment plans, none of which is a price-cap category; or, for Great Britain, how much aligning the collection date with pay day reduces failures. Outside Great Britain, a bill arriving when benefits land cut late payment by about a third in a US study and a payday after the due date cut on-time payment by about thirty per cent in an Argentine natural experiment; both are analogues, not evidence for a GB direct debit. What the record does bound: in February to April 2022 over 7 million direct debits rose by 62% on average, and about 0.4% of the largest rises (above 100%) were found to be wrong (Ofgem, 2022), so households were meeting large but mostly correct increases; and the share of customers paying by direct debit rose 3 to 4 points between September 2020 and September 2025 (DESNZ Quarterly Energy Prices), so any lasting move off direct debit after those rises was small. How many households cancel their own mandate after an increase is not published anywhere.

It does not establish, for GB energy: the share of failed collections by reason; the chance of default after a first failed collection or a cancelled mandate; how often a re-presented collection succeeds; how many repayment plans are kept or broken; whether early contact raises repayment; or what share of Breathing Space registrations involve energy debt. Those figures sit in suppliers' own data or behind the payment scheme's member login.

meta.title: What happens to a supplier when a household moves home
meta.subtitle: A move is two events at two addresses, often weeks apart, and in Britain the energy keeps flowing to whoever walks in. Between a fifth and two-fifths of all domestic energy debt starts there.
meta.wall_placement: Public-reality commons only. So several gaps on this page are gaps in the public record, not only in ours.
