headline.heading: The claim, in one sentence
headline.body: About one household in fourteen in England moves home each year, and about one in five in private renting. A British supplier must keep supplying whoever moves in, on a deemed contract, before it knows who they are. That is why 20 to 40 per cent of all domestic energy debt arises at a change of tenancy.

plain.heading: In plain terms
plain.body:
When a household moves, the meter stays where it is and the electricity and gas keep flowing. What changes is who should pay. The old occupier is liable until shortly after they tell the supplier they are leaving. The new occupier is liable from the day they arrive, whether or not they ever get in touch.

So a supplier does not see one move. It sees two separate events. At one address a customer leaves: there is a final reading, a final bill sent to a forwarding address, and sometimes a debt that is never paid. At another address somebody it has never heard of starts using energy. The law puts them on a 'deemed contract' at the supplier's standard rate. Bills go to 'The Occupier', and nobody may read them for weeks or months.

These are different problems, with different people and different fixes, and they should never be counted as one number. Most other countries switch the supply off between occupiers. Britain does not, and that one difference is why home moves are a debt problem here.

theory.heading: How it works
theory.body:
THE CASES. Five situations need keeping apart, and three of them split further.

(A) Move-out. Our customer leaves. We send a final bill, and any unpaid balance becomes debt on a closed account.

(B) Move-in, unnamed. Someone new starts using energy at a premises we supply. A deemed contract arises automatically (Gas Act 1986 Sch 2B para 8; Ofgem Guidance on Deemed Contracts 2023, para 2.10), at a rate held to the price cap (para 2.19).

(B') The new occupier registers with us. That is a customer we never paid to acquire.

(B'') The new occupier signs with another supplier. That switch carries a Change of Occupier indicator, and a correctly flagged switch leaves us 'no valid grounds to object' on debt (Ofgem, non-domestic objections decision, Jul 2016, fn 26).

(C) Our customer moves and takes us with them. This is the moment a passive customer is most likely to be lost.

(D) Void. Nobody lives there, and the owner or landlord is liable.

(E) A landlord or letting agent handles the changeover.

LIABILITY FOLLOWS THE PERSON, NOT THE PREMISES. A new occupier does not owe for energy used before they arrived. A departing occupier pays until about two days after giving notice (Citizens Advice). Debt left on a closed account stays with the person who left, and has to be traced to a forwarding address.

WHY IT MAKES DEBT. In Ofgem's words, because the supply continues, 'the obligation on the supplier to continue to provide energy takes away the incentive for the new occupier to contact their energy supplier' (call for input, Dec 2025). The share of debt it causes 'has been stable since before the energy crisis', which suggests behaviour is a cause, not only affordability.

THE READ AT THE BOUNDARY. The same meter reading closes one account and opens the next. If it is an estimate, any error moves money between two households who never meet. A smart meter can take an actual reading remotely on the day. About 64 per cent of meters were running in smart mode by late 2025.

THE MOVE-WITH-US OFFER (case C). The household must give at least two Working Days' notice for its contract to end on the move date (SLC 24.1(a)). That notice is the only moment a supplier can make an offer before the household goes. A mover has no licence exemption from a fixed-term exit fee (SLC 24.3), so waiving it is the supplier's own choice. Many suppliers waive it if the tariff moves with the customer, according to comparison-site summaries of their moving pages. At the new home another supplier holds the meter, so taking the old supplier along is an ordinary switch gained there. Whether carrying a tariff is a variation or a new contract is not established in the licence text read so far. Nor is how a regional tariff is re-rated at another address.

THE FINAL BILL AND THE BALANCE. The supplier must take all reasonable steps to send a final bill or statement of account within six weeks of the contract ending (SLC 27.17). A statement of account states the balance, so the closing balance is a figure the supplier has already issued. If the household is owed money, the credit must be refunded within 10 working days of that final bill (Standards of Performance regulation 6D, SI 2019/218). A debt stays with the person who left.

A CREDIT BEFORE THE MOVE. The licence defines a credit as the amount by which a customer's payments exceed all the charges due under that contract (SLC 27.16). It is a running account, kept per fuel. Each bill must say what is owed and what the household has to pay (SLC 31H.12). So when a household pays what each bill asks, a credit from one bill comes off the next charges. It does not wait for the move. Before the move, a credit is refunded only if the customer asks for it (SLC 27.16). On a fixed direct debit the fixed amount carries on, so a credit can build up until the next review (SLC 27.15), and Ofgem expects the supplier to lower that debit.

expected_shape.heading: What the data should look like
expected_shape.body:
Moves should be concentrated by tenure. The English Housing Survey 2023-24 counts about 1.8 million moving households out of 24.7 million, which is about 7 per cent a year. Each year, roughly 18 to 21 per cent of private rented homes take in a new household. For owner-occupied homes it is about 4 per cent, and for social rented homes about 4 to 6 per cent. A supplier whose book leans towards private renters should therefore see several times the change-of-tenancy volume of one that serves owner-occupiers.

About a sixth of moves (17 per cent in 2023-24) are newly formed households. Each creates a move-in with no vacated home behind it. Deaths and households merging do the reverse: they leave vacated homes with no matching move-in.

Debt should build up on unnamed and closed accounts far beyond their share of accounts: 20 to 40 per cent of domestic debt, out of a total of £4.43 billion in June 2025. That share should stay roughly steady through a price shock, because the main driver is people not making contact, not only people being unable to pay.

At first, a new occupier should look like the previous one. The settlement estimate of annual use belongs to the meter point, so a supplier's first estimate for a newcomer is someone else's consumption.

Moving should take customers out of the book in a way that no price signal explains. In Ofgem's 2024 survey, 4 per cent had changed supplier passively in the past six months 'by moving house or a supplier changing hands', against 6 per cent who switched actively.

live_evidence.heading: Live evidence
live_evidence.body:
WHAT IS SOURCED.
- How often households in England move, overall and by tenure, in 2023-24 (English Housing Survey).
- The deemed contract, its legal basis, and its cover by the price cap (Ofgem guidance, 2023).
- Britain's unusual policy of keeping supply going through a change of tenancy (Ofgem call for input, Dec 2025, para 1.6).
- The 20 to 40 per cent share of debt that suppliers put down to change of tenancy and unnamed accounts, and the £4.43 billion total it is a share of.
- That switch requests carry a Change of Occupier indicator, and that a flagged switch cannot be blocked for debt.
- The rules consumers are told: 48 hours' notice, a final bill within six weeks, and credit refunded within ten working days of the final bill (Citizens Advice).
- Movers as a named acquisition channel at all six large suppliers (CMA 2016; the figures are redacted).

WHAT THE PUBLIC RECORD DOES NOT HOLD.
- How many accounts are unnamed, how long they stay unnamed, and how much each owes. Ofgem asked suppliers for exactly these figures in December 2025.
- How many movers take their supplier with them.
- How long homes stand empty, and how much energy they use while empty.
- A month-by-month pattern of moves from an official source.
- What share of a supplier's lost customers are movers rather than switchers.

A NEAR MISS, RECORDED. A scope brief in this repository says about 10 per cent of households move each year, with no source. The English Housing Survey gives 7.3 per cent of households in England. A 2016 Ofgem survey found 11 per cent of consumers had moved in the past year, but it counts people, not households. The three figures measure different things and should not be averaged.

WHERE MOVERS GO, AND WHAT THEIR NEW HOME USES.
- Of moves that change local authority, 51.9 per cent stay inside the same ONS region (year ending June 2020). So at least 51.9 per cent of all moves stay in-region; this is a lower bound, because the same-authority share is not published.
- By tenure, the share moving within 5 miles of their previous home: social renters 70 per cent, owners 51 per cent, private renters 45 per cent (English Housing Survey 2021-22).
- A home's dwelling explains more of its energy use (about 39 per cent of the variance) than its occupants' socio-demographics (about 24 per cent) (Huebner et al., 2015, 924 English homes). No study follows the same household's use before and after a move.
- No published figure says how many movers take a move-with-us offer, which Ofgem's June 2026 summary of responses confirms.

residuals.heading: Where our picture is still weak
residuals.body:
The rates by tenure are for England only, though the 2023-24 and 2024-25 survey editions agree on them. Figures for Scotland and Wales, and the 2016-2025 time series, still have to be extracted from each nation's own survey tables.

The 20 to 40 per cent debt share is a range suppliers gave Ofgem, not a measured statistic, and it may be a share of a different total from Ofgem's published £4.43 billion. Multiplying the two gives roughly £0.9 to £1.8 billion. That figure is an inference: state it with that caveat or not at all.

No official monthly series of moves was found. Removal firms' claims that August is the peak month are marketing, not evidence.

This pass did not establish which industry data flows carry a change-of-tenancy reading or flag for domestic electricity and gas, apart from the switching indicator. Nor did it check three timings against the law itself: the statutory source of the two-day notice rule, and the licence clauses behind the six-week final bill and the ten-day refund.

Nothing published says how often a household that takes its supplier to a new home takes only one fuel, or how often its two fuels start there on different dates. Before July 2022 a supplier sent two separate registration requests, one for each fuel, so the dates could differ. Nor does anything say what the previous occupier's gas annual quantity was at the new meter. The world draws no previous occupier there.

No published source says how a variable direct debit treats a credit brought forward: whether the supplier takes it off the next collection, or collects the bill and keeps the credit. This page follows the billing rule (SLC 31H.12), and a practitioner check is still owed.

scope_delta.heading: What this page does not yet establish
scope_delta.body:
It gives no figure for the value of a home-mover retention offer, for how long people stay on a deemed contract, or for how much an empty home uses. That is deliberate: each is a gap in the published record. Any simulation figure for them has to show that gap openly, not cover it with a plausible number.

It describes, but does not assess, Ofgem's 2026 proposal to let suppliers switch SMETS2 meters to prepayment mode when the previous occupier leaves. That rule comes after the 2016-2025 record the company runs against. For that period the regime is simple: supply continues, a deemed contract arises, and there is no remote switch to prepayment.

It does not say what our own supplier should do when a customer moves. That is the company's decision to get right or wrong. The world has to supply the moves, the tenure behind them, and the delay before a supplier finds out. The company has to see each move only the way a real supplier would: a phone call, a returned letter, a switch request with the occupier flag, or usage carrying on at an address with no named customer.

HOW THIS WORLD MODELS A MOVE WITH US, AND WHY (the choices, not results).
- The household answers the offer on its own next decision, against a stated multiple k of its own chance of staying at that price. No take-up rate exists, so the multiple runs from 0 (nobody takes us) to 1 (a mover stays as often as a household renewing at that price), and both ends are reported.
- The destination keeps the origin's region at least 51.9 per cent of the time, the published lower bound; otherwise another region is drawn. The weather follows the new address. Prices in this world are national, so the tariff re-rating gap does not bind it yet.
- The new home's consumption comes from a newly drawn dwelling, not from the old home's use, because the dwelling explains more of a home's use than its occupants do. Its use switches to the new dwelling on the move date. How fast it really changes is not published, so this is an assumption.
- Today only the electricity supply moves with the household, and a gas supply ends at the move. That falls short of the rule that a household moves as a household. The rules for the gas supply were written down first, on 22 October 2026. A gas supply belongs to a meter, so following a mover means taking on the new home's gas meter on the same date as its electricity. A new home with no gas meter (about one home in seven) takes electricity only. The company's first estimate of the new home's gas use is that meter's annual quantity.
- Every later term of a household that moved with us is kept out of the margin history that sets other customers' prices, so customers who stay never pay for the offer.

meta.title: Choosing what to do for each customer, and when doing nothing is the best choice
meta.subtitle: Next best action means choosing, for one customer at one moment, the action that changes the outcome most. The question is not who is likely to leave or buy. Contact can make things worse, and the evidence says it often does.
meta.wall_placement: Public-reality commons only. Every figure here comes from a published source: Ofgem licence conditions and decisions, Ofgem's randomised consumer-engagement trials, the FCA's general insurance pricing evaluation, peer-reviewed field experiments, and supplier annual reports. No figure on this page was produced by this project's simulation. Where the published record is silent, the page says so instead of supplying a number.

claim_freshness.source: Ofgem, Decision: Renewing the BAT after March 2026 (13 November 2025); Ofgem, Insights from Ofgem's consumer engagement trials (September 2019) and Prompting sustained engagement in energy tariff switching (October 2020); Ofgem, State of the Market: Energy Retail Highlights (January 2026); Ofgem Standards of Conduct Guidance OFG1163 (April 2024); FCA EP25/2 (July 2025); Ascarza, Iyengar and Schleicher, JMR 2016; Ascarza, JMR 2018; Prince and Greenstein, JEMS 2014; Shah, Kumar, Qu and Chen, JM 2012; Centrica Annual Report 2025; Telecom Plus FY2025 results; Octopus Energy Limited Annual Report FY2025. Full citations in docs/market_research/next_best_action_and_cross_sell.md.
claim_freshness.note: Written for step 1 of the director's priority order of 5 October 2026. The simulation has a renewal-pricing optimiser and a catalogue of add-on products with no callers. It has no estimate of what an offer changes. Its world cannot respond badly to an offer. This page is here so that whatever gets built next has the published evidence to answer to.

headline.heading: The claim, in one sentence
headline.body: Next best action means choosing, for each customer at each moment, the action whose effect on that customer is largest net of its cost, and doing nothing is always one of the options. In randomised trials the customers most likely to leave were not the ones a retention contact helped most, and a well-meant 'you could save money' contact raised churn from 6% to 10%. So the quantity to rank on is what the action changes, not how likely the customer is to leave.

plain.heading: In plain terms
plain.body:
A supplier can do many things for a customer: offer a better price when their fixed deal ends, move them to a tariff that suits their electric car, help them onto direct debit, call them about a debt, sell them boiler cover or put them in touch with a solar installer. Or it can leave them alone. Next best action is the habit of choosing among these one customer at a time.

The common mistake is to aim at the customers most likely to do something anyway. Someone who was going to stay takes the discount and stays, so the discount is just money handed over. Someone who was going to leave takes the call and leaves. What matters is the difference the action makes. Some customers stay because they were asked. Some leave because they were reminded they could. The second group is real, and it is large enough to matter.

Upselling and cross-selling are different things. An upsell is a better version of what the customer already has, such as an EV tariff for a customer who has just bought an electric car. A cross-sell is a different product, such as boiler cover or broadband. A cross-sell brings a second contract, sometimes a second regulator, and its own marketing-consent rules.

theory.heading: How it works
theory.body:
PROPENSITY AND UPLIFT. Propensity is how likely a customer is to do something. Uplift is how much more likely they are to do it because you acted. Customers split four ways: those who respond only if asked (persuadables), those who would anyway (sure things), those who will not either way (lost causes), and those whom asking pushes the wrong way (sleeping dogs). Only the first group is worth the cost. Radcliffe and Surry set this out in 1999. Ascarza (Journal of Marketing Research, 2018) showed in two field experiments that targeting on lift beats targeting on risk. Ascarza, Iyengar and Schleicher (JMR, 2016) found that recommending cheaper plans to about 65,000 mobile customers raised three-month churn from 6% to 10%. Uplift can only be measured against a group that was deliberately left alone, so a real programme keeps a random holdout.

WHAT A CONTACT DOES IN GB ENERGY. Ofgem's randomised trials give the scale. A letter listing cheaper market deals raised switching from 1% to between 2.4% and 3.4%. A prompt sent just after a one-year fix ended raised it from 19% to 28%. A collective switch offer raised it from 2.6% to 22.4%. These figures count every switch, including switches away from the supplier that sent the letter. The effect also lasts: households who switched in the trial later switched again at 63%, against 33% for those who did not. An action that wakes a household up changes its behaviour for years.

THE RULES. Since April 2022, SLC 22B has banned deals offered only to new customers. Its Market-wide Derogation, extended to 31 March 2027, lets a supplier offer bespoke retention deals only to customers nearing the end of a fixed term. Which actions are available therefore depends on the customer's contract state. The Standards of Conduct (SLC 0) require fair treatment and attention to vulnerability. When a customer misses two monthly payments, SLC 27.5B requires the supplier to contact them, so debt support is an obligation and cannot be ranked against a sales offer. The FCA banned pricing insurance renewals on predicted reluctance to switch from January 2022, and found the renewal premium in home insurance almost halved, from £95.38 to £49.17. The smart-meter data rules (SLC 47) require explicit consent before consumption data is used for marketing. Electronic marketing without consent is limited to 'similar products' under PECR. So the population a cross-sell can lawfully reach is smaller than the customer book.

HOW OUR RULE RANKS (2026-10-12, the director's ruling). The company ranks on joint value: the household's benefit over the horizon plus the change in the company's own forward value, and it takes no action that leaves either side worse off. At realistic margins and churn, every advice action we can model is worth more to the household than it costs us, yet it still costs us something, so the rule advises nobody. Whether such an action should come with a price that shares the value it creates is an open question for the director.

What is published about such a price (read 2026-10-14). The licence is silent on a savings-share fee, and the Standards of Conduct (SLC 0.6) do not bound a fee's amount. Recovering a share by instalments is consumer credit, as the Green Deal was. The one computable GB energy split is Octopus's Demand Flexibility Service test events in 2022/23: of the £3.00/kWh NESO paid, households got £2.25 (75%) and Octopus kept 25%, on Octopus's own account. ECO runs the other way: the supplier funds the measure and the household keeps the whole saving. No GB supplier publishes an advice-savings-share scheme. Detail: docs/market_research/how_a_supplier_prices_a_share_of_value_it_creates_for_a_household_2026-10-14.md. HOW OUR RULE LEARNS WHAT AN ACTION DOES (2026-10-16). The first estimate comes from the company's own holdout: some customers get the contact, a coin-drawn group does not, and the company compares who stayed. The estimate is used only when its 95% interval is clear of zero. If the holdout says the contact made people leave, the rule refuses it. At realistic sizes, telling apart a 2-point difference in staying over a year takes about 3,000 customers in each group. A run can now keep a coin-drawn share of default-tariff customers out of the letter; none has been run that way yet.

A retention price that shares the value (measured 2026-10-16). SLC 22B has not been lifted: Ofgem proposed removing it in May 2024 and reversed that in July 2024, citing the loyalty penalty, and it now runs to 31 March 2027. Its carve-out lets a supplier offer a fixed-term tariff to existing customers only, and names no price rule, so such a tariff may cost more than the household's present one. The price cap reaches default tariffs only. Across the 18 cases above, a rise on a fixed retention tariff of £0.01 to £2.73 a month brings our side to zero in all 18, if staying does not respond to the price. Adding the published response of staying to price (about 0.15 points per £ a year) leaves 10 of 18, and none of the six highest-margin cases. On a default tariff already at the cap, none. The rise moves value; it creates none. Detail: docs/market_research/a_retention_price_that_shares_the_value_an_action_creates.md.

expected_shape.heading: What the data should look like
expected_shape.body:
Retention offers should cluster at the end of fixed terms, because that is both when the law allows bespoke deals and when the trials show the largest response. A retention programme run against a holdout should show uplift varying across customers and turning negative for some. The customers with the highest predicted churn should not all be the ones with the highest uplift.

Smart and EV tariffs should be growing fast from a small base. Ofgem counted 835,000 domestic customers on smart time-of-use tariffs in July 2025 (2.8% of the market), of whom 653,000 were on EV tariffs, up 84% in a year. Uptake should follow the moment a household buys the kit.

Customers holding several products should churn less. Utility Warehouse supplies about 2.9 services per customer, and British Gas retains 87% of protection contracts. Most of that gap should be expected to shrink once selection is controlled for. The one careful causal study, of US telecoms bundles, found a real effect, but only in turbulent markets. A minority of cross-buyers should lose money: 10-35% of them across five firms in Shah and colleagues' study.

live_evidence.heading: Live evidence
live_evidence.body:
WHAT IS SOURCED. The legal shape of retention offers (SLC 22B and its derogation, Ofgem decision of November 2025). Contact effect sizes in GB energy from Ofgem's randomised trials, 2017-2018, and their persistence (Ofgem, October 2020). The existence and size of negative contact effects (Ascarza et al. 2016, telecoms). Lift-based targeting beating risk-based targeting (Ascarza 2018). Smart and EV tariff take-up (Ofgem, January 2026; Octopus FY2025: 278,000 EVs on Intelligent Octopus Go). Product holding and retention at the two GB multi-product suppliers (Centrica 2025: 2.94m Home Services customers, 87% retention, about 7% of nearly 600,000 free members converting to a paid contract; Telecom Plus FY2025: 3.39m services across 1.16m customers, energy churn up from 8.7% to 13.7%, partly blamed on not having an EV tariff).

WHAT IS NOT. No GB source measures how many more customers stay because their own supplier made them a retention offer, or how that depends on the size of the discount. Ofgem itself records that no evidence on the derogation's pricing effect was put to it. No GB source separates the causal part of the multi-product churn gap from selection. No source gives conversion rates or supplier economics for heat-pump, solar or battery offers to existing customers.

ONE NUMBER DELIBERATELY NOT USED. A vendor-commissioned study of a commercial decisioning platform reports churn falling 5%, 10% and 15% over three years. It describes a composite organisation, is not energy-specific, and was paid for by the vendor. It is the kind of figure that becomes load-bearing by accident.

residuals.heading: Where our picture is still weak
residuals.body:
The biggest gap is the one a supplier would most want filled: the uplift of its own retention offer, by size of offer, for its own customers. Every GB trial measured market-wide prompts, and the sending supplier's gain and loss are mixed together in the figures.

There is no energy-specific measure of contact fatigue, meaning how much a further message reduces the response to the next. The best available evidence is from online retail, where halving email frequency cut unsubscribes by 59% at a cost of 5-8% of short-term revenue.

Two legal readings are open. One is whether 'similar products' under PECR covers boiler cover, broadband or a heat pump offered by an energy supplier. The other is how far the FCA's insurance pricing rules reach home-emergency cover. Both need someone who works in the trade, not another search.

scope_delta.heading: What this page does not yet establish
scope_delta.body:
It does not establish an uplift figure for any offer, and that is deliberate. The honest output is a shape: uplift varies across customers, can be negative, depends on timing, and lasts. Measuring it needs a holdout.

It does not establish what the simulated supplier should offer anyone. That is a decision the simulation should be free to get wrong.

It does not cover the cost of a contact by channel, which is an open gap recorded elsewhere, or debt collection practice, which has its own research.

And it records something about our own model that matters more than any single figure. In the simulated world today, a retention offer can only help, helps the same whatever its size, and leaves no lasting trace. A decision engine trained against that world would learn the opposite of what the field experiments found.

meta.title: EV, solar and batteries: what a supplier gains, loses and can see
meta.subtitle: An electric car adds to what a household buys and solar panels take it away. A battery only moves it in time. They are three different products, and a supplier relates to each in three different ways.
meta.wall_placement: Public-reality commons only. Every figure is from a published source or is marked as a gap. Figures read only through a secondary report are said to be so. No figure produced by this project's simulation is used as evidence; the one place the simulation's code is described, it is described as code.

claim_freshness.source: Ofgem Smart Export Guarantee Annual Report, Year 5 (April 2024 to March 2025); Ofgem State of the market reports (April 2025, January 2026); SMMT annual registrations 2024 and 2025; DfT vehicle licensing statistics (VEH0142); DESNZ solar photovoltaics deployment and solar cost data; MCS annual installation figures; Electric Nation smart charging trial; McKenna, Pless and Darby (2018), Energy Policy 118:482-491; English Housing Survey energy reports. Full list with links in docs/market_research/ev_solar_and_batteries_as_products.md
claim_freshness.note: Written for step 1 of the director's priority order of 5 October 2026. Several figures were read through secondary reports that quote the primary source. Those are marked in the research document and should be opened at source before any of them becomes a constant.

headline.heading: The claim, in one sentence
headline.body: For a supplier, an electric car is extra demand that lands at the evening peak unless a tariff moves it overnight; rooftop solar is lost daytime demand plus exported energy that rival suppliers compete to buy; and a battery is worth whatever the tariff lets it shift. So the money a supplier can make here comes from tariffs that move energy in time and from keeping the households that own the kit, much more than from the energy volumes themselves.

plain.heading: In plain terms
plain.body:
There are three products, and they pull in different directions. A car charged at home adds roughly 1,800 to 3,500 kWh a year to what a household buys, which is more than half again of a typical home's electricity. Solar panels cut what the household buys from the grid by about a quarter, and the rest of what they generate is sent back to the grid. A battery makes or uses nothing of its own: it stores cheap or home-grown electricity and uses it later.

A supplier can relate to each product in three ways. The customer may buy the kit without the supplier's involvement, and the supplier simply sees demand change. The supplier may sell or install the kit, or be paid for passing on a lead. Or the supplier may offer a tariff built around the kit: a cheap overnight rate for charging a car, or a payment for exported solar. Only the last of these uses what a supplier actually is, a licence to sell electricity.

Who can take part is limited before preference comes into it. Around a third of households have nowhere off the street to park, so they cannot charge a car at home. Tenants rarely have panels on their roof: in England in 2023, 7% of owner-occupied homes had solar, 5% of socially rented homes and 2% of privately rented ones.

theory.heading: How it works
theory.body:
ELECTRIC CARS. The Electric Nation trial found that people mostly plug in when they get home: charging peaks between 7pm and 10pm, which is exactly when electricity costs most to buy and move. A time-of-use EV tariff with smart charging moves that load into the night. The value this creates is the difference between peak and night prices multiplied by the energy moved, and the cheaper overnight rate is the customer's share of it. Ofgem counted 653,000 households on smart EV tariffs in July 2025, up from 243,000 in January 2024, against a fleet of plug-in cars charged at home that is probably one and a half to two million. Somewhere around a third to a half of EV households therefore pay a tariff built for the car. The rules on new home chargers since June 2022 set a default of avoiding peak hours, but owners can override it, so the default alone does not settle when charging happens.

SOLAR. Measured across 302 homes, households use about 45% of what their panels generate and export the rest (McKenna and colleagues, 2018). For a typical home that is about a quarter less electricity bought. Since January 2020, any supplier with 150,000 or more domestic customers has had to offer an export tariff under the Smart Export Guarantee, at a rate that is always above zero. In the year to March 2025, 270,395 installations were registered for it, 443 GWh was exported, and suppliers paid £57 million, an average of about 12.9p a kWh. Tariffs open only to a supplier's own import customers averaged about 15.4p; tariffs open to anyone averaged about 4.5p. Before 2019, the Feed-in Tariff simply assumed half of what an unmetered system generated was exported.

BATTERIES. Batteries went from about 270 certified installations in 2022 to about 41,000 in 2025. Paired with solar, a battery raises the share of generation the home uses. Paired with a time-of-use tariff, it can charge cheaply overnight and supply the home at the peak, which creates value in the same way an EV tariff does.

THE PAYBACK. For solar, it depends on four things: the price the household pays for electricity (each kWh it uses itself saves that price), the export rate (which varies about threefold depending on which supplier buys it), how much of the generation the household uses itself, and the installation cost. The Energy Saving Trust gave 9 to 13 years in 2023. The median installed cost for small systems peaked around £2,250 to £2,260 per kW in 2022 to 2024 and has fallen to about £1,780.

expected_shape.heading: What the data should look like
expected_shape.body:
Solar installations should be high in 2016 at the end of the subsidy, fall to roughly 35,000 to 45,000 a year in 2019 to 2021, then step up after the 2022 price shock to about 190,000 to 200,000 a year in 2023 and 2024 and about 255,000 to 267,000 in 2025. Battery installations should be near zero until 2022 and then roughly double each year. Home charging of electric cars should grow with the fleet: new battery-electric cars took 19.6% of the market in 2024 and 23.4% in 2025, though fewer than one in four of them were bought by private buyers.

A household that gets solar should buy about a quarter less electricity, with the drop in daytime hours, and export about half of what it generates. A household that gets an electric car on an ordinary tariff should buy more in the evening; on an EV tariff, it should buy more overnight. A supplier's export payments should be close to the wholesale value of midday power on open tariffs, and well above it on tariffs tied to an import contract.

live_evidence.heading: Live evidence
live_evidence.body:
WHAT IS SOURCED. Smart Export Guarantee registrations, export volume, payments and tariff counts, from Ofgem's own report. Smart time-of-use and EV tariff customer numbers, from Ofgem's State of the market reports. New car registrations, from SMMT. Solar site counts and installation costs, from DESNZ. Certified installations, from MCS. Measured solar self-consumption, from a peer-reviewed study. When and how much people charge at home, from the Electric Nation trial. Solar by tenure, from the English Housing Survey.

WHAT CANNOT BE DIVIDED. The average export per Smart Export Guarantee installation cannot be read off Ofgem's totals, because they include non-domestic generators of up to 5 MW. The average registered capacity is 5.9 kW, above a typical home's 3.5 to 4 kW.

ONE FIGURE HELD BACK. A widely repeated summary of the Energy Saving Trust's savings figures implies a typical home exports more than 4,500 kWh a year, which a home-sized system cannot do. It is not used here until the source itself has been read.

residuals.heading: Where our picture is still weak
residuals.body: Nobody publishes how many households have an electric car, as opposed to how many cars are registered, and company cars charged at home blur the line. No published figure says what share of a car's charging moves off-peak on an EV tariff. Battery counts before 2023 are only a floor, because certification was not required, and estimates of how often new solar comes with a battery range from about 30% to over 90%. No published source gives what suppliers earn from installation leads, the margins on kit they sell, or how often households with the kit change supplier. How batteries are actually run, on solar alone or charging from the grid at night, is not measured anywhere public.

scope_delta.heading: What this page does not yet establish
scope_delta.body: It does not give a single number for the value of an EV tariff, a solar customer or a battery. Those depend on the price shape and on the tariff, and should be measured on the real half-hourly price record rather than chosen. It does not cover heat pumps, which belong with heating. It does not establish the margin a supplier loses when a customer installs solar. The structure of the price cap suggests that loss is small, because the standing charge is unaffected, and suggests the larger risk is the customer leaving for a rival's tied export tariff. That is an inference from how the cap is built, not a published figure.

meta.title: What a GB energy customer's satisfaction, complaints and recommendations are, and what they do
meta.subtitle: Satisfaction, NPS, sentiment, complaints, Ombudsman cases and trust are six different things. Complaining is something a household does; being dissatisfied is a state it is in. On the published record they point opposite ways on whether the household leaves.
meta.wall_placement: Public-reality commons only. Every figure on this page comes from a published source: Ofgem surveys and complaints data, the Energy Ombudsman, Citizens Advice, the Institute of Customer Service, the CMA, Ofgem's randomised trials, and peer-reviewed work on NPS. No figure produced by this project's simulation appears here.

claim_freshness.source: Ofgem supplier-level satisfaction findings Jul-Aug 2025 (n=3,790); Ofgem/GfK Complaints to energy companies 2014 (domestic n=2,457, Figures 54-56); Ofgem biennial complaints survey 2016 (n=3,049); Ofgem CIM wave 6 (n=3,458, Table 56); Energy Ombudsman annual data 2019-2025; Littlechild 2021, EPRG WP 2027; Keiningham et al. 2007, Journal of Marketing 71(3); Ofgem CMOC trial 2019; BIT CMOL 2017; SI 2008/1898; Ofgem SLC 23 guidance; Ofgem Consumer Standards decision 2023; Citizens Advice star-rating methodology
claim_freshness.note: Written as step 1 knowledge for the area the director's 2026-10-05 order puts last. The page exists so that the world's satisfaction and complaint physics have something published to be checked against, before anyone builds sentiment or NPS on top of them.

headline.heading: The claim, in one sentence
headline.body: When a GB household complains and the complaint is handled badly, it is about two and a half times as likely to leave as when it is handled well (23% against 9% within two months in Ofgem's 2014 survey). A household that is merely dissatisfied and never complains switches less than a satisfied one (3.0% against 5.4% over six months in Ofgem's 2025 survey). So the thing that drives departure is a bad complaint experience, not unhappiness in general.

plain.heading: In plain terms
plain.body:
Six measures get used as if they were one. Satisfaction is what a household says when asked how happy it is with its supplier. NPS is whether it would recommend the supplier to a friend. Sentiment is the tone of what it says when it calls or writes. A complaint is a recorded act: in law, any expression of dissatisfaction that expects a response. An Ombudsman case is a complaint that was still unresolved after eight weeks and that the household chose to take further. Trust is whether it expects the supplier to treat it fairly.

The difference that matters most is between the act and the state. A household that complains is already engaged: it has picked up the phone. If the supplier then handles the complaint slowly, or without keeping it informed, a large share of those households leave. A household that is unhappy but says nothing tends to be disengaged. It is more often on a default tariff, on prepayment, or struggling to pay, and it is the least likely of anyone to move. A model that says 'unhappy customers leave' gets this backwards.

Routine service is broadly fine. About 82% of households are satisfied and 6% dissatisfied, and the dissatisfied share ranges from 3% to 10% across the seven largest supplier groups. Things go wrong when something breaks and has to be put right, and the published evidence says most of what breaks is billing.

theory.heading: How it works
theory.body:
COMPLAINTS. Under the Gas and Electricity (Consumer Complaints Handling Standards) Regulations 2008, a supplier must record every complaint, signpost its procedure and the Energy Ombudsman, and publish an annual report. Ofgem publishes complaints per 100,000 accounts every quarter: 1,011 across the market in Q4 2025 and 1,038 in Q1 2026, which is roughly 1% of accounts each quarter. In Q4 2019, among large and medium suppliers, the rate varied fourteen-fold. After eight weeks, or a deadlock letter, the household may go to the Energy Ombudsman within 12 months. The Ombudsman can award up to £10,000. It accepted 122,829 cases in 2023, 92,938 in 2024 and 80,256 in 2025. Billing makes up 56-58% of them; disputed usage is 22% of billing disputes and disputed balances 8%. Suppliers correctly signpost the Ombudsman in only about 45% of cases, so how many complaints escalate partly depends on the supplier's own conduct.

THE DOSE. Ofgem's 2014 complaints survey interviewed households about two months after they complained. Of those satisfied with how their complaint was handled, 9% had already switched; of those dissatisfied, 23%. Speed of resolution was the single strongest driver of satisfaction with handling. Only a quarter of complainants were given a timetable, and only half of those had it kept. The 2016 survey's figure that 52% 'had or were planning to switch' mixes intention with behaviour: in 2014 the equivalent figure was 44%, but only 18% had actually switched.

NPS. NPS is the percentage of promoters (scores of 9-10) minus the percentage of detractors (0-6). Ofgem's 2019 survey published it only by supplier size: Large -15, Medium +17, Small -16. No regulator publishes it per supplier. Keiningham and colleagues (2007) found satisfaction predicts company growth as well as NPS does. The CMA treated customer service as a 'hygiene factor': it matters below a minimum standard and stops mattering above it.

COMMUNICATIONS. The best published evidence is Ofgem's randomised trial with about 600,000 default-tariff customers, in which households got a letter from their own supplier listing cheaper tariffs (CMOC, 2018). Within 30 days, switching went from 2.9% to 6.8%. A reminder took it from 5.9% to 7.5%. Each £100 of potential saving added 1.2 percentage points. Every communication with a published effect makes households more likely to move. None shows a communication reducing departures.

RULES. The Standards of Conduct (SLC 0) require fair, honest, transparent, appropriate and professional treatment. A price rise needs at least 30 days' notice (SLC 23). Since December 2023, a supplier must contact a customer after two missed monthly payments, or one missed quarterly payment. The Citizens Advice star rating weights complaints at 35%, ease of contact at 30%, billing at 25% and commitments at 10%.

expected_shape.heading: What the data should look like
expected_shape.body: A credible world should produce complaints at around 1% of accounts per quarter, varying between suppliers by an order of magnitude and driven mostly by billing: disputed usage, disputed balances and catch-up bills, not by price rises alone. Only a small, supplier-dependent fraction should reach the Ombudsman. Among complainants, departure should rise steeply as handling gets worse, from roughly one in ten after good handling to roughly one in four after poor handling, and vulnerable households should leave less after the same bad experience. Satisfaction should sit around 80% satisfied and 6% dissatisfied, should dip during a price crisis and recover afterwards, and on its own should not raise departure. Households that answer surveys should over-represent the extremes.

live_evidence.heading: Live evidence
live_evidence.body:
WHAT IS SOURCED. Satisfaction levels by wave and by supplier group, published twice a year since 2018. Complaints per 100,000 accounts, per supplier, every quarter. Ombudsman volumes and categories each year. Within-complainant switching by handling quality (Ofgem 2014, n=2,457). Switching by satisfaction band (Ofgem CIM wave 6, Table 56). NPS by supplier size band (Ofgem 2019). Two randomised trials of supplier-sent letters (2017, 2018). The rules on complaint handling, notice periods and proactive contact.

WHAT OUR WORLD DOES TODAY. It generates complaints and their resolution times, but they are triggered only when a unit rate rises by more than 20%, which is a price change rather than the billing failures that make up most real complaints. How well a complaint is handled is decided by a random draw in the world rather than by the company. None of it reaches the household's decision to leave: the resentment stock, reputation index and journey state are logged and read only by reports. The one path from experience to departure is a satisfaction score built from rate shocks and household characteristics, and it raises the hazard for dissatisfied households, which the published record contradicts. Nothing in the code generates or reads sentiment.

residuals.heading: Where our picture is still weak
residuals.body: No published GB source gives a per-unit dose from a satisfaction, NPS or sentiment score to an individual household's chance of leaving; all published links compare bands or whole suppliers. The best evidence on handling-to-departure is self-reported ('as a result of'), comes from 2013, and is partly reverse causation, since 15% of those complaints were about the switch itself. There is no base switching rate for the same window. No distribution of sentiment in energy-supplier contacts has been published. No trial measures whether proactive contact, a DD-change notice or a price-rise notice reduces complaints or departures. Per-supplier NPS and trust are not published. The 2018-2024 quarterly complaints series exists on Ofgem's portal and has not yet been captured.

scope_delta.heading: What this page does not yet establish
scope_delta.body: It does not give a number to set for satisfaction, NPS or sentiment, and that is deliberate. What it establishes is a set of shapes a world can be checked against: complaint incidence, which is driven by billing; a steep handling-to-departure gradient among complainants; a flat or inverted link between satisfaction and departure; and a selected, extreme-heavy survey response. It does not cover prepayment self-disconnection, which is a different experience with its own measurement. It does not cover non-domestic customers.

meta.title: Where a gas-heated home's carbon comes from, and which measures save it
meta.subtitle: On today's grid the gas boiler is five to six times the carbon of all the home's electricity. The measures that save both money and carbon are mostly heating measures; the timing measures are small on both.
meta.wall_placement: Public-reality commons only. Every figure is from a published source (Ofgem, DESNZ, the Energy Saving Trust, DfT, ICCT, IPCC, the Electrification of Heat and RHPP field trials, Nesta, the Behavioural Insights Team, IEA 4E) or computed from NESO's published half-hourly carbon intensity as held in the repository. No figure produced by this project's simulated company appears on this page.

claim_freshness.source: Ofgem TDCV decisions 2015, 2017, 2020, 2021 (postponement), 2023 and 2026; DESNZ Greenhouse gas reporting conversion factors 2016-2025 (flat files); NESO national carbon intensity via sim/grid_carbon_history.py; DfT National Travel Survey 2024; ICCT July 2025 EU life-cycle update; IPCC AR5 WGIII Annex III; Energy Systems Catapult EoH interim report March 2023; DECC RHPP final report March 2017; EST in-situ condensing boiler trial 2009; EST advice pages (current and June 2016 archive); Nesta boiler flow temperature reports 2022-2023; BIT Nest evaluation 2017; IEA 4E home energy storage report Feb 2025. Working: docs/market_research/household_carbon_and_the_measures_that_save_it.md
claim_freshness.note: Written because the project's carbon knowledge and code were built almost entirely around electricity timing, while the carbon a gas-heated home actually emits is mostly gas. The company's only live household footprint counts electricity only.

headline.heading: The claim, in one sentence
headline.body: For a typical gas-heated British home on the 2024-25 grid, the gas burnt for heating and hot water is five to six times the carbon of all the home's electricity — up from about two and a half times in 2016 — so the measures that save the most carbon, and most often save money too, are heating measures, not changes to when electricity is used.

plain.heading: In plain terms
plain.body:
Take Ofgem's 'typical' home: 11,500 kWh of gas and 2,700 kWh of electricity a year. Burning that gas releases about 2.1 tonnes of CO2. The electricity, on 2025's grid, comes to about 0.37 tonnes. In 2016 the same electricity would have been about 0.84 tonnes, because the grid then still burnt a lot of coal and gas; since then wind and solar have roughly halved the carbon in each unit. Gas has not changed at all: a unit of gas burnt today emits what it did in 2016.

That changes which advice matters. Turning the thermostat down a degree, lowering a combi boiler's flow temperature, fitting heating controls, insulating a loft or a cavity wall: each saves gas, and every unit of gas saved is worth about 183 grams of CO2. Moving a unit of electricity from the early evening to the middle of the night is worth about 36 grams on today's grid — and even a perfectly timed shift, every day, is worth about 80. Per unit, saving gas beats shifting electricity about five to one, and a typical home has four times as many gas units as electricity units to work on.

Three bigger decisions behave differently. A heat pump saves about 1.6 tonnes a year against a gas boiler, but on ordinary flat tariffs it usually costs a little more to run, so it is chosen mainly for carbon unless a heat-pump tariff makes it cheaper. Solar panels now save mostly money: each panel displaces far less carbon than in 2016, because the grid they displace is cleaner. An electric car saves about 1.8 tonnes a year compared with a petrol one — but it nearly doubles the home's electricity use, so the household's electricity carbon goes up, and the energy supplier can see the extra electricity but never the petrol that was not bought.

theory.heading: How it works
theory.body:
TWO FUELS, TWO KINDS OF FACTOR. Natural gas has a fixed emission factor because its chemistry is fixed: DESNZ's factor for gas, per kWh on a gross calorific value basis (the basis gas bills use), was 0.1840 in 2016 and 0.1830 in 2025. Electricity's factor is whatever the grid burnt that half hour. NESO publishes it half-hourly; DESNZ publishes an annual figure that lags two years (its 2025 figure describes the 2023 grid) and adds a separate factor for transmission and distribution losses. On the 2025 grid the two bases differ by about 45%, so any statement about electricity carbon must say which it uses. Gas has no such ambiguity.

WHY THE RATIO MOVED. The ratio of gas carbon to electricity carbon for the same home went from 2.5 in 2016 to 5.8 in 2025, and all of the movement is the grid. The household's electricity, weighted by when a typical home uses it, fell from 312 to 135 grams per kWh over the decade.

WHY TIMING IS WORTH LITTLE PER UNIT. The value of shifting a unit of electricity is the difference in grid carbon between two times of day, not the level. That difference has been fairly stable — about 40 grams from a day's average to its cleanest four hours, about 80 from its dirtiest four hours to its cleanest — and it narrowed to 28 grams between evening and night in 2022. A home battery has to beat its own losses (it returns 80-95% of what it stores), so its carbon effect is close to nothing and was negative in some years.

WHY A HEAT PUMP IS CARBON-LED. A boiler in a real home turns about 82% of its gas into heat (Energy Saving Trust field trial); a heat pump in a real home delivers about 2.8 units of heat per unit of electricity (Electrification of Heat trial median). It is cheaper to run than the boiler only if electricity costs less than about 3.4 times as much as gas per unit. Under the price cap the ratio has been 3.5 to 5.7, so on a flat tariff the heat pump has cost £60-260 a year more to run while saving 1.0 tonne (2016) rising to 1.6 tonnes (2025) of CO2. A heat-pump tariff, or replacing an old inefficient boiler, is what makes it save money as well.

WHY SOLAR TURNED INTO A MONEY DECISION. A kilowatt of panels generates about 800-900 kWh a year in Britain. It displaces grid electricity in the hours it generates, which are already the cleanest hours. That displaced carbon fell from about 250 kg per kilowatt in 2016 to about 90 in 2025, while the money saved per unit used at home roughly doubled with the electricity price.

expected_shape.heading: What the data should look like
expected_shape.body:
A gas-heated home's carbon should be dominated by its gas, and increasingly so each year as the grid cleans up: roughly 70% gas in 2016, about 85% by 2024-25.

Gas savings should translate into carbon at a constant rate — about 0.18 kg per kWh — in every year, so a measure that saved 3,000 kWh of gas in 2016 saved the same carbon in 2025. Its money value, by contrast, should track the gas price: loft and cavity insulation saved about 40% more in pounds in 2025 than in 2016 for the same physical saving.

Electricity savings should be worth less carbon every year. An LED bulb or an efficient fridge saving the same kWh in 2025 as in 2016 should save less than half the carbon.

A heat pump should show up in a household's meters as gas falling to zero and electricity rising by about 3,400 kWh. Its carbon saving should be about three-quarters of the heating carbon on today's grid.

An electric car should show up as about 2,400 kWh a year of extra electricity, mostly overnight if smart-charged — close to the whole of a typical home's other electricity use.

live_evidence.heading: Live evidence
live_evidence.body:
THE RATIO, BY YEAR (gas ÷ all electricity, Ofgem medium home, NESO grid weighted by the domestic load shape): 2016 2.4 · 2017 2.7 · 2018 2.7 · 2019 3.2 · 2020 4.1 · 2021 3.9 · 2022 4.1 · 2023 4.9 · 2024 5.9 · 2025 5.8. On DESNZ's lagged factors with losses the 2025 figure is 4.0.

MEASURES THAT SAVE BOTH MONEY AND CARBON (typical figures, 2025 prices): turning the thermostat down 1°C, about £120 and 350 kg a year (EST); heating controls, about £100 and 290 kg (EST); loft insulation from nothing, about £200 and 580 kg in a semi-detached house (EST 2016 carbon, re-priced); cavity wall, about £220 and 650 kg (same basis); draught-proofing, about £55 and 160 kg; lowering a combi boiler's flow temperature, up to about £65 and 190 kg if done fully (Nesta modelling), though a 61,000-home trial of advice alone found about 0.4% of gas; a smart thermostat, about 4.5-5% of gas (Behavioural Insights Team trial); LED spotlights, £45 and 35 kg (EST); smart-charging an electric car, about 85 kg.

MEASURES LED BY CARBON: a heat pump on a flat tariff (about 1.6 tonnes saved, £60-260 a year more to run, ~£12,000 installed before a £7,500 grant); solid-wall insulation (about 1,100 kg, £12,000-15,000); an electric car, judged on the household's energy bills (about 1.8 tonnes saved, battery manufacturing repaid in about 17,000 km, ICCT).

MEASURES LED BY MONEY: solar panels (about 90 kg of carbon per kilowatt a year in 2025 against 250 in 2016); home batteries (roughly carbon-neutral); efficient appliances (small electricity savings, worth less carbon each year).

WHAT A SUPPLIER CAN SHOW. It sees its own gas and electricity meters. It can evidence a fall in gas use, and a shift in half-hourly electricity. It can only estimate an electric car's avoided petrol or a solar panel's generation. It cannot see a heat pump's benefit at all once the gas account closes: on electricity alone, a heat pump looks like a carbon increase.

GRID LOSSES, 2016-2025. The electricity figure is per unit generated. What the grid loses delivering it is published each year by the government as its own factor: 0.03727 kg CO2e per kWh in the 2016 set, falling to 0.01769 in 2022 and 0.01853 in 2025 (BEIS/DESNZ conversion factors, read from each year's own file). Since 12 October 2026 a household's year shows those losses on their own line beside its electricity, and they are not added into its electricity figure or its total.

residuals.heading: Where our picture is still weak
residuals.body:
The Energy Saving Trust's current pages give money savings for fabric measures but have dropped their carbon figures, and some (cavity and solid wall) no longer state a saving at all; the carbon figures here come from its 2016 archived tables for a semi-detached house that lacks the measure. How many typical homes still lack each measure is not established here.

The share of gas used for cooking rather than heat, the efficiency of today's boilers in real homes (the measured figure is from 2009), the share of solar output a typical home uses itself, the petrol cost of the car an electric car replaces, and the money a battery saves on its own are all open.

Every displacement figure here uses the grid's average carbon. If the electricity saved or shifted actually displaces gas-fired generation at the margin, solar, batteries and timing would all be worth more carbon — up to about 3.7 times more for solar. No published half-hourly marginal series for Britain is held.

DESNZ's 2022 gas factor could not be read from its spreadsheet; the 2021 and 2023 values, which differ by 0.1%, bracket it.

scope_delta.heading: What this page does not yet establish
scope_delta.body:
It does not establish what any one customer saved. A supplier can see a fall in a meter, not its cause, and every 'you saved' statement needs weather correction and a stated counterfactual.

It does not set a carbon price or turn carbon into money. Carbon here is shown, not optimised.

It does not cover oil, LPG or electrically heated homes, whose ratios and best measures differ sharply, nor homes off the gas grid. It does not establish heat-pump tariff prices across 2016-2025, which decide when a heat pump became cheaper to run as well as cleaner.

meta.title: Back bills: who pays for energy that was never charged for
meta.subtitle: Since May 2018 a supplier can only ask a household to pay for energy used in the twelve months before it asks. What counts as asking decides who carries the rest.
meta.wall_placement: Public-reality commons only. Every figure here comes from a published source: Ofgem's 2017 open letter, statutory consultation and 2018 decision on licence condition 21BA, Ofgem's 2020 letter to suppliers, the Energy Ombudsman's published stance and annual data, and Energy UK. No figure produced by this project's simulation appears as evidence on this page, and nothing here was chosen because a number was needed.

claim_freshness.source: Ofgem, open letter on back billing, 3 April 2017; Ofgem, Protecting consumers who receive backbills, statutory consultation, 16 November 2017 (with draft SLC 21BA); Ofgem, decision of 5 March 2018; Ofgem, open letter on SLC 21BA, 7 May 2020; Energy Ombudsman, Our backbilling stance; Energy Ombudsman annual data 2025; Ombudsman Services energy sector reports 2017-2019; Energy UK Explains: Back billing, February 2025. Full citations in docs/market_research/back_billing_and_liability.md; Electricity Act 1989 Sch 6 para 3 and Gas Act 1986 Sch 2B para 8 (legislation.gov.uk); Ofgem electricity supply licence conditions consolidated to 1 August 2025, SLC 6, 7, 21BA.6-21BA.9 and 24; Ofgem, Tackling Energy Debt in the Supplier Home-Moves Process, call for input, 9 December 2025, and its summary of responses, June 2026; Energy Ombudsman, Deemed contracts and rates; Citizens Advice, Check if you're responsible for paying an energy bill; MHCLG, Social housing lettings in England, tenancies, 2023/24 and 2024/25; Scottish Housing Regulator, National Report on the Scottish Social Housing Charter, 2023-24 and 2024-25; Goodlord Rental Index, 2020-2026; MHCLG, English Private Landlord Survey 2024; MHCLG, Council Taxbase 2025 in England
claim_freshness.note: Written at the director's request of 6 October 2026, which asked for back-billing to be treated as knowledge rather than as a toggle value. Writing it showed that the simulated company measured what it may not recover against the wrong thing for direct-debit customers: against its estimated bills, where the rule measures against the money it has actually asked for or taken. That was corrected the same day; on 16 October 2026 a census of every run of more than twelve estimated bills found none billed past the twelve-month limit, and found that nothing in the company asks for a read when a run grows long. Extended on 8 October 2026 at the director's request to cover empty properties between tenants: who the customer is during a void, whether the twelve-month limit protects a landlord, and change-of-tenancy practice (section 9 of the research file).

headline.heading: The claim, in one sentence
headline.body: A GB supplier may only demand payment for energy a household or microbusiness used in the twelve months before the demand, unless the customer obstructed it; and because the rule is about the demand, not the bill or the meter reading, a direct debit set too low can cost a supplier money even when every bill it sent was right.

plain.heading: In plain terms
plain.body:
A back bill is a catch-up: the supplier asks you to pay for energy you have already used and were never correctly charged for. It happens when estimated bills were too low and a real reading finally arrives, when nobody read the meter for years, when the supplier's billing system failed, when you were billed on the wrong meter, when you moved in and nobody sent you a bill, or when your direct debit was too low and nobody raised it.

Since 1 May 2018 for households, and 1 November 2018 for microbusinesses, the supplier can only ask for the last twelve months of that. The rest is the supplier's loss. Not sending a meter reading does not make it your fault. Blocking access to the meter after being asked and warned can. So can stealing energy.

The twelve months count back from the day the supplier asks for the money: a bill asking for payment, a higher direct debit, or a debt set on a prepayment meter. A statement that only shows a growing balance does not count as asking. So a supplier that reads your meter correctly every month, but lets your direct debit fall short and never raises it, loses whatever shortfall is more than a year old when it finally asks. If the payments it took covered what you used, nothing is lost, however wrong the bills were.

theory.heading: How it works
theory.body:
THE RULE. Standard licence condition 21BA, in both the gas and electricity supply licences. When a supplier 'issues a Bill … or otherwise seeks to recover (including via a Prepayment Meter) Charges', which the condition calls a 'charge recovery action', it may do so only for units 'which could reasonably be considered to have been consumed within the 12 months preceding' that action, and standing charges accrued in the same window. There are four exceptions: a demand made before the rule began; a compliant demand that is still being chased because it was not paid; the customer's 'obstructive or manifestly unreasonable behaviour'; and anything Ofgem later adds after consultation (none found). The supplier must prove an exception, and the Ombudsman will not look for one on its behalf. Deemed contracts are covered, so an occupier who never opened an account is protected too. Refunds of overcharges are not limited at all.

BEFORE 2018. From 2007 a voluntary principle applied only where the supplier was at fault, and counted twelve months back from when the error was found. It sat in Energy UK's Billing Code, whose signatories were the six largest suppliers, with 81% of domestic gas and 83% of domestic electricity customers in 2017. Microbusinesses had voluntary limits of three years for electricity and four for gas. Ofgem replaced the 'supplier at fault' test with 'customer not at fault' because the old one left customers unprotected when the fault was a third party's. Ofgem did not publish an impact assessment.

DIRECT DEBITS. Ofgem counts setting a direct debit as charge recovery action. The Ombudsman's published stance gives two worked cases. In the first, monthly bills on actual readings show a direct debit falling short, and the supplier raises it after 17 months: the shortfall from more than twelve months back cannot be recovered. In the second, no bills are sent for 17 months, but the direct debit covers the use: nothing is barred, because 'backbilling is not intended to refund customers' payments made for energy that they have used.' Energy UK and Ofgem's own consumer page list 'your Direct Debit amount was previously set too low' as one of the cases the rule covers. In 2019 the Ombudsman reported suppliers failing to apply the reduction when they had not completed an accurate direct-debit review within twelve months.

WHO ELSE PAYS. The supplier is still charged in industry settlement for energy it cannot bill. Electricity is reconciled up to about fourteen months, gas up to about four years. So a supplier can be paying wholesale for gas it may only bill twelve months of. Energy that settles without a reading is spread across all suppliers as a correction.

EMPTY PROPERTIES. A move-out followed later by a move-in is three periods with three different customers. First, the outgoing tenant: their contract ends on the move-out day if they gave two working days' notice, otherwise two working days after they tell the supplier or when someone else moves in, whichever is first, and they are liable until then (licence condition 24.1-24.2). Second, the void: for electricity the law deems a contract with 'the occupier (or the owner if the premises are unoccupied)' (Electricity Act 1989, Schedule 6, paragraph 3). For gas the deemed contract is with 'the consumer' (Gas Act 1986, Schedule 2B, paragraph 8), and whether the owner of an empty home counts is not settled in anything we read. Third, the incoming occupier, from the day they move in and not before.

THE LIMIT AND LANDLORDS. Deemed contracts are covered by the twelve-month limit, and the test is whether the premises are domestic, not who the customer is. So the owner of an ordinary domestic let looks protected for a void, though Ofgem has not said so in terms. Two landlord cases are expressly non-domestic and get no domestic protection: a landlord who holds the account and charges tenants for energy as part of a commercial accommodation service (licence condition 6.2(a), the usual bills-included or shared house), and a landlord whose homes sit on a multi-site business contract (6.6). Such a landlord is protected only if it is a microbusiness, and only from November 2018. In 2017-18 suppliers asked Ofgem whether a tenant who 'has not told the landlord they are moving in or out' or a landlord holding the only key to a meter cupboard is at fault; Ofgem answered only that each case is judged on its facts.

expected_shape.heading: What the data should look like
expected_shape.body:
Back bills should be rare and concentrated. In the first half of 2017 just over 7% of households went more than a year without an accurate bill, and the median supplier gave about 95% of its customers a bill on a reading within the year. The losses under the rule should sit almost entirely on accounts left unread or unchased for more than a year, and they should grow by roughly a month of under-charge for every month a found shortfall goes unasked-for.

For customers who pay each bill when it arrives, the loss should track how far estimates fell short. For direct-debit customers, most of the credit book, it should track how far collections fell short, and it should be near zero when direct debits are reviewed and raised on time.

Complaints should be few against the population and large per case. In 2016 Citizens Advice took over 6,000 back-billing cases and the Ombudsman over 4,000, about 15% and 12% of their caseloads. The median complaint back bill was £1,160, covering 24 months. Ofgem estimated that £0.8m to £2.3m a year should have been written off for Citizens Advice's clients alone. In 2024 and 2025 the Ombudsman took 3,238 and 3,216 back-billing cases, about 3.5% and 4% of all its cases.

Voids should cost a supplier mostly standing charges, because an empty home uses little. A tenant who leaves without telling anyone stays liable through the void until they do, so the landlord's share is only the void the supplier knew about. Energy used before an incoming tenant moved in can never be charged to them. When nobody is identified, the supplier pays for the void in settlement and can bill no one.

How long a void lasts depends on who owns the home. In England a social home stood empty for a median of 35 days between general-needs tenancies in 2024/25. The median across all social lettings was 21 days a year before Covid and about 30 since. In Scotland the average was 61 days, up from 32 in 2019/20. Privately let homes re-let through agents stand empty for about 20 to 21 days, ranging from 9 to 24 in a month (Goodlord Rental Index, an industry figure). Nobody publishes the void for a home that is sold, or what an empty home uses, so a void should cost its owner mainly standing charges, for about one month on a social let and three weeks on a private one.

live_evidence.heading: Live evidence
live_evidence.body:
WHAT IS SOURCED, AND READ IN THE PRIMARY DOCUMENT. The licence wording, its exceptions and their intent (Ofgem consultation, November 2017, appendices 2 and 3). The start dates and the 'obstructive or manifestly unreasonable' threshold (Ofgem decision, March 2018, and the Ombudsman's stance). The 2016 complaint counts, the £1,160 median and 24-month median, the £0.8m-2.3m estimate and the published case studies (consultation). The 94.8% and 94.4% read-based billing medians (decision). The finding that 34 of 63 suppliers' terms misstated the rule (Ofgem, May 2020). The 2024 and 2025 Ombudsman counts (Energy Ombudsman annual data 2025). The direct-debit cases (Ombudsman stance; Energy UK, February 2025; Ofgem consumer page).

WHAT CAME FROM A SUMMARY RATHER THAN THE SOURCE. Citizens Advice's 2016 estimate that up to 2.1 million households received large late bills, averaging £206 (the survey method is not given). The settlement reconciliation windows, taken from the project's earlier research rather than from the industry code texts.

A NOTE ON WHAT THE CASES SHOW. All six case studies Ofgem published in 2017 are billing failures, ignored readings or unloaded prepayment debt. None is simply a meter nobody could reach. The long back bills in the complaint record are at least partly a supplier's own failures, not only meters left unread.

ADDED 8 OCTOBER 2026, READ IN THE PRIMARY TEXT. The deemed-contract paragraphs of the Electricity Act 1989 and Gas Act 1986. Licence conditions 6 (which premises are domestic), 7 (deemed contracts), 21BA.6-21BA.9 (the deemed leg is covered; the microbusiness part started on 1 November 2018) and 24 (when a mover's contract ends), consolidated to 1 August 2025. Ofgem's home-moves call for input (9 December 2025): suppliers bill 'the occupier' on a deemed contract, that group may hold 20-40% of domestic energy debt, and Great Britain is unusual in keeping supply on when the occupier changes. Ofgem's summary of responses (June 2026), where suppliers asked for better notice from landlords and agents. The Energy Ombudsman's stance on deemed contracts. Citizens Advice's guidance on who pays after a move.

residuals.heading: Where our picture is still weak
residuals.body:
Nobody publishes how many back bills are sent, how big they are across all households rather than just complaints, or how much suppliers write off under the rule. The Ombudsman's back-billing counts for 2017 to 2023 were not found.

Two questions that decide real money have no written answer. Does a bill addressed to 'The Occupier' count as asking a later-named occupier to pay? Does a normal annual direct-debit review raise the debit to recover arrears, or only reset it to future use? These are things people in the trade know and do not write down.

No source covers crossed meters under the rule; the treatment here is inferred from it. How often suppliers successfully claim customer obstruction is not counted anywhere; Ofgem expected 'very few cases'.

On empty properties: how long social and private lets stand empty is now published, but nobody publishes how long a sold home stands empty, or what any empty home uses. Whether the owner of an empty home is the gas 'consumer' is not settled. Whether the twelve-month limit protects a landlord of an ordinary let for a void is our reading of the licence, not something Ofgem has stated. Court cases on landlords' liability for voids were not searched. A practitioner question is held: how long are voids on a domestic let, and are they billed to the landlord in practice or written off?

scope_delta.heading: What this page does not yet establish
scope_delta.body:
It gives no figure for what a supplier loses to the rule. The quantity depends on how a supplier reads meters, estimates and reviews direct debits, and no supplier publishes it.

It does say what our simulated company currently gets wrong. It writes off the old part of a catch-up by comparing true use with its estimated bills for every customer. For direct-debit customers, the rule compares true charges with the money actually asked for or taken. So the company writes off money it is still owed when a direct debit has covered the use, and writes off nothing when a direct debit has fallen short on accurate bills for more than a year. Its direct-debit review resets payments to future use and never asks for the balance it finds, which is exactly the failure the Ombudsman reported in 2019. It counts a twelve-month window by days rather than by its own seasonal profile, and it starts the microbusiness rule in May 2018 rather than November 2018. Until the company keeps the date it last asked each customer for money, it cannot tell what the rule bars.

The simulated company's change-of-tenancy record treats the void and the unnamed incoming occupier as one 'occupier' account. In law they are different debtors: the owner for the void (in electricity), the new occupier from the day they arrive. The world does not draw a void length, because none is published, and says so in its code.

meta.title: Getting to the meter, and energy that is stolen
meta.subtitle: A supplier must try to read every meter once a year, but it cannot enter a home without consent or a warrant. It must look for theft, but finding theft costs it money. This page explains both duties, who pays when they fail, and what a supplier can see.
meta.wall_placement: Public-reality commons only. Every figure here comes from a published source: the Electricity Act 1989, the Gas Act 1986, the Rights of Entry (Gas and Electricity Boards) Act 1954, Ofgem's supply licence conditions and decisions, the Retail Energy Code, the Retail Energy Code Company's theft estimate, and the gas industry's Unidentified Gas statement. No figure produced by this project's simulation appears as evidence on this page. Where nothing is published, the page says so and gives no number.
