Writing it found that the two-yearly meter inspection duty was abolished in April 2016, before most of our window. It also found that the simulation has no way for a supplier to ask for access, and that the world generates no theft. So the company cannot use the one back-billing exception a real supplier earns by trying to get in. Extended on 8 October 2026 at the director's request to cover what half-hourly settlement changes about reads and unbilled energy, and whether hard-to-read meters cluster (sections 8 and 9 of the research file).

headline.heading: The claim, in one sentence
headline.body: A GB supplier must take all reasonable steps to read every credit meter once a year. It has a legal power to enter to read the meter, but it cannot use that power against a refusal without a magistrate's warrant. It must look for theft, but each theft it finds costs it money, because theft nobody finds is shared across all suppliers by market share.

plain.heading: In plain terms
plain.body:
Reading the meter is the supplier's job. The rules ask it to try to get a reading at least once a year. A reading the customer sends in counts, and so does one a smart meter sends by itself. Until April 2016 there was also a rule to inspect every meter every two years. Ofgem removed it, because the yearly reading rule and safety law did the job better.

A customer does not break any law by refusing to let a meter reader in. The supplier has a legal right to come in at reasonable times. But without the occupier's consent, that right can only be used with a warrant from a magistrate. In practice warrants are used for suspected theft, for safety, and (until 2023, and on tighter rules since) to fit prepayment meters for debt. They are not used just to read a meter.

The access question matters because of the 12-month back-billing limit. A supplier normally cannot bill for energy used more than 12 months ago. The limit does not apply if the customer was obstructive: for example, they stole energy, or kept refusing a meter reader after reasonable requests. Simply not sending in readings does not count. The supplier has to show it asked.

Theft is the other half of the page. Every supplier must detect, investigate and prevent theft, and treat vulnerable households carefully when it does. But theft nobody finds never shows up on any one supplier's meters. Its cost is shared across all suppliers through the settlement system. Theft a supplier does find, it must pay for in settlement, and it usually recovers only a fraction from the person who stole it. That is why an industry incentive scheme pays suppliers for each detection.

theory.heading: How it works
theory.body:
THE READ DUTY. Standard licence condition 21B.4 in both fuels has applied since 31 December 2014. It requires 'all reasonable steps to obtain a meter reading (including any meter reading transmitted electronically from a meter … or provided by the Customer) … at least once every year'. Prepayment meters are exempt. It is a duty of effort, not a guarantee. In electricity a second pressure comes from settlement. The Balancing and Settlement Code expects at least 97% of non-half-hourly energy to be settled on actual reads by the final run, 14 months on, and charges suppliers that fall short. The two-yearly inspection conditions were repealed from 1 April 2016. Ofgem's reason was that 21B.4 meets 'the objectives of billing accuracy in a more effective and efficient way than a static meter inspection interval'.

ENTRY. Electricity Act 1989 Schedule 6 paragraph 7(2) and Gas Act 1986 Schedule 2B paragraph 23(2) let a supplier's authorised officer enter 'at all reasonable times' to read or inspect a meter. Obstructing that power is an offence, with a fine of up to level 3. But the Rights of Entry (Gas and Electricity Boards) Act 1954 says no such right can be used without the occupier's consent or a warrant, except in an emergency. It also says nobody can be penalised just for refusing entry to someone who has no warrant. A magistrate grants a warrant if admission is reasonably required, the operator would otherwise be entitled to enter, and notice was given. The current court directions require 10 business days' notice for theft, safety or tamper applications and 15 for debt.

OBSTRUCTION AND BACK-BILLING. SLC 21BA.2(c) lifts the 12-month limit where the supplier could not bill correctly 'due to obstructive or manifestly unreasonable behaviour'. Ofgem's 2018 decision gives two examples: stealing energy, and not letting a meter reader in 'without good reason' after reasonable requests. It says 'we do not consider a consumer to be obstructive … when he or she does not supply a meter reading'. It also says the supplier's backstop is to 'take a meter reading themselves', and that suppliers must keep evidence.

THEFT DUTIES. SLC 12A has applied to gas since January 2013 and to electricity since July 2014. It requires all reasonable steps to detect, investigate and prevent theft, and membership of the industry Theft Arrangement, now Schedule 7 of the Retail Energy Code. Paragraph 12A.11 sets the standards a supplier must meet. It must find out whether the household includes someone of pensionable age, disabled or chronically sick, or who would struggle to pay. It must set instalments the household can afford, and offer a prepayment meter before cutting off supply. It must take all reasonable steps not to cut off vulnerable households in winter. It must show, on the balance of probabilities, that the theft was the customer's intentional act or culpable negligence before asking them to pay. REC Schedule 7 provides three things. TRAS is a shared risk-scoring service. A tip-off service requires the supplier to read each tip within 10 working days. The Theft Detection Incentive Scheme sets each supplier a detection target by market share and pays a set value per detection.

WHO PAYS. Theft nobody detects is never metered, so it never lands on the thief's supplier. In electricity it is smeared across suppliers by market share through GSP group correction. In gas it is part of Unidentified Gas, which has run at about 2.5% of throughput since 2017. When a supplier detects a theft, it enters the assessed energy into settlement, pays for it, and bills the customer. Ofgem's 2014 model assumed only 20-30% of those charges are recovered.

HALF-HOURLY SETTLEMENT FOR EVERYONE (MHHS). In April 2021 Ofgem decided that every electricity meter point will be settled half-hourly, with the final reconciliation run at four months instead of fourteen and the dispute run at twenty months instead of twenty-eight. The new central systems went live on 24 September 2025, suppliers began moving meters on 22 October 2025, every meter is due to have moved by 7 May 2027, and the switch to the four-month timetable is planned for 2 July 2027. Gas is not part of it. Meters that are not read remotely stay in, and their readings are turned into half-hourly figures by a central load-shaping service. Ofgem did not add a duty to read traditional meters more often: it said manual readings 'should be the exception' and left it to the settlement code's performance targets to allow for the traditional meters that remain. Energy still unread at four months is spread across all suppliers through group correction. The licence's once-a-year reading duty is unchanged.

WHAT FOUR MONTHS DOES TO UNBILLED ENERGY. Today a supplier whose estimate was too low pays for the difference in settlement whenever a reading arrives within fourteen months, but may only bill twelve months of it, so energy twelve to fourteen months old is paid for and cannot be billed. Under the four-month timetable that band disappears, and a new one appears: energy four to twelve months old can still be billed to the customer, but is no longer re-settled to the supplier; its cost is shared across the market. That is our derivation from the decision and the back-billing rule; nobody has published its size.

DO HARD-TO-READ METERS CLUSTER? The evidence says yes in kind, and is silent on how much. In the English Housing Survey 2022-23, 57% of private renters and 44% of owner occupiers reported no electricity smart meter (68% and 55% for gas), and households paying on receipt of a bill were less likely to have one than those paying by direct debit. Every cause of persistent no-access that suppliers put to Ofgem is a trait of the building or the landlord: a locked cupboard whose key the landlord holds, a bank of meters in a block of flats, a bill sent to the building company. The same buildings are harder to fit with working smart meters: Alt HAN Co says a home-network range problem affects over 700,000 households, and crowded shared meter rooms block installation. No source links no-access to vulnerability.

expected_shape.heading: What the data should look like
expected_shape.body:
Reads: most credit meters read within a year, and a small group stays unread for years. In 2017 about 7% of domestic consumers had no bill based on a reading in 12 months. 97% of electricity energy is settled on actual reads by 14 months. Complaint back-bills had a median length of 24 months. Smart meters cut how many meters are left to estimate, but 2-15% of a supplier's smart meters are not sending reads. That share differs by supplier and persists. Access failures fall into several kinds (nobody home, refused, a locked meter cupboard), and only a refusal after documented requests is obstruction.

Theft: in progress at about 1% of domestic electricity meters (Ofgem 2014). Detected at a few per cent of that stock a year. About a quarter of investigations confirm theft: 15% of proactive investigations and 42% of reactive ones. Investigations lean heavily towards prepayment customers and deprived areas. Detected thefts have run for about two years. A supplier's cost of theft through prices is its market share of a national smear, not the theft in its own customer base.

Hard-to-read meters should persist at a property across tenants rather than appearing at random each year, and should be more common among private lets and flats. The size of that tilt is not published. Half-hourly settlement should leave billing for traditional meters unchanged and move the cost of late readings from the individual supplier to the market as a whole after four months.

live_evidence.heading: Live evidence
live_evidence.body:
WHAT IS SOURCED. The duties, entry powers and warrant rules are quoted from the statutes and licence conditions in force. The repeal of the inspection duty is from Ofgem's decision of 4 February 2016. The obstruction test is from Ofgem's 2018 back-billing decision, pages 9-10. The theft safeguards are SLC 12A.11.

THEFT SCALE. RECCo's Theft Estimation Methodology (2023) puts electricity theft at 1,703-2,837 GWh a year and gas theft at 636-1,059 GWh. That is £737m-£1,233m and £93m-£155m at December 2022 cap prices, or £29-48 a household. Ofgem (2025) gives £830m to £1.388bn. The gas industry's UIG expert assumes far more gas theft: 6,362 GWh, or 1.48% of consumption. It says this assumption is 'driven largely by the views of electricity theft' studies. The two gas estimates differ seven- to tenfold.

DETECTION. About 300,000 TRAS investigations ran between 2014 and March 2021, and 23% confirmed theft. For tip-off leads, 37% are investigated and 22% of those confirm theft (Ofgem 2025). Suppliers meet 40% of their incentive-scheme targets. In 2011 suppliers detected 15,956 domestic electricity thefts, against a stock Ofgem put at 275,000 in progress at any time. Reports to the public tip-off line grew from 2,613 in 2017-18 to 13,415 in 2024-25.

READS. Ofgem in 2015 found that meter inspections produced under 4% of suspected gas theft incidents. Tip-offs and suppliers' own analysis produced 85%. Large suppliers' smart meters at the end of 2024 were 85.1% to 98.0% in smart mode.

ADDED 8 OCTOBER 2026. Ofgem's half-hourly settlement decision and business case (20 April 2021), section 3 on the settlement timetable and manual reads. Elexon's announcement of 22 October 2025 on the migration dates. The programme's paper on moving to the new timetable (cut-over planned 2 July 2027, all earlier runs complete by 31 October 2027). English Housing Survey 2022-23, energy annex tables 3.7 and 3.9 (smart meters by tenure and payment method). Ofgem's back-billing decision (5 March 2018, page 8) for the access problems suppliers raised. Alt HAN Co's published figure for home-network range problems.

residuals.heading: Where our picture is still weak
residuals.body:
No published source gives the share of meter-reading visits that fail. Nor does any give the split of failures into nobody home, refusal and inaccessible meters. This is a question for someone who has run a meter-reading operation, and nothing has been invented to fill it. Also unpublished: how many warrants are sought for theft, safety or reading; the share of long-unread homes a supplier could show were obstructive; the domestic share of the theft estimate; theft rates on smart against traditional meters; and the recovery rate on theft since 2014. The size of electricity GSP group correction across 2016-2025 was not derived. We have not yet checked whether the price cap already allows for UIG and group-correction costs. Nor is it published when, in a run of estimated bills, a supplier should first ask for a read, or how: a letter, a text, a prompt to send one in, or a visit. The licence does not define 'reasonable steps', and Ofgem's 2018 decision names the supplier's own attempt to read the meter as the remedy without giving a schedule.

On half-hourly settlement: the settlement code's target for actual readings after the cut-over, any reading-frequency rule for traditional meters in the new design, and how the load-shaping service estimates an unread meter were not found. On clustering: no source measures how far no-access persists at a property, or how much more common it is by tenure, landlord, building type or vulnerability. We recommend drawing a persistent hard-to-read group tied to the property rather than the person, sized as now, and spread evenly until a practitioner says how much more often it sits in private lets and flats. That is a recommendation, not an established fact.

scope_delta.heading: What this page does not yet establish
scope_delta.body: It does not give a theft rate for any one supplier's customers, and that is deliberate. A supplier pays for theft mostly through a market-wide smear, and it learns about theft among its own customers only through its own investigations. It does not model how a household answers a request for access. The research shows that is what the supplier's reading effort and the obstruction exception both depend on, and the simulation does not yet have it. Changes after 2025 (market-wide half-hourly settlement, the 90-day smart repair rule of 2026) are explained above but fall outside the 2016-2025 window: every settlement day the simulation covers reaches its fourteen-month final run before the planned cut-over.

meta.title: How a GB energy supplier accounts for the bills it will never collect
meta.subtitle: A provision is an estimate made today about money owed today. A write-off comes years later. The cost a supplier reports, and the cost the price cap allows, is the first, not the second.
meta.wall_placement: Public-reality commons only. Every figure here comes from a published source: the text of IFRS 9, Centrica's annual reports for 2015 to 2025, the 2023-2024 statutory accounts of Octopus Energy, OVO Energy and E.ON Next, and Ofgem's May 2025 decision on debt-related costs. No figure produced by this project's simulation appears on this page. Where nothing published establishes a number, the page says so instead of supplying one.

claim_freshness.source: IFRS 9 (paragraphs 5.4.4, 5.5.15, 5.5.17, B5.5.35, B5.5.37, B5.5.52) as published in Commission Regulation (EU) 2016/2067; Centrica plc Annual Reports and Accounts 2016-2025, Note 17 and the Audit and Risk Committee reports; Ofgem, Decision - Appendix 2: Debt-related costs, May 2025; Lowell Group 2013 annual financial results; Arrow Global Group plc Annual Report 2017; Ofgem, Debt Relief Scheme policy update working paper, August 2025; Ofgem, Impact Assessment - Debt Relief Scheme, 6 November 2025; for capital and credit balances: Ofgem financial resilience decision 26 Jul 2023 (SLC 4A, 4B, 4D), CMA appeal decision 19 Jan 2024, docs/market_research/bad_debt_provisioning.md section "Capital target: the conflict settled"; IFRS 9 Appendix A (credit loss, lifetime expected credit losses), B5.5.28, B5.5.42 and B5.5.44, re-read at EUR-Lex 2026-10-11 for docs/market_research/bad_debt_provisioning.md section "An expected-loss provision from a forward cash forecast"; for the simulated world's write-offs coming from one payment record: docs/market_research/bad_debt_provisioning.md section "One payment truth" (2026-10-12), with the Limitation Act 1980 s.29(5), account_hierarchy_payment_allocation.md and DESNZ Annual fuel poverty statistics report 2025 s.3.4; for a provision matrix whose loss rates are learned from the company's own monthly roll rates, and the forward-looking overlay run at its two published ends: docs/market_research/bad_debt_provisioning.md section "A provision matrix whose loss rates come from the company's own roll rates" (2026-10-14); for when a supplier writes off closed-account debt, the unpublished clock from final bill to write-off and what recoveries count: docs/market_research/bad_debt_provisioning.md section "When the company writes off its own closed-account debt, and what the recoveries line counts" (2026-10-15)
claim_freshness.note: Written because the project carried four different bad-debt figures (three uncited provision tables, a flat 2% of revenue, a per-bill haircut, and the world's write-offs) and none of them was the quantity suppliers and Ofgem report. Working is in docs/market_research/bad_debt_provisioning.md. Extended on 8 October 2026 at the director's request to cover what written-off debt sells for and how that and near-zero recovery after write-off enter the provision, a customer's forward value and price (section 9 of the research file).

headline.heading: The claim, in one sentence
headline.body: A GB supplier's cost of bad debt is the change in its provision plus what it writes off, and at the one supplier that publishes the detail, the provision depends far more on how a customer pays and whether they have left than on how old the debt is: in 2025 Centrica held 7% against direct-debit debt over 90 days old, 50% against pay-on-receipt debt of the same age, and 88% against a closed account's.

plain.heading: In plain terms
plain.body:
Every energy supplier is owed money by some of its customers. At each year-end it has to estimate how much of that money it will never get. That estimate is the provision. It sits on the balance sheet against the money owed.

The yearly cost of bad debt is how much the provision went up, plus anything written off in the year, less anything recovered that had been written off before. It is not the amount written off. A write-off is the step of taking the debt off the books once there is no reasonable hope of collecting it, and it comes late. It does not mean the supplier has stopped chasing: Centrica says enforcement continues on written-off balances.

So three numbers that sound alike are different. The provision is a stock: how much of today's debt is expected to go bad. The bad-debt charge is a flow: what the year cost. A write-off is an event. A model that only books write-offs records the cost years late and misses the cost of customers who stay in debt without leaving.

theory.heading: How it works
theory.body:
THE RULE. IFRS 9 requires a supplier to hold, against every customer receivable, the loss it expects over the receivable's whole life (paragraph 5.5.15, the simplified approach). The estimate must weigh a range of outcomes, allow for the time value of money, and use reasonable information about the past, the present and forecasts (5.5.17). A supplier may use a provision matrix: rates by how overdue a balance is, in groups whose losses differ (B5.5.35). Historical losses are the anchor but must be adjusted for conditions now and expected (B5.5.52). Default is presumed by 90 days past due unless the supplier can show otherwise (B5.5.37).

HOW A SUPPLIER APPLIES IT. Centrica groups receivables by customer type and by payment method, separates live accounts from closed ones, and ages each customer's whole balance by its oldest unpaid invoice. Rates come from its own history of cash collected, re-estimated each year, plus internal ratings from payment history and credit-bureau data. On top it adds a separate macroeconomic provision when it believes the past understates what is coming: GBP 30m in 2020 and 2021, GBP 125m in 2022, GBP 175m in 2023, GBP 49m in 2024 and GBP 11m in 2025. It treats debt as in default from 60 days past due for some groups up to six to twelve months after a final bill, and writes off only once a period of time has passed since the final bill.

WHY ONE YEAR'S CHARGE IS NOISY. Ofgem, which sets the price cap's debt allowance from suppliers' reported charges, notes that a year's charge mixes provisions for this year's bills with corrections to earlier ones, and that suppliers change their models. One supplier told Ofgem it provided heavily in 2023 and corrected down in 2024.

SELLING DEBT. Debt that a supplier has given up collecting can be sold to a debt purchaser. Lowell paid on average 5.4p per pound of face value for the consumer debt it bought from 2004 to 2013, across all sectors, and began buying from utilities in 2013. Arrow Global paid £223.9m for £2.4bn of face value in 2017, about 9.3p, with 41% of the price for secured loans. Centrica reported money received from selling written-off debt in 2017 but not what it sold. Ofgem, valuing crisis-era energy debt still on suppliers' books for its debt relief scheme, took its worth as about a quarter of face value, the part suppliers had not provided for, and puts the cost of collecting at about 3p per pound.

WHAT THAT MEANS. For the provision: by the time a balance is written off, a supplier should already hold close to all of it, because what comes back afterwards is a few pence in the pound. For a customer's forward value: a likely leaver's closing balance is worth the 10-25p in the pound implied by provision rates on old closed accounts, not its face value, and the sale route adds only a few pence much later. For price: the cap's debt allowance is built from suppliers' bad-debt charges, which already net off recoveries and sale proceeds, so they cannot be priced in twice. On a capped tariff the allowance is the ceiling on bad-debt cost a supplier can recover through price; collecting or selling better improves its margin against the cap, not the cap.

Customer credit is not free working capital. Ofgem's financial resilience decision of 26 July 2023 set a Capital Target of £115 of Adjusted Net Assets per dual-fuel customer (£57.50 per fuel) and a Capital Floor of £0, binding from 31 March 2025. A supplier must also tell Ofgem when its cash falls below 20 per cent of its gross customer credit balances, and Ofgem may direct that credit balances be ringfenced. Gross means the trigger counts every customer in credit, not the book net of those in debit: credits and debits net out in the accounts but not in this test, so letting more customers carry credit moves a supplier toward the trigger even if its book is balanced overall.

A PROVISION IS A CASH FORECAST. IFRS 9 defines a credit loss as the difference between the cash a supplier is owed and the cash it expects to receive, probability-weighted and discounted (Appendix A; B5.5.28), and says the estimate may be simple: the average loss of a large group with shared risk characteristics can be enough (B5.5.42). The age-band matrix is a practical expedient for that quantity. So a supplier that forecasts, customer by customer and month by month, the bills it will send and the chance each payment arrives, given how the customer pays and their own payment record, can provision directly as the expected unpaid part of what is owed today. Two quantities must be kept apart: the provision covers only money already billed; the expected loss on next year's bills is a pricing and customer-value figure, not a provision. Centrica's 2025 change of provisioning model, audited against an "expected profile of the recovery" from two years of cash collection, is the nearest published practice.

LOSS RATES FROM A SUPPLIER'S OWN ROLL RATES. The standard says a matrix rests on "historical credit loss experience" but not how a ledger becomes a rate per age band. Two calculations are ordinary credit practice. A cohort loss rate asks what share of the money in a band at a past date was still unpaid at the write-off point; it needs the whole horizon to have passed, so it lags a shock by that horizon. A roll-rate chain asks what share of the money at each monthly age was still unpaid a month later, and multiplies those shares through to the write-off point; its early factors respond within a month. No GB supplier publishes its roll rates or the window it learns them over; Centrica's 2025 auditor tested its rates against two years of cash collection. Centrica's overlay was largest exactly when a learned matrix lags most (GBP 125m in 2022, GBP 175m in 2023, about 13% of its total provision in 2023) and was released as the matrix caught up, which is why leaving an overlay out asserts a value, zero, that the record shows was wrong in 2022.

expected_shape.heading: What the data should look like
expected_shape.body:
A credible supplier book, provisioned the way suppliers provision, should show these shapes:
- Coverage rising with age within each group, and the groups ordered direct debit, then pay on receipt, then closed accounts. Centrica 2019-2025: direct debit over 90 days 3-7% (34.8% in 2022, an outlier); pay on receipt over 90 days 38-63%; closed accounts over 90 days 75-90%.
- A closed account under 30 days old provisioned above a live pay-on-receipt account 30-90 days old, in every year.
- Provision coverage of the whole residential book of roughly a third to two fifths (Centrica 34-42%, 2019-2025).
- A bad-debt charge of roughly 1-3% of residential revenue, low in 2021 and high in 2023 (Centrica UK: 1.1% in 2021, 3.1% residential in 2023).
- From 2022, provisions growing much faster than write-offs: Centrica's residential charge was GBP 1,160m over 2022-2025 against GBP 391m written off.
- Recoveries after write-off of a few pence in the pound: Centrica recovered GBP 68m against GBP 1,482m written off over 2017-2025, about 4.6%.
- A cost that responds to the 2022-23 crisis through the provision and an overlay in the year it happens, not years later through write-offs.

- Sale proceeds of a few pence in the pound for written-off consumer debt: 5.4p (all sectors, 2004-2013) to about 9p (a 2017 book including secured loans).

live_evidence.heading: Live evidence
live_evidence.body:
WHAT IS SOURCED.
- The text of IFRS 9 on the simplified approach, the provision matrix, forward-looking adjustment, default and write-off.
- Centrica's UK residential provision by payment method, live or closed, and age band, for seven year-ends, 2019 to 2025, from each year's Note 17.
- Centrica's residential provision movements (charge, write-offs, closing balance), 2015 to 2025, and its recoveries of written-off debt, 2017 to 2025.
- Centrica's bad-debt charge as a share of UK energy supply revenue, 2019 to 2025, its macroeconomic overlay by year, and its provision against debt being recovered through prepayment meters (63-81%, not aged).
- Ofgem's definition of the bad-debt cost it allows in the cap, and its reasons for treating a single year's charge with caution.
- Three more suppliers' statutory accounts for 2023-2024. Octopus, OVO and E.ON Next describe the same method (rates by age, payment method and supply status, from their own collection history), report bad-debt charges of 1.6-3.9% of revenue, and hold provisions of 33-60% of their whole-book receivables. Octopus's 2023 accounts show overdue debt provisioned at 35% under three months old and 92% over twelve.

WHAT IS NOT. Only one supplier publishes its provision by method, age and live or closed status, and Ofgem considered and declined to build an industry table. No supplier publishes the roll rates or cure rates behind its matrix. The time from a final bill to write-off is not published. Coverage beyond 90 days is not split further, except one 2025 auditor's line: GBP 812m of Centrica's GBP 1,038m residential provision related to balances more than 360 days old. No price for selling GB energy debt specifically has been found; the sale prices above are for consumer debt across sectors (Lowell, Arrow Global), and Ofgem's quarter-of-face figure is a valuation of debt still held, not a sale price (Ofgem debt relief scheme working paper, August 2025, and impact assessment, November 2025).

residuals.heading: Where our picture is still weak
residuals.body:
Every coverage figure here is one supplier's, and that supplier has an unusually large standard-credit and legacy book. Before 2021 Centrica's residential figures include North America, and 2016-2017 are under the older incurred-loss standard, so the decade is not one series. Whether a balance on a repayment plan keeps its age or moves to its own group, and what a direct-debit balance over 90 days old actually is, are questions for someone who has run a supplier's credit function.

What GB domestic energy debt fetches when sold, by age and for live against closed accounts, is not published; nor is the share of written-off energy debt that is sold rather than kept with a collection agency. Whether energy debt sells above or below other consumer debt is not evidenced either way.

No GB supplier publishes a per-customer cash-forecast provision, or the monthly roll and cure rates it would rest on. A supplier building one learns them from its own book. Whether cash on a rolling balance should be treated as paying the oldest debt first when provisioning, and how a direct-debit balance that is behind its seasonal path should be provisioned, are practice questions no published source answers. In this project's simulated world, the bills it writes off can now come from the same record of who paid and when that every household behaviour acts on, so a household that keeps to a repayment plan or pays a missed bill late is not written off; that link is now how the simulated world runs. Checked against the record on 12 October 2026, the simulated world's stock of debt more than 91 days old matched Ofgem's, and it wrote off roughly a fifth to a seventh of what a large supplier writes off for each pound billed. Re-measured on 25 October on the same households, the world as it now runs writes off about 0.7p in every pound billed, at the bottom of the range worked out for that supplier, before allowing for that supplier having far more customers who pay on receipt of a bill. A household that has left no longer repays its old arrears after its final bill, as the published evidence says it mostly does not; that change explained only about a ninth of today's level, and which other changes since 12 October moved the rest is not yet known.

scope_delta.heading: What this page does not yet establish
scope_delta.body: It does not give a probability that any household will default. A coverage rate is a ratio of two balances at a year-end, and a charge rate is a ratio of two flows over a year; neither is a default probability. It does not say how long a supplier waits before writing off, or what written-off energy debt in particular sells for; it gives only the all-sector purchase prices and says so. It does not establish how the price cap's GBP 71 allowance splits between bad debt and the cost of chasing it.

meta.title: Why supplying a home costs more in some regions, under one national price
meta.subtitle: GB has one wholesale price, but the network charges and the energy lost in the wires are set region by region. Both are published, and our world carries neither by region. It carries no losses at all.
meta.wall_placement: Public-reality commons only. Every figure is read from Ofgem's price cap workbooks (Annex 3 network cost allowance v1.25; the demand and losses supplementary workbook v1.19; the cap level model v1.31) or from Elexon's BSC modification record. No figure from this project's simulation appears here except where the page says what our code does.

claim_freshness.source: Ofgem Annex 3 network cost allowance methodology, electricity, v1.25 (sheets 2a TNUoS, 2b DUoS, 2c BSUoS, 1a, 3b Losses); Ofgem supplementary workbook to Annexes 2, 3 and 4, demand and losses, v1.19 (1a Loss multipliers); Ofgem, Energy price cap methodology: group correction factors, consultation 22 Aug 2025 and decision Nov 2025; Elexon, BSC modification P350 (zonal transmission losses, live 1 April 2018); docs/market_research/regional_supply_cost_under_one_national_price_2026-10-25.md
claim_freshness.note: Written because the B5 regional basis atom was closed onto this gap on 24 Oct 2026: only London's DUoS had been extracted, and nothing in the record or the code modelled losses.

headline.heading: The claim, in one sentence
headline.body: Under one national wholesale price, supplying a home in N Wales and Mersey or the north of Scotland cost £14 to £44 per MWh more in network charges than supplying one in the cheapest region, usually London, in each year from 2016 to 2025. On top of that, a supplier buys more energy than its meters record, because some is lost in the wires: about 10 per cent in the median region, between 3 and 15 per cent across regions and years.

plain.heading: In plain terms
plain.body:
Every unit of electricity a household uses has travelled through the transmission grid and a local distribution network. The companies that own those networks charge for their use, and the charges are set separately for each of the 14 regional networks. Rural, sparse networks with long lines cost more per home than dense city ones, so the same household would pay more for its network in Merseyside and North Wales or in the Highlands than in London.

Some electricity is also lost on the way, as heat in cables and transformers. A supplier cannot sell what was lost, but it still has to buy it. The industry's settlement rules therefore scale each supplier's metered volume up to what actually left the grid. The uplift is about a tenth, and it differs by region too.

These are two different things. A network charge is a fee on a meter. A loss is extra energy the supplier must buy at the wholesale price. They are kept apart here.

theory.heading: How it works
theory.body:
NETWORK CHARGES. Three charges make up the network cost of a domestic electricity customer. DUoS, the distribution charge, is published by each of the 14 distribution network areas in its charging statement. It is the part that differs most by region. TNUoS, the transmission charge, is published by NESO with a locational element by zone. BSUoS, the balancing charge, is GB-wide. Ofgem's price cap builds its network allowance for each of the 14 regions from those statements, and publishes the build-up back to April 2015.

TWO BREAKS IN HOW THEY ARE CHARGED. From April 2022 the DUoS residual moved from the unit rate to a fixed daily charge, so most of the regional difference now sits in the standing charge. From April 2023 the TNUoS residual moved to a per-site daily charge that is the same in every region (CMP343). A per-kWh regional figure from before 2022 cannot be differenced against one from after it.

LOSSES. Settlement turns metered volume into the volume a supplier pays for. Line Loss Factors do this for distribution losses; each distribution network publishes them every year. Transmission Loss Multipliers do it for the transmission grid; they have been zonal since BSC modification P350 went live on 1 April 2018. A GSP Group Correction Factor then scales every supplier in a region, each half-hour, so the total matches what entered the region. Ofgem found in 2025 that correction factors had risen enough that line loss factors alone no longer reflected real losses. From the November 2025 update it adds a GB-average uplift of about 1.46 per cent.

THE CAP ALREADY PRICES LOSSES. The cap's wholesale allowance for each region is scaled by that region's loss multiplier. The ratio of each region's wholesale allowance to London's equals the ratio of their loss multipliers to four decimal places (Eastern 1.0122 against 1.0122, Southern Western 0.9767 against 0.9767).

expected_shape.heading: What the data should look like
expected_shape.body:
Network cost, all-in per MWh at 3,100 kWh a year (DUoS, TNUoS and BSUoS, including the fixed part). In 2016/17 the median region was £44.7, London the cheapest at £39.2, and Northern Scotland the dearest at £57.7. In 2025/26 the median was £66.6, London £51.3, and N Wales and Mersey £95.0. The gap between the cheapest and dearest region was £14 to £20 per MWh before 2023 and £24 to £44 from 2023. London was the cheapest region in 8 of the 10 years.

DUoS alone varies most. The dearest region paid 1.4 to 1.9 times the cheapest each year from 2016/17 to 2024/25, and 3.1 times in 2025/26. That ratio is not a constant.

Losses. Ofgem's demand-weighted transmission and distribution loss multiplier for a single-rate home was 1.07 to 1.11 in 2016/17 (median 1.095). It rose to a median of 1.121 by 2025/26 and runs 1.08 to 1.17 for 2026/27. So in the median region a supplier buys about 9 to 12 per cent more energy than its domestic meters record. The lowest of any region in any year is about 3 per cent (Northern Scotland, 2025/26). The regional spread is 4 to 12 percentage points. At a normal wholesale price that is £2 to £6 per MWh. At the 2022-23 peak it was more than the whole regional DUoS spread.

live_evidence.heading: Live evidence
live_evidence.body:
WHAT IS SOURCED. Every figure above was read on 25 October 2026 from Ofgem's Annex 3 v1.25 and demand and losses v1.19 workbooks, with their URLs and checksums recorded in the research note. Two checks passed. London's 2016/17 DUoS (£75.70 a year, 24.4 per MWh) matches the figure read from a 2019 edition of the same annex. Each region's network allowance equals DUoS plus TNUoS plus BSUoS to the penny.

WHAT OUR CODE DOES. The world prices the network at one national figure per year, close to the regional median, with no regional spread and no regional standing charge. The supplier's DUoS ledger holds one national unit rate and is reached by no production caller. No code anywhere in the world or the supplier applies a loss factor. The world settles metered kWh. A real supplier pays for about 1.09 to 1.12 times those kWh, and the cap it is priced against includes them. That flatters margin. At the cap's own allowances, losses were about £13 per customer a year in 2016 and about £134 a year at the January-March 2023 peak, annualised. That is an estimate from the cap's figures, not a measurement of our book. The measurement is filed as a finding.

residuals.heading: What is still unexplained
residuals.body: Figures before January 2019 are Ofgem's "historical examples, for illustration only". They were built with the same method but were never cap levels in force. One April cap period stands for each charging year, so BSUoS movements within a year, which were large in 2022-23, are not averaged. The London DUoS fall from £101 to £67 a year in April 2025 is read as Ofgem published it and has not been checked against the network's own 2025/26 charging statement. Actual settled correction factors were read only as Ofgem's two-year summary, not from Elexon's files.

scope_delta.heading: What this page does not yet establish
scope_delta.body:
It does not map an address to a network region. The world draws households in 11 ONS regions. Network charges and losses are set for 14 GSP groups, and the two do not nest: Scotland is two groups, and N Wales and Mersey crosses the border. Until a mapping is sourced (the published one is the distributor ID by postcode), any regional figure applied by ONS region is an approximation and must say so.

It does not cover Economy 7 or other multi-rate meters, which are in the same workbooks, or gas, whose network charges are set by gas distribution zones.

It does not change the world. The national loss uplift is the larger error and needs no region key, so it comes first, as a fidelity fix to the baseline world decided without reference to company results. The regional spread comes after the mapping.

meta.title: How a household pays for energy: direct debit, the other methods, and what a supplier owes the customer for getting the amount right
meta.subtitle: Roughly seven in ten accounts pay by direct debit, and that is the cheap way to serve them. The rule that the amount be right is absolute since 2022, and getting it wrong in either direction is what turns a payment method into a bill-shock, a debt or a regulator's letter.
meta.wall_placement: Public-reality commons only. Every figure here comes from a published source: Ofgem decisions and indicators, DESNZ Quarterly Energy Prices, Bacs scheme guidance and Pay.UK statistics. The one statement about the simulation (what its population draw does) is about the code and is marked as read, not run. Where nothing published establishes a number, the page says so.

claim_freshness.source: Ofgem decision letter on DD rules (26 Aug 2022); Ofgem DD market compliance review and progress update (Feb 2023); Ofgem letter to the ESNZ Committee (29 Nov 2023); Ofgem customer credit balance note (Mar 2024); Ofgem payment method uplift (2018) and Appendix 2 Debt-related costs (May 2025); Ofgem debt and arrears indicators Q2 2026; DESNZ Quarterly Energy Prices Mar 2018, Dec 2023-Dec 2025; Bacs scheme and Pay.UK 2024 statistics. Full citations, URLs and derived figures in docs/market_research/payments_and_direct_debit_2026-10-25.md.
claim_freshness.note: Step 1 of the owed pages in the director's map steer of 24 Oct 2026, from the advisor's cited evidence pack. It adds the method mix, the cost by method and the Bacs mechanics to what debt-and-collections already says about collection and arrears.

headline.heading: The claim, in one sentence
headline.body: A GB supplier's payment method decides most of its cost to collect: in the 2025 price cap, debt-related cost is £57 a year for a direct-debit customer, £160 for standard credit and £19 for prepayment, and a fixed direct debit has had to rest on the best current information, with no exception, since 21 October 2022.

plain.heading: In plain terms
plain.body:
Three ways of paying carry most households. Direct debit (DD) is the large one: 72% of standard electricity and 73% of gas customers in September 2025, against about 61-66% in 2017-18. Standard credit, where the customer pays each bill when it comes, was 16-21% in 2017-18. Prepayment (PPM) was 15-16%. The mix moved slowly, by 3 to 4 percentage points over the five years to 2025.

The method matters because it changes what a customer costs. Ofgem's 2018 estimate put the extra cost of standard credit over DD at £80 against £11 per dual-fuel account (working capital, bad debt and administration), and its 2025 decision set the debt allowance at £57, £160 and £19 for DD, standard credit and PPM. The standard credit premium in the cap is about £135 a year from July 2025. Only 43% of standard credit customers know it costs more than DD, and only 20% of those surveyed wanted to change.

A fixed monthly DD is the supplier's estimate of the year's use, spread over twelve months. If it is too low, the customer builds a debt that is recovered later. If too high, the supplier holds the customer's money: domestic credit balances were about £8.1bn gross at the end of 2023, of which Ofgem's policy measure (fixed-DD customers, net of unbilled use) was £3.76bn. In February to April 2022, more than 7 million standard variable tariff customers saw a DD rise averaging 62%, and 500,000 households saw one above 100%. That is what the 2022 rule change answered.

theory.heading: How it works
theory.body:
SETTING THE AMOUNT. Until 21 October 2022, standard licence condition 27.15 required the supplier to take "all reasonable steps" to base a fixed DD on "the best and most current information available", unless a clear and express principal term of the contract provided otherwise. Ofgem's decision of 26 August 2022 removed the principal-term exception and, per the decision letter, the "all reasonable steps" qualifier, making the duty absolute. GAP: the licence notice as extracted still shows "all reasonable steps"; the strike-through may have been lost, so the consolidated licence should be checked. Ofgem did not prescribe a review frequency. Its follow-up work named the practices it wants: more frequent adequacy checks, an extra review when a DD rises beyond a tolerance, surplus credit refunded or counted into a lower DD, and, in its words, "Where a consumer is in a credit position, we expect suppliers to reduce the associated Direct Debit level". Since 20 September 2023 a supplier must hold cash of at least 20% of gross domestic credit balances net of unbilled consumption, or Ofgem may direct ringfencing. Ofgem's position is that a customer can ask for a refund of a net credit balance at any time; the licence text for a refund duty was not found.

THE BACS CYCLE. A debit is submitted on day 0, the payer's bank hears on day 1 and the money moves on day 2. A failure can still arrive on day 4, in about 1% of cases, so a payment is not final until then. Advance notice defaults to 10 working days. Three message types carry the exceptions. AUDDIS answers a new instruction (for example 5 = no account, B = account closed, L = incorrect details). ADDACS reports changes by the payer or bank (cancelled, deceased, account transferred, amended). ARUDD reports a failed collection, with code 0 ("refer to payer", mostly insufficient funds), 1 (instruction cancelled), 2 (deceased), 3 (account transferred), 4 (advance notice disputed), 5 (no account), 6 (no instruction), 7 (amount differs), 8 (not yet due), 9 (presented late) and B (account closed). Under the Direct Debit Guarantee the payer's bank refunds a payment taken in error at once and recovers it from the supplier by an indemnity claim, with no strict time limit on the payer.

THE REASON CODE IS THE POINT. Code 0 is a household that could not pay this month. Codes 1, 2, 3 and B are the instruction ending, which is a different event with a different cure. 4, 5, 6, 7 and 9 are the supplier's or bank's error. A single "DD failure rate" folds these together, which is why no single published failure rate can be used as a belief about whether a household can pay.

MIGRATION. A household leaves DD by cancelling, by failing payments until the supplier moves it off, or by moving supplier. It reaches PPM through debt: Ofgem's review covered more than 150,000 PPMs fitted under warrant or switched remotely between January 2022 and January 2023, and suppliers committed £18.6m in redress. The rules now require at least 10 attempts to contact a customer and a welfare visit before an involuntary install. No published matrix gives the yearly flow between methods.

expected_shape.heading: What the data should look like
expected_shape.body:
A credible world and book should show these shapes against the record:
- A DD share of about 61-66% of customers in 2017-18, rising to 71-74% by 2025, with prepayment at 15-16% in 2017-18 and standard credit 16-21%.
- Standard credit about 20-25% of standard variable accounts in 2025 (8m of 35m accounts, derived), because fixed tariffs are mostly paid by DD.
- Unpaid debits near 2-3% of collections (Bacs, all sectors, 2024; energy-specific rate unpublished, a secondary source says about 2.2%).
- Customers in arrears with no arrangement at about 4% of accounts in 2026, with about 3% repaying under an arrangement; average arrears with no arrangement £1,500-1,900.
- Net credit balance per fixed-DD household between about £180 and £400.
- A standard-credit book that costs two to three times a DD book to serve, in debt and administration.
- A rise in DD adjustments in winter-to-spring after a price step, with the tail of very large rises close to zero once the 2022 rule bites.

live_evidence.heading: Live evidence
live_evidence.body:
WHAT IS SOURCED. The method mix at 2017-18 and 2025 (Ofgem; DESNZ), Ofgem's 2018 and 2025 payment-method cost decisions, the 2022 DD review and its 2023 update, the credit balance bridge to end-2023, the Bacs cycle and reason codes, Bacs volumes, and Ofgem's debt and arrears indicators to Q2 2026. Every figure and URL is in docs/market_research/payments_and_direct_debit_2026-10-25.md.

WHAT THE SIMULATED WORLD DOES, read from code and not yet run. simulation/population_draw.py draws direct debit with probability 0.72 (electricity) and 0.75 (gas), the DESNZ March 2026 values, and puts every other household in one class called "other". Two consequences. First, standard credit and prepayment are one class, so the payment-method cost differences above (£160 against £19) cannot arise from the draw. Second, a constant share is 6-14 points above the 2017-18 record, if it is used for the early years of a run; whether it is re-dated per window was not checked.

residuals.heading: Where our picture is still weak
residuals.body:
Nine things are not published, and each is a research task that is closed only by someone who has run a collections book. (1) A consistent 2016-2025 mix series for credit and prepayment: DESNZ Quarterly Energy Prices Table 2.4.1 holds it and only 2018, 2020 regional, 2023 and 2025 figures were read. (2) The current wording of SLC 27.15. (3) The licence text, if any, behind "refund at any time". (4) The share of energy DDs returned, by ARUDD code: Bacs, Pay.UK and Ofgem do not publish it, and the 2.2% figure is a secondary source with no stated method. (5) Cancellation and indemnity-claim rates. (6) How often suppliers review a DD, by trigger. (7) The yearly flow between payment methods and the reasons. (8) Arrears incidence by payment method other than PPM repayment shares. (9) The seasonality of arrears, which exists only as qualitative statements.

The practitioner question that sits under all of them: does a failed DD in a given month mean a household cannot pay, or will not? The record cannot separate them, and the codes only partly do.

scope_delta.heading: What this page does not yet establish
scope_delta.body: It does not give a failure probability for a debit, for any group of households, and supplies none. It does not say how much a large DD change raises failed payments, complaints or churn. It does not say how the payment mix would respond to a change in the standard-credit premium, because the only evidence is a 20% stated willingness to change. It does not grade the simulated world against the headline bands, which is owed: the world has no separate standard-credit or prepayment class to grade. It does not cover the supplier's own treatment of a failed debit, which is on debt-and-collections, nor the setting of the amount from the supplier's side, which is in the research note what_a_supplier_holds_to_size_a_direct_debit.md.

meta.title: How a household changes supplier: the switch, the objection, the save and the switch that goes wrong
meta.subtitle: Switching is a regulated process with a fixed clock, and the losing supplier's room to act inside it is narrow: an objection only for debt, a save only if the household cancels, and since February 2026 no annulment to keep a customer.
meta.wall_placement: Public-reality commons only. Every figure comes from a published source: Ofgem decisions and impact assessments, the Retail Energy Code, DESNZ Quarterly Energy Prices, ElectraLink, Energy UK and the NAO. The statements about the simulation are about its code and are marked as read, not run. Where nothing published establishes a number, the page says so.

claim_freshness.source: Ofgem as-is switching map (2018), objections policy update (2017), domestic objections impact assessment (2016), erroneous transfers paper (2016), three-week switching consultation (2014), switch-speed GSoP decision (2024), REC R0287 decision (Feb 2026), BAT decisions (2024, 2026); REC Registration Services schedule; DESNZ Quarterly Energy Prices 2019-2026; ElectraLink (2025); NAO (2023)
claim_freshness.note: Step 2 of the owed pages in the director's map steer of 24 Oct 2026, from the advisor's cited evidence pack.

headline.heading: The claim, in one sentence
headline.body: Since the Central Switching Service went live on 18 July 2022 a GB domestic switch completes within five working days, the losing supplier may object only for a debt over 28 days old (about 5-6% of switches met an objection before 2022, over 90% of them for debt), and it may keep a leaving household only by an offer the household accepts and then cancels the new contract for.

plain.heading: In plain terms
plain.body:
A household agrees a deal with a new supplier. Unless it asks to start sooner, a 14-day cooling-off period runs first. The new supplier then registers the meter points, and the old one is told. Before 2022 the old supplier had about a week to object and a switch took 15-16 days on average; since CSS the whole thing must finish within five working days, with £30 compensation if it does not.
The old supplier cannot simply refuse. It may object if the household owes it money that has been outstanding for more than 28 days after it asked for it, if the switch was made in error, or at the customer's request. A prepayment household with under £500 of debt can usually take the debt with it instead. Before 2022 about one switch in twenty met an objection, and roughly 70% of indebted households switched without one.
The old supplier may contact a leaving customer and make an offer, but the price is limited: since April 2022 a supplier may not offer new customers a deal its existing ones cannot have, and a retention-only deal is allowed only to a customer reaching the end of a fixed term. If the household changes its mind, it is the new supplier that withdraws the switch; since February 2026 the old supplier may not annul it to keep the customer.

theory.heading: How it works
theory.body:
THE CLOCK. Before CSS, electricity registered on MPAS and gas on UK Link; objection windows were up to 5 working days for electricity and 7 for gas, and the 2014 three-week rule bounded the whole switch. Under CSS (REC Schedule 23) a domestic switch can start at least one complete working day after the request and up to 28 days ahead; the objection window closes at 17:00 on the first working day after the request; the registration becomes Secured Active at 17:00 the day before supply starts, after which it cannot be withdrawn or annulled. SLC 14A.1 requires completion within five working days of the relevant date.
THE LOSER'S MESSAGES. Under CSS the losing supplier receives an Invitation to Intervene when the request goes Pending, and a Secured Inactive notice when it can no longer be cancelled. Its only regulated responses are an objection or, in narrow cases, an annulment.
OBJECTIONS. SLC 14.4 allows a domestic objection for outstanding charges, erroneous transfer, at the customer's request, or where related meter points have not all moved. Ofgem's 2016 review kept debt blocking. Under CSS a dual-fuel switch is linked one-fail-all-fail: an accepted objection on one fuel cancels the other.
SAVES. SLC 22B (from 14 April 2022, extended to March 2027 and proposed to March 2028) makes a new-customer deal available to existing customers too; a market-wide derogation allows retention-only deals at the end of a fixed term. REC R0287 (27 Feb 2026) removed annulment as a way to keep a customer.
ERRONEOUS TRANSFERS. About 0.5-1% of switches went to the wrong meter or the wrong person before CSS, mostly from address and meter-number mismatches; the household gets £30 automatically since May 2020.
DUAL FUEL. About 70% of electricity and 80% of gas customers held dual-fuel accounts in 2016; gas transfers run at about 0.75-0.80 of electricity transfers.

expected_shape.heading: What the data should look like
expected_shape.body:
A credible world and book should show these shapes against the record:
• Domestic electricity transfers of about 1.4-1.5m a quarter (about 5% of customers) at the 2019-20 peak, falling to about 0.22m (0.8%) in 2022, and 0.75-0.86m (2.5-2.8%) in 2024-26.
• Gas transfers at about 0.75-0.80 of electricity transfers.
• Peaks in April and October and a trough in December.
• Before CSS, about 5-6% of switch attempts meeting an objection, over 90% of them for debt, and about 30% of indebted switch attempts blocked.
• Erroneous transfers at 0.5-1% of switches before CSS.
• No reactive save before 18 July 2022 that relied on a notice the loser did not have in time, and none by annulment after 27 February 2026.

live_evidence.heading: Live evidence
live_evidence.body:
WHAT IS SOURCED. The process before and after CSS, the objection grounds and rates, the save rules (SLC 22B and REC R0287), erroneous-transfer rates, quarterly switching volumes 2016-2026 and the SoLR episode. Every figure and URL is in docs/market_research/switching_mechanics_2026-10-25.md. The objection rates and their three denominators are read in full in domestic_debt_objection_rates_gb.md; the save offer against the rules in a_save_offer_against_the_switching_rules_and_the_seam.md; internal against external switching in gb_domestic_switcher_split_cim_2022_2025.md; the monthly series in gb_domestic_switching_by_calendar_month.md.
WHAT THE SIMULATION DOES, READ FROM CODE AND NOT RUN. The loss notice crosses the wall as REC Schedule 23's own messages, the Invitation to Intervene dated at the latest day the rules allow. The world blocks an indebted credit-meter household's departure with probability 0.283 (Ofgem 2016: about 170,000 blocked against 430,000 allowed a year), never a prepayment one; the company does not yet decide its own objection. The company's save offer is answered by the household's own renewal roll at the offered price, for fixed-term leavers from 18 July 2022. A dual-fuel household leaves on one decision. No switch ever fails: there is no erroneous transfer, cooling-off cancellation or customer-requested objection.

residuals.heading: Where our picture is still weak
residuals.body: Nine things are not published. (1) Objection rates after CSS, and how many are withdrawn: the world applies 2013-15 rates to 2022-25. (2) Erroneous-switch rates after CSS. (3) The share of switches completed next day rather than in two to five working days, which decides how much warning a loser gets. (4) The share of switches that are dual fuel. (5) Save rates on loss notices, and any domestic rule on win-back contact. (6) Cooling-off cancellation rates. (7) Exact annual QEP totals per fuel for 2018-2025. (8) Ofgem's 2026 "fell slightly" against QEP's Q2 2026 rise of 15.2%. (9) CMA 2016 and the DCC's CSS performance reports were not read.

scope_delta.heading: What this page does not yet establish
scope_delta.body: It does not grade the simulated world's switching level against the quarterly bands; gb_switching_rate_denominators.md holds the matched numerator and denominator for that grade. It does not give a save rate, an objection rate after 2022 or an erroneous-transfer rate after 2022, and supplies none. It does not cover non-domestic switching, where contractual objections apply, or the economics of acquiring and keeping a customer, which are on the acquisition and retention page.

meta.title: What a supplier must hold: revenue it has not billed, debt it will not collect, customers' money and the capital behind them
meta.subtitle: A supplier earns revenue as energy is used, holds its customers' credit balances, and since 31 March 2025 must hold £115 of adjusted net assets for every dual-fuel customer. The 2021-22 failures were what happened when none of that was watched.
meta.wall_placement: Public-reality commons only. Every figure comes from a published source: Ofgem decisions, data and resilience reports, audited supplier accounts (Centrica, Octopus) and their Consolidated Segmental Statements, and CRA's report for Energy UK. The statements about the company are about its code and are marked as read, not run.

claim_freshness.source: Ofgem financial resilience decision (Jul 2023), FRC transparency report (Apr 2025), supplier financial resilience report (Jun 2026), customer credit balance data (2025, 2026), debt-related costs Appendix 2 (May 2025) and historical review (Mar 2026), EBIT allowance decision (Aug 2023), CSS modification (Sep 2025); Centrica 2019 and 2024 accounts and CSS 2016-2023; Octopus Energy Ltd FY2024 accounts; CRA for Energy UK (2023)

headline.heading: The claim, in one sentence
headline.body: Since 31 March 2025 a GB domestic supplier must hold at least £0 and aim for £115 of adjusted net assets per dual-fuel customer (Ofgem consulted on £130 and decided £115), and Ofgem may ringfence its customers' credit balances if its cash falls below 20% of the balances held for fixed direct debit customers.

plain.heading: In plain terms
plain.body:
A supplier's books differ from its bills in three ways that matter. First, it earns revenue as the energy is used, not when it sends the bill, so at any year end it carries energy supplied and not yet billed: about 5-8% of a year's revenue at Centrica and Octopus. Second, some of what it bills is never paid; it sets aside a provision for that and writes it off later. In normal years that cost about 1-2% of residential revenue; in 2023-24 British Gas's was 2.3-3.1%. Third, its direct-debit customers pay ahead in summer, so it holds their money: about £3bn across the market on average, £1.9bn at the March low.
When 28 suppliers failed in 2021-22, many had spent those credit balances and held almost no capital. Ofgem's answer, in force since 31 March 2025, is a capital rule (a floor of zero net assets and a target of £115 per dual-fuel customer) and a power to ringfence customers' money. By March 2026, 21 of 24 suppliers were above the target.

theory.heading: How it works
theory.body:
REVENUE. Under IFRS 15 energy supply is recognised as it is delivered; the gap between delivered and billed is accrued (unbilled) income, estimated from reads, consumption history, weather and settlement data, and trued up by industry reconciliation (up to £30m at Centrica in 2019).
BAD DEBT. Under IFRS 9 a supplier provides for lifetime expected credit loss on what it is owed, by a matrix of customer age, payment method and live or final status. The price cap counts the profit-and-loss charge: write-offs and recoveries plus movements in provisions. Octopus's provision covered about 44% of gross trade debtors in FY24.
CREDIT BALANCES. Fixed direct debits level a seasonal bill, so balances rise in summer and fall in winter. Since 2023 Ofgem may direct ringfencing when a supplier is below its Capital Target or its cash is below 20% of gross fixed-DD credit balances (the Cash Coverage Trigger). In March 2026 the market held £2.7bn of cash against £1.9bn of balances.
CAPITAL. Adjusted Net Assets are tangible fixed assets plus current assets less liabilities, plus approved Alternative Sources of Capital (rated guarantees and facilities with at least 12 months' tenor). Below the £0 Floor is a breach; between Floor and £115 Target a supplier needs a credible Capitalisation Plan and faces Transition Controls.
MARGINS. SLC 19A requires an audited Consolidated Segmental Statement that separates supply from everything else down to EBIT. The cap allowed the CMA's 1.9% EBIT until September 2023, then capital employed (£358 per customer) at 12.3%, about 2.5-2.6% of the direct debit cap in 2026.

expected_shape.heading: What the data should look like
expected_shape.body:
A credible company book should show these shapes against the record:
• Unbilled income at year end of about 5-8% of annual revenue.
• A bad debt charge of about 1-2% of residential revenue in normal years and 2.3-3.1% in the crisis years.
• A provision covering about a third to under half of gross trade debtors in a stressed book.
• Direct debit credit balances high in late summer and low in late winter.
• Adjusted net assets of at least £115 per dual-fuel customer from 31 March 2025, and cash above 20% of fixed-DD credit balances.
• A domestic EBIT margin near the cap allowance (1.9% to 2023, about 2.5% after), with single-fuel years anywhere from about -4% to +15%.

live_evidence.heading: Live evidence
live_evidence.body:
WHAT IS SOURCED. Revenue policy and unbilled shares (Centrica, Octopus), bad debt charges and coverage, the cap's debt allowances, credit balances and ringfencing, the capital rule and outcomes to March 2026, segmental margins and the EBIT allowance, working capital and collateral. Every figure and URL is in docs/market_research/suppliers_accounts_and_capital_2026-10-25.md; Centrica's and EDF's segmental statements are read in CSS_BENCHMARKS.md; the P&L cost structure and IFRS 9 practice in supplier_financial_reporting.md.
WHAT THE COMPANY DOES, READ FROM CODE AND NOT RUN. It sizes growth against the £115 Capital Target from 31 March 2025, in one place. Nothing computes cash against fixed-DD credit balances. An uncalled capital module states thresholds no source supports (a 1.5%-of-revenue wind-down reserve, a 10% equity ratio); no run reads them. Six documents that still called £130 the decided target were corrected on 25 October 2026.

residuals.heading: Where our picture is still weak
residuals.body: Eight things are missing. (1) Debt sale prices: no primary source. (2) E.ON, EDF and OVO accounts were not read. (3) A British Gas bad-debt series for 2016-2022, so the normal-years band is thin. (4) Market-wide segmental margins for 2016-2024. (5) The text of IFRS 15 and IFRS 9 was not fetched. (6) Centrica's 2022-2025 accrued income. (7) A monthly credit-balance series. (8) No source supports a 2.4% EBIT allowance, and none is used.

scope_delta.heading: What this page does not yet establish
scope_delta.body: It does not grade the company's own book against these bands; that is owed. It does not explain unbilled revenue or bad-debt provisioning in depth, which have their own pages. It does not cover the hedge book's collateral beyond the per-customer figures, which belong to the hedging page.

The weather-to-demand engine and the advice on solar, batteries and EVs carry over; the price replay, settlement and billing do not.

headline.heading: The claim, in one sentence
headline.body: Of the GB build, the weather-driven demand engine and the advice on solar, batteries and EVs transfer to Australia, while the price replay, settlement and billing would need rebuilding: Australia prices power every five minutes in five regions with no day-ahead market, bills at least every 100 days in arrears, and has almost no prepayment.

plain.heading: In plain terms
plain.body:
Australia's east-coast National Electricity Market covers Queensland, New South Wales with the ACT, Victoria, South Australia and Tasmania. Each of the five regions has its own price, set every five minutes. There is no day-ahead market. Prices may fall to minus A$1,000/MWh and rise to a cap of A$20,300/MWh in 2025-26 (AEMC). In the last quarter of 2025, 31% of five-minute intervals had a negative price (Energy Magazine, citing AEMO).
Households are billed at least every 100 days, so usually quarterly, on meter readings and in arrears. Bill smoothing is opt-in. GB's model of a fixed monthly direct debit that builds a credit balance is not the norm. Prepayment is close to absent.
The default price works differently. The Default Market Offer and the Victorian Default Offer cap standing offers only, about 12% of Victorian households, and serve as the reference price that every advertised market offer must quote against. In GB the cap covers every default tariff.
Solar is the ordinary customer, not the edge case: 4.3 million rooftop systems and 28.3 GW at the end of 2025, and 454,473 home batteries (Clean Energy Council, July-December 2025).

theory.heading: How it works
theory.body:
PRICE AND SETTLEMENT. Generators bid into five-minute dispatch, and five-minute settlement replaced half-hourly averaging in October 2021. Since May 2022 global settlement shares unaccounted-for energy among all retailers in each local area in proportion to their load. The spot price is the settlement price; there is no separate imbalance price. Hedging is by over-the-counter and exchange-traded caps and swaps.
NETWORKS AND EXPORT LIMITS. Thirteen distribution businesses set per-phase export limits on rooftop solar, typically 5 kW per phase and up to 10 kW at Ausgrid. South Australia runs dynamic export limits from 0 or 1.5 kW up to 10 kW per phase, and several states can curtail solar remotely in an emergency (Amber, May 2025; SA Power Networks). A household's connection can therefore bind what its assets earn.
METERS. Outside Victoria the retailer appoints a competitive Metering Coordinator; Victoria kept network-owned meters. 57% of meters were remotely read across the market, from 99.1% in Victoria to 39.2% in New South Wales, and the rules set universal smart metering by 2030 (AEMC).
DEBT. Retailers must run approved hardship programmes and offer payment plans. About 2.9% of residential customers had debt older than 90 days in 2023-24 and 1.9% of electricity customers were in hardship programmes. Disconnections for non-payment were about 0.06% of small customers (AER, via Energy Magazine). The retailer asks for a disconnection; the network carries it out. Debt stays with the old retailer when a customer leaves.
MOVES AND FAILURE. A move-in customer who has not chosen can take a standing offer from the area's designated retailer, which must act by the next business day (National Energy Retail Rules r17-19). When a retailer fails, its customers go to a retailer of last resort; five small retailers failed this way in May-July 2022.

expected_shape.heading: What the data should look like
expected_shape.body:
Against GB, an Australian book would show these shapes:
• Prices at five-minute resolution in five regions, with frequent negative prices at midday in spring and rare spikes towards the cap.
• Household electricity use around 3,900-4,900 kWh a year in the 2025-26 default-offer benchmarks, against about 2,700 kWh in GB (the GB figure is from the pack, unverified).
• Two demand peaks: winter evenings in the south and summer air-conditioning in the north. About 74% of homes had some cooling in 2014 (ABS).
• Bills every quarter in arrears, not monthly advances, and no prepayment segment.
• Solar on a large share of homes, with export limits per phase, and a fast-growing battery fleet.
• Annual switching of about 16% of households in the year to June 2025 (Roy Morgan).

live_evidence.heading: Live evidence
live_evidence.body:
WHAT IS SOURCED. The market design and price bounds (AEMC, Wikipedia), the 2025 generation mix and price outcomes (Energy Magazine reporting AEMO and AER), export limits (Amber, SA Power Networks), smart meter shares (AEMC), billing and hardship rules (National Energy Retail Rules v20; ESC Victoria), arrears and disconnections (AER via Energy Magazine), solar and battery counts (Clean Energy Council), switching (Roy Morgan) and housing (ABS Census 2021 and ABS 2014). Every figure and URL is in the research note.
WHAT WAS CHECKED ON 25 OCT 2026. Six fetches were tried to check the pack's unverified items. The Australian regulators' and tax office's sites refused or timed out, so none of the pack's unverified items could be confirmed or corrected; all stay open and are marked unverified below. Wikipedia's market article agrees that half-hourly averaging ended in October 2021 and that the price floor is minus A$1,000/MWh.
WHAT THE GB BUILD DOES, READ FROM CODE AND NOT RUN. The demand model already carries a cooling term on a 22°C base. Everything else here assumes GB: 48 settlement periods a day in about ten modules, a single national price, monthly direct debit and prepayment, a supplier-wide price cap and a deemed contract on move-in.

residuals.body: Twelve things are missing. (1) City heating and cooling degree days. (2) Heating, cooking and heat-pump shares newer than 2014. (3) The settlement revision timetable and how accumulation meters are profiled. (4) The rule text for disconnection timing, life support, cooling-off, transfer and deemed contracts. (5) Current market shares (the latest is 2019). (6) Credit support and how bad debt is treated. (7) Standing against market offers outside Victoria. (8) The network share of the bill. (9) The tax and levy breakdown, including whether GST is 10% on energy. (10) Meter data granularity by meter type. (11) Feed-in tariff levels. headline.heading: The claim, in one sentence
headline.body: Belgium's weather and wholesale market are close enough to GB's that the demand and price engines transfer, but its supplier rules differ at the root: three regional rulebooks, no default price cap, monthly advances with an annual true-up, 15-minute settlement, and a drop procedure that hands a non-paying household to the network operator as social supplier.

plain.heading: In plain terms
plain.body:
Belgium splits energy powers. The federal level runs the transmission system, the wholesale market, nuclear policy, VAT and a social tariff. The three regions, Flanders, Wallonia and Brussels, each license suppliers, set network tariffs, run smart meters and write their own debt and disconnection rules. A Belgian world is three rulebooks in one federal shell.
There is no default price cap. Most household electricity contracts are variable, about 75%, and spot-indexed products make up about 46% of electricity and 48% of gas contracts (CREG study F3188, March 2026). Households pay monthly advance invoices and then an annual true-up bill.
The largest difference is debt. In Flanders a supplier that has followed the reminder and notice steps may end the contract, and the network operator, Fluvius, then supplies the household as social supplier, using a prepaid function on the digital meter. Debts to the former supplier stay with that supplier. In Wallonia and Brussels the network operators play the same part. The costs they cannot recover are carried in network tariffs, so the worst credit risk leaves the competitive supplier's book.

theory.heading: How it works
theory.body:
SETTLEMENT. Electricity settles in 15-minute periods and gas hourly. Continuously metered points are allocated on their own quarter-hour data; index-read points are split with synthetic or real load profiles, a climate correction and a residue factor. Allocation is monthly and reconciliation is the basis for final settlement, with a compensation step that spreads residual error across all suppliers in proportion (MIG6 reconciliation method, via the Flemish regulator). The central clearing house, Atrias, went live from 1 November 2021 for more than 9.6 million access points.
NETWORK CHARGES BY PEAK. Since 1 January 2023 Flemish households pay network charges mainly on capacity: the average of the last twelve monthly peaks, each the highest quarter-hour of its month, with a 2.5 kW minimum. A 4 kW average peak cost about €161.60 a year before VAT in 2023 (Test-Aankoop). EV charging, heat pump running and kettle timing change the bill directly.
METERS. The network operator owns and runs the meters, not the supplier. Fluvius had installed 4.40 million electricity and gas digital meters by the end of February 2025, in nearly seven in ten Flemish connections. Wallonia and Brussels are slower.
SOLAR. Net metering ended in Flanders in 2021 and Brussels in November 2021; Walloon systems from before 2024 keep it to 31 December 2030. Owners still on analogue meters pay a prosumer tariff per kVA or kWe of inverter.
SOCIAL TARIFF AND WINTER. A federal social tariff, set quarterly by the federal regulator, reached 9.7% of electricity and 10% of gas customers in 2020, with allocation more than 90% automatic. Each region bans winter disconnection on its own dates: Wallonia 1 November to 15 March, Brussels 1 October to 31 March, Flanders from 1 December to 1 March or 1 April (the sources conflict).

expected_shape.heading: What the data should look like
expected_shape.body:
Against GB, a Belgian book would show these shapes:
• Heating degree days of about 2,340-2,770 a year in 2020-24 (Eurostat), and negligible cooling, about 12 cooling degree days in 2024.
• Comparison households of 3,500 kWh electricity and 17,000 kWh gas a year (CREG), with only about 57% of electricity points also having gas.
• Oil supplying about a third of residential building heat (IEA 2022).
• Monthly advances with an annual true-up bill, not monthly direct debits on smart reads.
• Concentrated regional markets: the top three suppliers held 73.9% of Flemish, 80.2% of Walloon and 92.2% of Brussels electricity in September 2025.
• Non-paying customers leaving the supplier's book for the network operator, rather than staying as debt.

live_evidence.heading: Live evidence
live_evidence.body:
WHAT IS SOURCED. The structure and regulators (joint regulators' market report 2024), the generation mix (Elia 2024; Connaissance des Énergies for 2025), the Flemish capacity tariff (Solar Magazine, Test-Aankoop), access points and distribution volumes (joint report 2024), supplier counts, concentration and product mix (CREG F3188, March 2026), settlement (MIG6 reconciliation method), smart meters (Solar Magazine, Test-Achats), the social tariff and energy poverty (IEA 2022, VVSG, Chamber papers), winter rules (regional sources) and the drop procedure (Vlaanderen.be, Selectra, Brugel 2024). Every figure and URL is in the research note.
WHAT WAS CHECKED ON 25 OCT 2026. Heating degree days were corrected from the pack's remembered 2,600-2,900 a year to 2,339-2,771 for 2020-24 from Eurostat's own series; the series has no UK values after 2019, so the GB comparison stays open. The federal regulator's page says the social tariff is set every three months from the most advantageous market prices; the pack's 'lowest commercial tariff' and its funding by a federal levy are not stated there and stay unverified. The 6% VAT rate could not be reached and stays unverified.
WHAT THE GB BUILD DOES, READ FROM CODE AND NOT RUN. It settles in 48 half-hours a day, bills monthly direct debits against a credit balance, keeps every debtor on the supplier's book, has no capacity-based network charge, and sends a new occupant to the supplier on deemed terms.
