headline.heading: The claim, in one sentence
headline.body: France transfers the GB build's physics but not its market: 55.8% of residential electricity sites were on a regulated tariff that only EDF and local distributors may sell at the end of 2025, every home subscribes to a power limit that its Linky meter enforces, 37% of homes heat with electricity, and households are settled on profiles, not their own half-hours.

plain.heading: In plain terms
plain.body:
France had 35.02 million residential electricity sites at the end of 2025. 19.54 million (55.8%) were on the regulated tariff, which only EDF and the local distributors may sell. Alternative suppliers held 31.8% of sites (energy regulator CRE, Q4 2025 observatory). Market offers are commonly priced as the regulated tariff minus a percentage, so the regulated tariff is the price anchor.
Every home chooses a subscribed power, in 3 kVA steps from 3 to 36 kVA. It sets the standing charge, and the meter trips if the home draws more. The network operator also sets each home's off-peak hours, and from November 2025 is moving about 11 million homes to a new timetable with three daytime hours, zone by zone to the end of 2027.
Electricity heats 37.2% of main residences, including 5.1% with heat pumps, against 35.8% on mains gas (SDES, 2020). National demand rises about 2,400 MW for each degree of cold in winter, and about 400 MW per degree at the summer afternoon peak.
Households pay monthly instalments on estimated use with an annual true-up. There is no prepayment market (unverified). A non-paying household's supply can be reduced rather than cut, and nobody may cut a main residence from 1 November to 31 March.

theory.heading: How it works
theory.body:
THE REGULATED TARIFF. The regulator proposes it and the government decides. It is built from a published cost stack: energy bought evenly over 24 months in forward products, capacity, balancing, retail costs (18.11 €/MWh for households, of which energy-saving certificates 9.80 €/MWh), a 2.5% margin, catch-up for past error, the network tariff and taxes. It changed −15% in February 2025 and −0.83% in February 2026, and +2.5% was proposed for August 2026 (CRE).
NUCLEAR REVENUE. The old regulated access to nuclear power ended on 31 December 2025. Since 1 January 2026 the state takes 50% of EDF's nuclear revenue above 78 €/MWh and 90% above 110 €/MWh and returns it to every consumer as a bill line. At 2026 forward prices it pays nothing (EDF; derived).
SETTLEMENT. The distributor rebuilds each site's consumption at 30-minute resolution and allocates it to the balance responsible party each supplier names. Households are profiled: 29 profiles in four families, about 90% of sites on dynamic profiles updated at least weekly. Imbalance settles at 15 minutes since January 2025. Runs go from two weeks to 14 months after delivery (Sia Partners, 2020; CRE).
METERS AND DATA. 37.3 million Linky meters were installed by 31 August 2024. Daily readings flow by default; the half-hourly load curve needs consent, and only about 30% of meters have it on (CRE, February 2026). The distributor operates the meters; there is no central data body.
DEBT. From 14 days after the due date the supplier writes; after 15 more days and a second letter at least 20 days ahead, it may reduce power or cut off; social services are told five days in. There were more than 1.2 million debt interventions in 2025, 79% more than in 2019; power reductions grew 3.5-fold since 2019 while cut-offs fell 49%. A means-tested chèque énergie of 48-277 € reaches about 5.6 million households.

expected_shape.heading: What the data should look like
expected_shape.body:
Against GB, a French book would show these shapes:
• A large regulated-tariff base that drifts down slowly, from 19.54 million sites at end-2025 to 19.37 million by end-March 2026.
• Household electricity use around the regulator's 4.5 MWh reference, against about 2.7 MWh in GB (the GB figure is unverified), with electrically heated homes far higher.
• Strong winter electricity sensitivity, about 2,400 MW per degree, and a 2025 peak of 88 GW (RTE).
• Heating degree days of about 2,040-2,410 a year in 2020-24 on Eurostat's basis, and 63-116 cooling degree days in 2022-24.
• Quarterly switching of 2.78% for electricity and 3.6% for gas in Q4 2025.
• Debt handled by power reduction rather than prepayment, and no disconnections of main residences in winter.

live_evidence.heading: Live evidence
live_evidence.body:
WHAT IS SOURCED. Generation and demand (RTE Bilan électrique 2025), the regulated tariff, its cost stack and its changes (CRE deliberations and press releases, 2025-26), market shares and switching (CRE Q4 2025 observatory), the nuclear revenue scheme (EDF), housing, tenure and heating energy (SDES, INSEE), Linky and its consent rate (Connaissance des Énergies; Selectra reporting CRE), settlement profiling (Sia Partners), debt procedure and interventions (decree 2008-780; Connaissance des Énergies), the chèque énergie and fuel poverty (SDES). Every figure and URL is in the research note.
WHAT WAS CHECKED ON 25 OCT 2026. Eurostat's heating degree days for France, 2,036-2,413 in 2020-24, sit inside the pack's 2,000-3,000 range on France's own 17°C basis. The Linky consent figure of about 30% was re-read in the CRE's February 2026 wording. The end of the 5.5% VAT rate on the standing charge was confirmed for gas only (20% on both parts since 1 August 2025); the electricity leg stays unverified. Tempo's red-day count could not be reached.
WHAT THE GB BUILD DOES, READ FROM CODE AND NOT RUN. It has no per-home power limit, no per-home off-peak calendar, no regulated competitor price, settles on 48 half-hours a day, and sends a new occupant to the supplier on deemed terms. Its demand model already carries a cooling term on a 22°C base.

headline.heading: The claim, in one sentence
headline.body: Germany's household market runs on a different chassis from GB's: no regulator-set price cap, a local default supplier whose basic-supply tariff takes about a fifth of household consumption, monthly advance payments trued up once a year, smart meters in about 6% of metering points, and fifteen-minute settlement, so the GB build's physics and price replay would transfer but its billing, tariff, settlement and debt machinery would largely need rebuilding.

plain.heading: In plain terms
plain.body:
A German household pays an estimated monthly advance (Abschlag) and gets one true-up bill a year after an annual meter reading. There is no prepayment to speak of: 11,985 basic-supply homes in 2024 (Bundesnetzagentur monitoring report 2025).
In each network area the supplier with the most household customers is the default supplier. Anyone without a contract, including a new occupant, falls into its basic-supply tariff. That tariff is not capped by a regulator; it is only open to civil-law fairness review (section 36 of the Energy Industry Act).
Taxes and levies were 32% of a new-customer household price of 39.6 ct/kWh in 2025, with VAT at 19% (BDEW price analysis, Oct 2025).
When a household does not pay, the supplier instructs the network operator to disconnect. Network operators carried out 239,269 electricity disconnections in 2024 (Bundesnetzagentur monitoring report 2025). GB has no counterpart at that scale.
Switching is high: about 14% of households switched electricity supplier in 2024 and about 17-18% switched gas (same report).

theory.heading: How it works
theory.body:
MARKET. One bidding zone shared with Luxembourg. Day-ahead trades in 15-minute products since October 2025. The gas hub is Trading Hub Europe, formed in October 2021. Renewables were 55.9% of public net generation in 2025; lignite and hard coal still produced about 94 TWh, and the last three nuclear plants closed on 15 April 2023 (Fraunhofer ISE, Jan 2026).
NETWORK. Four transmission operators and 819 distribution operators answered the regulator's 2025 survey. Since 1 January 2024, heat pumps, wallboxes and batteries above 4.2 kW are 'controllable': the network operator may dim them to 4.2 kW, and the household gets a network-fee reduction in one of three forms (section 14a of the Energy Industry Act).
METERS. A separate meter operator, by default the network operator, owns the meter. At 30 June 2026 there were 3.17 million smart metering systems, 5.9% of 54.1 million metering points (Bundesnetzagentur, Sep 2026). Smart metering is mandatory above 6,000 kWh a year, for controllable devices and for generation above 7 kW.
SETTLEMENT. Most households are settled on standard load profiles that spread an annual volume across quarter-hours. Measured quarter-hour settlement for smart-metered homes began on 6 June 2025. Each network operator aggregates the data for its area.
DEBT. Basic-supply disconnection needs arrears of at least 100 euros, a reminder, a written threat, four weeks' wait and three working days' notice, and is barred where disproportionate (section 19 of the basic-supply regulation, read through a secondary source). The old supplier keeps the debt; nothing follows the customer to a new supplier.

expected_shape.heading: What the data should look like
expected_shape.body:
If the GB build were re-pointed at Germany, a credible German world would show:
• A gentler heating need than often assumed: Germany's heating degree days were 2,583 in 2024 against the UK's 2,812, and 2,580-3,130 over 2020-2025 (Eurostat). Cooling degree days were about 19 a year.
• A heating stock with gas 56.1%, heating oil 17.2%, district heating 15.5% and heat pumps 4.5% of dwellings (BDEW, 2025).
• Smaller households: 40.8 million at 2.02 people, 41.6% living alone (Destatis microcensus 2024).
• One bill a year that can move a household's finances sharply, instead of a monthly direct debit.
• Mass prosumers: 5.71 million PV systems, 2.4 million home batteries and 1.22 million balcony PV units (strom-report, 2026).
• Disconnection as a routine collections outcome: 4.6 million threats, 981,000 orders and 239,269 cuts in 2024.

live_evidence.heading: Live evidence
live_evidence.body:
WHAT IS SOURCED. The advisor's evidence pack, kept as the research note, cites the Bundesnetzagentur monitoring report 2025, BDEW price and heating-stock analyses, Fraunhofer ISE's 2025 generation figures, Destatis and Eurostat. On 25 October 2026 the drafting pass confirmed the 2023 price brakes (40 ct/kWh electricity and 12 ct/kWh gas on 80% of reference use, ended 31 December 2023, federal government page), the nuclear closure date, the smart-meter mandatory groups (Bundesnetzagentur metering page) and Eurostat's degree days. It corrected two items: Germany's heating degree days (about 2,600-2,900, not about 3,000) and the household smart-meter price cap, which the regulator's page gives as 30 euros a year for an intelligent metering system up to 6,000 kWh, not 20.
WHAT THE SIMULATION DOES. Nothing: this page is knowledge only. The director ruled on 25 October 2026 that other markets are for understanding how transferable the GB build is, not for building.

residuals.heading: Where our picture is still weak
residuals.body: The pack carried 70 unverified items; most are GB comparison figures and statute details that could not be fetched. Still missing: the statute texts for basic supply and billing, the reconciliation timeline for volume differences, air-conditioning and cooking-fuel shares, the payment-method mix, supplier concentration, a count of 2021-22 supplier failures, gas disconnection threats, dynamic-tariff uptake and the installed heat-pump base.

scope_delta.body: It does not rate the build component by component on the page itself; the research note keeps the advisor's transferability ratings and the lists of new world and supplier features a German build would need. It does not cover language, business customers or the district-heating market, and it changes no priority in the GB build.

headline.heading: The claim, in one sentence
headline.body: Italy differs from GB at the connection itself: a household contracts a power level, typically 3 kW, that its network-owned smart meter enforces and can cut to 15% for arrears, so the GB build's weather engine and debt principles would carry over but its connection model, zonal fifteen-minute prices, bimonthly reading-based billing, auctioned default service and arrears-follow-the-customer rule would all be new.

plain.heading: In plain terms
plain.body:
An Italian household chooses a contracted power, most often 3 kW, in steps of 0.5 kW up to 6 kW. The meter allows about 10% headroom and briefly cuts supply above it. Each kilowatt costs about 26 euros a year (ARERA consumer guide).
There is no prepayment meter. When a household does not pay, the supplier sends a formal notice, then the network operator limits the meter to 15% of its power for 15 days, then suspends supply. Customers on life-support equipment can never be disconnected (ARERA TIMOE rules, via luce-gas.it).
Regulated default prices ended for non-vulnerable households in 2024. Those who had not chosen a supplier were moved to a service whose suppliers were chosen by auction in 26 areas (ARERA 95/2025). Vulnerable households stay on a regulated tariff.
Free-market offers cost more than the regulated tariff in every consumption class in 2025 (ARERA annual report 2025), the reverse of the usual GB expectation that a fixed deal beats the default.
Switching is very high: 20.8% of household electricity customers switched in 2025 and 18.8% for gas (same report).

theory.heading: How it works
theory.body:
CLIMATE. Heating is regulated by law through six climate zones, A to F, each with permitted heating dates and maximum hours a day, and a 20 degree (plus or minus 2) indoor limit while heating runs (DPR 412/93). July 2026 set a monthly demand record of 32.5 TWh, with peak demand about 58 GW credited to air conditioning (Terna, reported).
MARKET. The day-ahead market is zonal, and final customers have been settled on zonal prices since 1 January 2025, with a PUN Index and a perequation mechanism easing the transition. Gas import dependence was 94.3% in 2025 (ARERA annual report 2025).
METERS. Network operators own and run second-generation smart meters, about 32.7 million in service at end 2023. They record 15-minute load curves for all customers, can limit power remotely, and offer an in-home data channel (ARERA smart-metering page).
BILLING. Domestic electricity is billed every two months on readings, and a bill must be issued within 45 days of the last day billed, with automatic indemnities of 6 to 60 euros if late (ARERA 463/16).
DEBT. The supplier holds the debt and starts the process; the network operator limits and suspends on its request. If a customer switches leaving arrears, the old supplier can have a charge (the CMOR) added to the new supplier's bill 6 to 12 months later. GB has no equivalent.
SOCIAL SUPPORT. The social bonus has been automatic since 2021, triggered by the household's means-test declaration; it reached 4.3 million households in 2025.

expected_shape.heading: What the data should look like
expected_shape.body:
A credible Italian world would show:
• Much less heating and much more cooling than GB: heating degree days 1,678-2,025 and cooling degree days 224-365 over 2020-2025, against the UK's 2,710-2,961 and under 7 (Eurostat).
• A summer electricity peak as well as a winter one; 56.0% of households had at least one cooling system in 2024 (ISTAT).
• More domestic electricity points (just over 30.5 million) than households (24.1 million), because of second homes.
• Typical use near GB's: ARERA's typical customer uses 2,700 kWh at 3 kW and 1,100 Smc of gas, about 11,600 kWh.
• 15.4% of homes heated by a building-level system, where the gas customer is the building, not the household (ISTAT 2024).
• Power limitation, not prepayment, as the first step in collections.

live_evidence.heading: Live evidence
live_evidence.body:
WHAT IS SOURCED. The advisor's evidence pack, kept as the research note, cites ARERA's annual report and decisions, ISTAT's 2021 and 2024 household energy surveys, Terna via the press, GME and the TIMOE rules. On 25 October 2026 the drafting pass confirmed Italy's heating and cooling degree days against Eurostat and replaced the pack's estimate with the published range. The ARERA and tax-agency pages for the gas VAT split and the GME page for the bidding-zone list could not be read, so those items stay unverified.
WHAT THE SIMULATION DOES. Nothing: this page is knowledge only. The director ruled on 25 October 2026 that other markets are for understanding how transferable the GB build is, not for building.

residuals.body: Still missing: tenure and building-age shares, the number of distribution operators and the largest one's share, the household network tariff components, the exact time-band hours, whether households are settled on measured intervals or profiles, the payment-method mix, disconnection and limitation volumes, how bad debt is socialised, how the arrears charge is sized, supplier licensing capital rules, cooking-fuel and cooling shares of use, home batteries, energy-community numbers, and the home-move rules from ARERA's own text.

scope_delta.body: It does not rate the build component by component on the page itself; the research note keeps the advisor's transferability ratings and the lists of new world and supplier features an Italian build would need. It does not cover language, business customers or the islands' separate systems, and it changes no priority in the GB build.

headline.heading: The claim, in one sentence
headline.body: Japan shares GB's thirty-minute settlement and has near-universal network-owned smart meters, so the GB build's clock and meter-data feed would transfer well, but its room-by-room air-conditioner heating, near-universal cooling, nine area prices, incumbent-only regulated tariff on about 65% of incumbent contracts, monthly actual-read billing, disconnection around day 51 and the absence of any default supplier for a new occupant would all be new.

plain.heading: In plain terms
plain.body:
Most Japanese homes heat a room at a time, with the same air conditioner that cools it; air conditioners were the main heating for 39% of households in 2023 (Ministry of the Environment). Kerosene heaters matter in the north. Average use in 2023 was 3,911 kWh of electricity and only 177 cubic metres of city gas, so gas is mainly for cooking and hot water.
In Tokyo Electric's area the household picks a breaker size from 10 to 60 amps, and the breaker sets its monthly basic charge.
Retail opened fully in April 2016, but incumbents still hold 44.4 million regulated contracts against 23.7 million free ones in their own areas: about 65% regulated (Electricity and Gas Market Surveillance Commission, 2025). Only the incumbent may sell the regulated tariff.
Bills are monthly on actual reads, with three price tiers, a monthly fuel-cost adjustment and a renewable surcharge of 4.18 yen/kWh in 2026. The government has paid per-kWh subsidies through bills in most winters and summers since 2023.
A household that does not pay is typically cut off around day 51 after the read, with no winter ban.
A new occupant must choose a retailer; with a smart meter and no contract, the breaker gives no power.

theory.heading: How it works
theory.body:
MARKET. The power exchange trades 48 half-hour products a day in a single-price auction and splits into nine area prices. The country is split between 50 Hz and 60 Hz grids joined by 2.1 GW of frequency converters. Gas is imported LNG, with no traded hub like GB's. In winter 2020-21 an LNG shortage and cold weather drove the exchange to 251 yen/kWh, and new entrants on fixed low tariffs failed.
NETWORK AND METERS. Ten general transmission and distribution operators, legally unbundled in April 2020, each combine the transmission and distribution roles and own the meters. Smart meters reached 99.9% coverage, about 81.5 million, by March 2025, reporting at 30 minutes; the next generation, from 2025 to 2034, records 5-minute data.
SETTLEMENT. Every balancing group submits 30-minute plans. The imbalance price cap of 200 yen/kWh rises to 300 from 2026.
SWITCHING. Switching runs through a central system: at least one business day plus two calendar days after matching for a smart-metered site. There is no debt objection, but the incumbent may refuse a new contract until arrears are paid.
LAST RESORT. The network operators provide last-resort supply only to high- and extra-high-voltage customers. A household whose retailer exits falls back on the incumbent's regulated tariff; 32% of exiting retailers in 2022 left some customers with no contract (METI).

expected_shape.heading: What the data should look like
expected_shape.body:
A credible Japanese world would show:
• A climate from subarctic to subtropical: January means of -3.2 degrees in Sapporo, 5.4 in Tokyo and 17.3 in Naha (JMA 1991-2020 normals), and real cooling degree days where GB has almost none.
• Twice GB's scale: 56.2 million households (Statistics Bureau, 2023), 44.9% of occupied dwellings flats.
• Electricity-led homes with little wet central heating, and a summer price peak: the day-ahead price reached 37.51 yen/kWh on 29 July 2025.
• About 3 million residential PV systems, 1.65 million of them off the feed-in tariff by 2023, and 1.14 million home batteries.
• A low switching rate of about 3.5% a year against meter count (derived from the surveillance commission's figures).

live_evidence.heading: Live evidence
live_evidence.body:
WHAT IS SOURCED. The advisor's evidence pack, kept as the research note, cites the Electricity and Gas Market Surveillance Commission, METI and ANRE, the national grid coordinator's switching rules, the Ministry of the Environment's household energy survey, the Statistics Bureau, JMA climate normals, JEPX and battery and PV industry bodies. Its own unverified items are mostly GB comparisons. On 25 October 2026 the drafting pass tried to confirm the 2020 census household size and could not read the census PDF, so it stays unverified; Eurostat publishes no Japanese degree days, so the pack's area-weighted series stays unmatched to GB's.
WHAT THE SIMULATION DOES. Nothing: this page is knowledge only. The director ruled on 25 October 2026 that other markets are for understanding how transferable the GB build is, not for building.

residuals.heading: Where our picture is still weak
residuals.body: Still missing: a population-weighted heating and cooling degree-day series, a current official air-conditioner ownership figure (the official one is from 2009 and the recent third-party figures conflict), the national cooking-fuel and all-electric shares, the total of low-voltage contracts, network tariff components, settlement and reconciliation timelines, LPG households, the payment mix, arrears data, owner-occupation, the low-voltage bad-debt treatment, whether arrears information is shared, and how many households fell back to regulated tariffs in 2022.

scope_delta.body: It does not rate the build component by component on the page itself; the research note keeps the advisor's transferability ratings and the lists of new world and supplier features a Japanese build would need. It does not cover the LPG and kerosene retail markets, language or business customers, and it changes no priority in the GB build.

meta.wall_placement: Public-reality commons only, and knowledge only. Every figure comes from a published source named in the research note, read on 25 Oct 2026. headline.heading: The claim, in one sentence
headline.body: Spain's household market inverts several GB defaults: the regulated price is a dynamic hourly-shaped tariff that only incumbents' regulated arms may sell, not a ceiling over everyone's tariffs; every home subscribes to a power level under a compulsory time-of-use network tariff; smart meters owned by the network have been universal since 2018; and bills are paid after an actual reading, so there is no prepayment and no direct-debit credit balance.

plain.heading: In plain terms
plain.body:
A Spanish household contracts a power level. In 2024, 43.2% contracted 4-6 kW and 30.3% up to 3 kW (CNMC household panel, Q2 2024). Since June 2021 every supply under 15 kW sits on one network tariff with three energy periods on weekdays and two contracted powers.
The regulated electricity price (PVPC) follows the wholesale market hour by hour, now blended with futures: 25% in 2024, 40% in 2025, 55% in 2026 (Royal Decree 446/2023). Only the incumbents' regulated suppliers may offer it. About 8.2 million households, 27.4%, were on it at end 2025.
Bills use actual meter reads and are paid after the bill, usually by direct debit. There is no prepayment meter and no fixed monthly payment building a credit balance.
VAT on electricity is 21%, plus a 5.11% electricity tax; both were cut during the crisis and have been restored.
When a household does not pay, the supplier sends a formal demand and can ask the network operator to cut supply two months later. Households on the social bonus instead drop to a 3.5 kW minimum supply for six months, during which they cannot be cut (MITECO).
Switching was 23.9% for electricity and 19% for gas in 2024 (CNMC).

theory.heading: How it works
theory.body:
MARKET. Spain shares one bidding zone with Portugal. Day-ahead moved to 15-minute products on 1 October 2025. Renewables were 56% of 2024 generation and nuclear 19%, with the nuclear plants due to close between 2027 and 2035. Solar growth pushed prices to zero or below for 797 hours in 2025.
REGIME BREAK. From May 2022 to the end of 2023 the 'Iberian exception' capped the gas price used in power bids at 40 euros/MWh, rising 5 euros a month to 70, with gas plants compensated (IEA policy page). Replayed 2022-23 Iberian prices are not a pure market series.
METERS. By end 2018 about 27 million meters up to 15 kW were read remotely, 99.14% integrated (CNMC). The network operator owns them; most record hourly and quarter-hour values are interpolated.
SETTLEMENT. The grid operator runs five settlement runs, from about one month to about eleven months after delivery. The supplier is the settled party and lodges guarantees with the grid and market operators.
DEBT. The supplier holds the debt and the network operator cuts supply at its request, bearing the cost of cutting and reconnecting. Debt does not follow the customer [unverified]. A ban on cutting basic supplies to vulnerable households runs to 31 December 2026.
SELF-CONSUMPTION. 683,719 self-consumers by 2024. Under simplified compensation the supplier credits exports on each monthly bill, never above that period's consumption, so there is no cash payout (Royal Decree 244/2019).

expected_shape.heading: What the data should look like
expected_shape.body:
A credible Spanish world would show:
• Half GB's heating need and real cooling: heating degree days 1,497-1,730 and cooling degree days 236-387 over 2020-2025, against the UK's 2,710-2,961 and under 7 (Eurostat).
• Two demand peaks, winter evening and summer afternoon.
• Gas as optional: only about 40% of households on mains gas, and a gas-heated home using about 7,921 kWh a year, 57% of it for heating (SPAHOUSEC II).
• Two-thirds of people in flats, and 73.3% owner-occupation (INE, 2025).
• 19.3 million households averaging 2.50 people (INE, 2024).
• Every bill from an actual read, and no credit balances on the book.

live_evidence.heading: Live evidence
live_evidence.body:
WHAT IS SOURCED. The advisor's evidence pack, kept as the research note, cites CNMC's retail and household-panel reports, MITECO's disconnection and licensing pages, INE, REE, the IEA, and the 2026 consumer-protection decree through law-firm summaries. On 25 October 2026 the drafting pass checked Spain's degree days against Eurostat: cooling degree days 383 in 2022 and 304 in 2024 match the pack; Eurostat's current release gives 1,537 heating degree days for 2022, not 1,478.
WHAT THE SIMULATION DOES. Nothing: this page is knowledge only. The director ruled on 25 October 2026 that other markets are for understanding how transferable the GB build is, not for building.

residuals.body: Still missing: air-conditioning ownership after 2015, typical household electricity use by climate zone, the 2025 generation mix, the distribution-operator count and phase split, the billing period and fallback-supply rules under the 2026 decree, home-move default rules, how the social bonus is funded and capped, how exports are valued, butane penetration, the payment-method mix and arrears after 2018.

headline.heading: The claim, in one sentence
headline.body: An English household car drove about 7,100 miles in 2025, but the spread is wide (a third of cars under 5,000 miles, one in eight over 12,000) and it follows the driver, not the fuel; and about 72% of household vehicles are kept off the street overnight, which is what decides whether an electric car can be charged at home.

plain.heading: In plain terms
plain.body:
Most cars do modest mileage. In England in 2025 the average household car did about 7,100 miles a year, and about 56% of cars did between 5,000 and 12,000. A small group of drivers does a great deal more: company cars, people who drive for work, and people in the countryside.
Electric and diesel cars show higher mileage than petrol cars, but that is mostly because high-mileage drivers choose them, not because the fuel makes people drive further. So a simulated home has to start with the people in it, draw how far they drive, and only then decide what car they own.
Where the car sleeps matters as much. About seven in ten household vehicles are parked on a driveway or in a garage overnight, but in the cities far fewer are. Nine in ten electric car drivers can charge at home; the rest rely on public chargers, which cost several times more per mile and add nothing to the home's electricity bill.

theory.heading: How it works
theory.body:
MILEAGE. Annual mileage per car is heavily skewed. The National Travel Survey puts the 2025 England mean at 7,100 miles (petrol 6,200, diesel 8,000, battery electric 9,400). MOT readings for 2025 give medians of about 4,900 miles for petrol and 6,900 for diesel, with upper quartiles of 7,800 and 10,400, so a lognormal fits the shape. Mileage falls as a car ages: a 13-year-old car does about half what a car under three does.
WHO DRIVES. The drivers who do the most miles are men in their fifties, people in work, people on high incomes, company car holders and people in rural areas. Company cars did about 2.4 times the miles of private cars when last measured (2010) and are about 3.7% of household cars in 2025. Commuting is about 2,200 of the average car's 7,100 miles, business 500 and everything else 4,500.
WHEN. Car traffic is lowest in January (about 15% below an average month) and highest in early summer (about 6% above), and it peaks on Fridays and falls away on Sundays.
PARKING. In 2024, 64% of household vehicles in England were parked on private property overnight and 9% in a garage; 25% were on the street. In the most rural areas only about 8% are on the street; in towns near a major city about 29% are. Among battery electric car drivers, 87% have off-street parking and 89% can charge at home; about one in nine rely on public charging alone.

expected_shape.heading: What the data should look like
expected_shape.body:
A simulated population of drivers and homes should show these shapes against the record:
• Mean household car mileage near 7,100 a year in 2024-25 (7,900 in 2016, 5,400 in the 2021 lockdown year).
• About 31% of cars under 5,000 miles, about 56% at 5,000-12,000, about 13% over 12,000.
• Battery electric cars driving more than petrol cars because of who owns them, not because of the fuel.
• About 22% of English households with no car, 44% with one and 34% with two or more, and car ownership rising steeply with income.
• About 72% of vehicles kept off-street overnight, far fewer in conurbations than in villages.
• Close to nine in ten electric car owners able to charge at home.
• January traffic about 15% below the average month and early-summer traffic about 6% above it.
These are population checks. None of them is a target for any one home.

live_evidence.heading: Live evidence
live_evidence.body:
WHAT IS SOURCED. Mileage by fuel, purpose and ownership, and the mileage-band distribution, from DfT's National Travel Survey tables, fetched on 25 Oct 2026. Overnight parking by area type, from the same survey. Monthly and day-of-week traffic indices, from DfT's road traffic tables. Charging access among electric car drivers, from DfT's EV driver tracker, years 1 and 2. Car ownership by income and area, commuting and working from home, from the survey and the Census. Every figure and link is in docs/market_research/who_drives_how_far_and_where_they_park_2026-10-25.md.
WHAT THE SIMULATION DOES, READ FROM CODE AND NOT RUN. No household is drawn with a driver's mileage. Every simulated home starts without an electric car; one can arrive later by a yearly probability, and only in a detached or semi-detached house, which is how the world stands in for a driveway. On the main demand path an electric car adds a fixed 2,143 kWh a year, from 7,500 miles at 3.5 miles per kWh, for every owner alike. A second path draws daily miles around a fixed 20-mile mean. Neither path knows who drives, so neither can reproduce the spread on this page.

residuals.heading: Where our picture is still weak
residuals.body: Seven things are missing. (1) How one driver's mileage persists from year to year: no source publishes it, so any persistence the world uses is a named design choice. (2) The share of all homes, not vehicles, with off-street parking: the 65% (7% in Westminster, 84% in Flintshire) comes from the RAC Foundation's Standing Still report (2021), whose per-local-authority PDF is the lookup to use; corrected 25 Oct on the advisor's second read, which read the report itself. (3) Off-street parking by dwelling type and tenure from the English Housing Survey: not found in a published table. (4) Driver miles by age, sex, employment and income together: the tables exist but were not read. (5) How often drivers make trips over 100 miles: half of electric car drivers make one about once a month or less, and nothing finer. (6) Working from home after 2021 beyond the Census week. (7) Company car mileage since 2010.

scope_delta.heading: What this page does not yet establish
scope_delta.body: It does not say which car a driver owns or how much energy it uses; that is on the page about which cars households run. It does not cost charging against petrol or diesel; that is on the EV charging page. It does not grade the simulated world against these bands; that waits for the world to draw drivers at all.

meta.title: Which cars households run, and how much energy each one really uses
meta.subtitle: Britain's 31 million household cars are mostly petrol and diesel, about ten years old, and use more fuel on the road than their official figures say. An electric car's energy per mile depends on its model, the day's temperature and how it is charged. None of that is a single number.
meta.wall_placement: Public-reality commons only. Every figure is from a published source: DfT vehicle licensing statistics, SMMT parc and registration figures, EV Database model specifications, winter range studies (Recurrent, Geotab, What Car?), ADAC charging-loss tests, ICCT and Fraunhofer plug-in hybrid studies, and the European Commission's on-board fuel consumption data. Most are UK-wide rather than GB, and several winter studies are from North America; both are said where they matter. The statements about the simulation are about its code, read and not run.

claim_freshness.source: DfT vehicle licensing statistics 2024 and Q3 2025, VEH0103 (fetched 25 Oct 2026); SMMT Motorparc 2025 and 2025 registrations; EV Database consumption and battery cheatsheets; Recurrent (2025), Geotab, What Car? 2024 winter test; ADAC charging-loss tests (2026); ICCT/Fraunhofer PHEV fact sheet (2022); Fraunhofer/Oeko-Institut OBFCM analysis (2025); European Commission OBFCM release (2024); ICCT Lab-to-Road. Full list with links in docs/market_research/which_cars_households_run_and_what_they_use_2026-10-25.md
claim_freshness.note: One of the six distribution packs for the personalised asset world (director, 25 Oct 2026: vehicle energy is derived from 'miles driven and car type', never looked up as a percentage).

headline.heading: The claim, in one sentence
headline.body: An electric car's energy is its model's base efficiency (about 220 to 310 Wh a mile for mainstream models) times a temperature penalty of roughly 1.2 to 1.3 in a British winter, plus 5-7% lost charging on a wallbox or 13-24% on a three-pin plug; and the petrol or diesel car it replaces uses 8% to 39% more fuel on the road than its official figure, depending on its age.

plain.heading: In plain terms
plain.body:
Most household cars in Britain are petrol (about 58%) or diesel (about 32%). Fully electric cars were about 5% of cars at the end of 2025, and more than half of them belong to companies rather than households. The typical car is about ten years old, and nearly half are older than that.
An electric car does not use a fixed amount of electricity per mile. A small efficient model uses about a third less than a large SUV. In cold weather the same car uses more, because the battery is less efficient and the cabin needs heating: about a fifth more at 10 degrees and over a quarter more at freezing. A car with a heat pump loses less. Charging also wastes some energy: very little on a wallbox, but up to a quarter on a three-pin socket.
A plug-in hybrid is only as electric as its owner's charging habits. Private owners drive about half their miles on electricity; company car drivers, whose fuel is often paid for, about one mile in seven.
The car an electric car replaces matters for any saving. Older petrol and diesel cars use 8% to 39% more fuel than their official figure, and post-2018 cars about 17% to 21% more.

theory.heading: How it works
theory.body:
THE PARC. DfT counted 34.5 million licensed UK cars in September 2025, 1.63 million of them zero-emission (4.7%); company keepers hold 10.4% of all cars but 55.4% of zero-emission ones, so the private electric share is lower than the headline. Northern Ireland is about 3% of UK cars. The 2025 parc is a third superminis, a quarter lower-medium and a fifth SUVs; the average car is 9.7 years old.
ELECTRIC ENERGY PER MILE. EV Database gives real-world consumption by model, averaging 303 Wh a mile across all listed models, 218-309 for mainstream ones. Range studies give the cold penalty: 78% of ideal range at 0 degrees and 70% at minus 7 (Recurrent, 2025), which is 1.28 and 1.43 times the energy per mile; a heat pump recovers about 8-10 points at 0 degrees. A UK winter test at 6-11 degrees found real range 21-38% below the official figure. ADAC's 2026 tests put AC charging losses at 5-7% on an 11 kW wallbox and 13-24% on a 2.3 kW socket.
PLUG-IN HYBRIDS. Measured electric driving is 45-49% for private owners and 11-15% for company cars (ICCT and Fraunhofer, 2022), against 70-85% assumed in the official test. Across nearly a million European PHEVs the energy-based electric share was 31% (2025).
PETROL AND DIESEL ON THE ROAD. The gap between official and real fuel use grew from 8% in 2001 to 39% in 2015-17 under the old NEDC test, then reset under WLTP to about 17% for diesel and 21% for petrol (2022 registrations). So real consumption of 2010-17 cars fell much less than their official figures suggest.

expected_shape.heading: What the data should look like
expected_shape.body:
A simulated fleet should show these shapes against the record:
• A private electric share at end-2025 below the 4.9% all-keeper share, because companies hold more than half of zero-emission cars.
• Mean car age about 9.7-10 years, with about 46% older than ten.
• Superminis, lower-medium cars and SUVs together about 77% of the parc.
• A year-round electric efficiency of about 3.0-3.5 miles per kWh at the battery, or 2.8-3.3 at the wall.
• January electricity per mile about 1.2-1.3 times July's.
• A plug-in hybrid fleet driving about 31% of its energy electrically overall, and 45-49% among private keepers.
• Petrol and diesel cars using 8-39% more fuel than their official figures, by registration year.
These are population checks, never targets for one home.

live_evidence.heading: Live evidence
live_evidence.body:
WHAT IS SOURCED. Licensed car counts and fuel shares, from DfT and SMMT; segment mix and top models, from SMMT; per-model consumption and usable battery, from EV Database; the cold-weather penalty, from three range studies and one UK winter test; charging losses, from ADAC; plug-in hybrid electric shares, from ICCT, Fraunhofer and the EU's on-board meter data; the petrol and diesel real-world gap, from ICCT and the European Commission. Every figure and link is in docs/market_research/which_cars_households_run_and_what_they_use_2026-10-25.md.
WHAT THE SIMULATION DOES, READ FROM CODE AND NOT RUN. The world has no car model, no battery size by model, no temperature effect and no plug-in hybrid: an electric car is one flag, with a fixed 3.5 miles per kWh, a fixed 55 kWh battery and a fixed 90% charging efficiency. No household has a petrol or diesel car to compare against. Home charger power is drawn from 3.7, 7 or 22 kW, and 22 kW is beyond what most cars accept on AC and what a single-phase home supplies.

residuals.heading: Where our picture is still weak
residuals.body: Six things are missing. (1) DfT's fuel-by-year and make-and-model tables for 2016-2025 were not read, so the parc mix before 2024 is interpolated. (2) A sales- or parc-weighted distribution of battery size and onboard charger limit: it needs those tables joined to model specifications. (3) Whether EV Database's consumption is measured at the battery or the wall: its page does not say. (4) A GB split of plug-in hybrid electric share by keeper type: only European figures exist. (5) What fuel an electric car replaces: no GB source. (6) Most cold-weather evidence is North American, and GB winters sit at 0-10 degrees, where the evidence is thinnest.

scope_delta.heading: What this page does not yet establish
scope_delta.body: It does not say how far a household drives; that is on the page about who drives how far. It does not cost electric miles against petrol and diesel; that is on the EV charging page. It does not grade the simulated fleet, which does not yet hold cars at all.

meta.title: Charging an electric car at home: when it happens, what it costs, and what it saves against petrol and diesel
meta.subtitle: Where a car is charged decides almost everything about its cost. At home on an off-peak tariff an electric mile costs a few pence; on a public rapid charger it can cost more than petrol. A supplier sees only the home part, and has to work out the rest or ask.
meta.wall_placement: Public-reality commons only. Every figure is from a published source: SMMT and Zapmap market statistics, DfT's EV driver tracker, the Electric Nation trial, Zapmap's charging price index, Ofgem's price cap, HMRC's VAT notice, DESNZ greenhouse gas factors, the Smart Charge Points Regulations 2021, and published EV-detection studies. Tariff and product figures are from the suppliers' own pages. The worked cost table is our arithmetic on those figures and is marked as such. The statements about the simulation and the company are about their code, read and not run.

claim_freshness.source: SMMT and Zapmap market statistics (to Sep 2026); DfT EV driver behaviours and attitudes tracker, years 1 and 2 (Ipsos, 2025 and 30 Jul 2026); Electric Nation; Zapmap Charging Price Index (Sep 2026); Ofgem price cap Oct-Dec 2026; HMRC VAT Notice 701/19 (zero rate 1 Oct 2026-31 Mar 2027); DESNZ GHG conversion factors 2026; Smart Charge Points Regulations 2021; Otago/Vector, SINTEF and Bidgely detection studies; Ofgem TDCV decision (May 2026). Full list with links in docs/market_research/ev_charging_and_the_saving_against_petrol_and_diesel_2026-10-25.md
claim_freshness.note: From the advice-roadmap evidence pack (director, 25 Oct 2026: 'Home charge versus venue. Cost and carbon savings versus petrol and diesel for different mileages. Then the actual charging and usage patterns'). The EV, solar and batteries page covers what the supplier gains and loses; this page covers the car's own charging and the household's saving.

headline.heading: The claim, in one sentence
headline.body: A home-charged electric car adds roughly 1,750 to 3,500 kWh a year to a household's electricity, plugs in two or three times a week but draws power for only about an hour and a half each time, and at October 2026 prices costs about 2p a mile on an off-peak EV tariff and 9p on the capped standard rate, against about 18p for petrol, while a driver who can only use public rapid chargers pays about 24p.

plain.heading: In plain terms
plain.body:
About a quarter of new cars sold in 2026 are fully electric. Nine in ten electric car drivers can charge at home, and most of their charging happens there, usually overnight once or twice a week.
What a mile costs depends on where the car is charged. Home electricity at the capped rate in late 2026 is about 26p a kWh; an off-peak EV tariff is 7-9p; a public rapid charger is about 79p, and public charging carries 20% VAT where home electricity carries none until March 2027. So the same car can cost a quarter of what petrol costs per mile, or more than petrol.
For the household's bill, an electric car is the biggest single addition most homes ever make: 2,000-3,000 kWh a year is about as much again as a typical home uses. A smart tariff can move nearly all of it to the night, which saves the household about £350-510 a year against charging at the standard rate.
A supplier sees only what passes through the home meter. It can spot a car charging in half-hourly data with good accuracy after a year of readings, but not the car's mileage, its public charging, or what the household drove before. To prove a saving, it has to ask.

theory.heading: How it works
theory.body:
UPTAKE. Battery electric cars were 0.7% of new cars in 2018, 16.6% in 2022, 23.4% in 2025 and 26.2% in January-September 2026, under a ZEV mandate rising from 22% in 2024 to 80% in 2030. Plug-in cars were 8.2% of the parc at the end of 2025.
WHERE. DfT's tracker found 89% of battery electric drivers can charge at home and about 11% rely on public charging (year 2, 2026). In its two-week diary, drivers charged about 4.3 times at home and 1.3 times in public.
WHEN. In the Electric Nation trial, unmanaged plug-in peaked at 5-7pm on weekdays; cars stayed plugged in about 12 hours but drew power for about 1.5, and battery cars plugged in 2-3 times a week with 55-70% charge left. Since 2022 new home chargers must default to charging outside 8-11am and 4-10pm on weekdays, add a random delay of up to ten minutes, and be able to respond to demand-side signals. On a smart EV tariff about 97% of charging is scheduled by the supplier or its platform.
COST. Pence per mile is price per kWh times kWh per mile. At 0.33 kWh a mile at the meter: 26.32p standard gives 8.7p; 7p off-peak gives 2.3p; a rapid charger at 79p (0.30 kWh a mile, 20% VAT included) gives 23.7p. Petrol at 173.8p a litre and 45 mpg is 17.6p a mile.
CARBON. On DESNZ's 2026 average grid factor (0.144 kg a kWh with losses), an electric mile emits about 0.05 kg against about 0.21 kg for petrol; the marginal factor of the plant that meets extra demand is higher, and is not yet sourced here.
SEEING IT. With a year of half-hourly reads a detection model found home chargers with precision 0.87 and recall 0.81 (0.91 and 0.96 for fast chargers); with a month, 0.55 and 0.62. Immersion heaters, storage heaters, heat pumps and electric showers confound it.

expected_shape.heading: What the data should look like
expected_shape.body:
A simulated book of electric car households should show these shapes against the record:
• Home charging of about 1,750-3,500 kWh a year per car, central about 2,300, spread by mileage rather than fixed.
• About nine in ten owners charging at home and about one in ten never doing so.
• Plug-in 2-3 times a week for battery cars; sessions of about 10 kWh on average.
• Unmanaged charging starting 5-7pm on weekdays; on a smart tariff, almost all of it overnight.
• January charging per mile about 1.2-1.3 times July's.
• A household on an off-peak EV tariff saving about £350-510 a year against the standard rate at 2,000-2,640 kWh.
• A public-only driver paying more per mile than a petrol driver at 2026 prices.
These are population checks, never targets for one home.

live_evidence.heading: Live evidence
live_evidence.body:
WHAT IS SOURCED. Registration and parc shares, from SMMT and Zapmap; charging access and frequency, from DfT's EV tracker; charging patterns, from the Electric Nation trial; public prices, from Zapmap's index; the price cap and the VAT zero rate, from Ofgem and HMRC; carbon factors, from DESNZ; charger defaults, from the 2021 regulations; detection accuracy, from three published studies. Every figure and link is in docs/market_research/ev_charging_and_the_saving_against_petrol_and_diesel_2026-10-25.md.
WHAT THE SIMULATION AND THE COMPANY DO, READ FROM CODE AND NOT RUN. In the world, no household starts with an electric car; one arrives by a fixed yearly probability, only in a detached or semi-detached house, so no owner ever charges in public. On the main path each car adds the same 2,143 kWh a year, 90% of it overnight. The company assumes a different fixed 2,500 kWh, learns of a car only when the customer asks for an EV tariff, and does not try to detect one from meter data. Explore shows one electric car household whose use rose 8% (99 to 108 kWh a month); both of the world's paths should add about 180 kWh a month, so that figure is not yet explained.

residuals.heading: Where our picture is still weak
residuals.body: Seven things are missing. (1) The share of charging energy by place (home, work, public, rapid): the diary gives charge counts, not kWh. (2) Street-level diversity of charging (after diversity maximum demand) from the distribution networks. (3) How much a time-of-use tariff without automation moves charging. (4) Any GB study of detecting a car in half-hourly data, and none tests heat pump or storage heater confusion. (5) Total cost of ownership: servicing, insurance and depreciation. (6) The marginal and time-of-day carbon factor of charging. (7) Real-world diesel mpg for the counterfactual: the 55 mpg in the worked table is unsourced, so the diesel column is indicative only.

scope_delta.heading: What this page does not yet establish
scope_delta.body: It does not say how far each household drives or which car it owns; those have their own pages. It does not value an EV tariff to the supplier; the EV, solar and batteries page covers that. It does not grade the simulated world's charging, which draws neither mileage nor public charging yet. The worked cost table is an illustration at one set of prices, not a saving to promise any household.

meta.title: How a gas boiler and its controls turn into the gas a home uses
meta.subtitle: Most GB homes heat with a condensing gas boiler that seldom condenses, because it runs too hot. Thermostats, timers and smart controls save far less in the field than on the box, and a supplier sees almost none of it in the meter data.
meta.wall_placement: Public-reality commons only. Every figure comes from a published source and was checked against it on 25 October 2026 where the advisor's pack could not fetch it; figures still unconfirmed are named as gaps. The statements about the simulation and the company are about their code and are marked as read, not run.

claim_freshness.source: EFUS 2017 heating patterns; GASTEC for EST in-situ condensing boiler trial (2009); BRE S10TP-12 seasonal efficiency of condensing boilers (SAP 10); BEIS Boiler Plus factsheet (2018); Nesta Money Saving Boiler Challenge evidence and flow-temperature RCT (2022); BIT evaluation of the Nest thermostat (2017); BRE and UWE/BSRIA reviews of heating controls for BEIS (2017); Ofgem cap summaries (Jul and Oct 2026)
claim_freshness.note: Drafted from the advisor's cited evidence pack of 25 Oct 2026 for the advice roadmap and the personalised asset world. Its headline bands are calibration for the whole population, never targets for one home.

headline.heading: The claim, in one sentence
headline.body: A GB condensing gas boiler measured in homes delivers about 82-85% of its fuel as heat, not the 90%+ on its label, mainly because most are set to a 70-80°C flow that keeps the return water above the roughly 55°C at which it condenses; and the controls households are sold save between nothing and about 6% when measured, against claims of up to 31%.

plain.heading: In plain terms
plain.body:
About 22 million UK homes heat with gas central heating; about six in ten of them have a combi boiler that heats water on demand, and the rest feed a hot-water cylinder. Since 2005 new gas boilers have had to be condensing, and since April 2018 in England they must be rated at least 92%.
In practice they do worse. A field trial of 43 boilers measured 85% for regular boilers (about 80% once pipe and cylinder losses are counted) and 82.5% for combis, and recommended scaling rated figures by 0.95. The reason is the water temperature: a boiler only recovers the heat in its flue gas when the water coming back to it is below about 55°C, and most are set to send water out at 70-80°C.
Turning the flow temperature down from 80°C to 60°C saved about 9% of gas in a test house. In a randomised trial of 7,000 homes, advice to do it saved 1.4%, which was not statistically significant. The same gap runs through every control: smart thermostats were measured at about 5% and possibly nothing; timer-based proportional control at 0-0.5%. A typical home heats for about 7 hours on a weekday at a median setting of 20°C.

theory.heading: How it works
theory.body:
EFFICIENCY. Seasonal efficiency falls as the design flow and return temperatures rise. SAP 10's modelled figures for a modulating boiler without compensation are 87.1% at 80/60°C, 89.3% at 55/47°C, 92.8% at 45/39°C and 95.3% at 35/30°C; ideal weather compensation adds 1-4 points. The industry standard label overweights part load, which implies a 34.5°C return; hourly analysis supports nearer 48°C, so the label overstates.
HOT WATER. A combi heats water only when a tap opens. Its hot-water efficiency was measured at about 73%, and very short draws are much worse. A cylinder loses heat standing still: in the field trial as little as half the heat put into a cylinder reached the taps, about 900 kWh a year of losses.
CONTROLS. A room thermostat ends a heating period when the room is warm; a timer sets when periods start; radiator valves cap individual rooms; weather or load compensation lowers the flow temperature when less heat is needed, which is what lets a boiler condense. Boiler Plus requires a timer and room thermostat with every new boiler and, for combis, one of flue gas heat recovery, weather compensation, load compensation or smart controls.
IN THE METER DATA. Daily gas is close to a baseload (hot water and cooking, about 7 kWh a day on a typical home) plus a slope times heating degree-days. The slope mixes the building's heat loss, the boiler's efficiency and the setpoint, so a setpoint cut and a flow-temperature cut look the same in daily data.

expected_shape.heading: What the data should look like
expected_shape.body:
A credible simulated population of gas-heated homes should show these shapes against the record:
• About 62% combi boilers and 38% regular or system boilers (2017).
• A median thermostat setting of 20°C with an interquartile range of 19-21°C before 2022, and a weekday median of 7 hours heating (5-10), 8 hours at weekends.
• Of homes that heat at set times, 58% twice a day, 23% once and 19% three or more times on a weekday.
• 87% with a room thermostat, 79% with radiator valves on most radiators, 46% mainly using a timer.
• In-use boiler efficiency for space heating around 82-85%, and combi hot water around 73%.
• Space heating about 77%, hot water about 21% and cooking about 2% of household gas.
• Typical gas use of 11,500 kWh a year before July 2026 and 9,500 kWh after, as Ofgem's medium figure.

live_evidence.heading: Live evidence
live_evidence.body:
WHAT IS SOURCED. Boiler stock and types, measured and modelled efficiency, the flow-temperature evidence, control prevalence, the controls evidence and the advice economics are in the research note behind this page, with every link and the outcome of each check made on 25 October 2026.
WHAT THE WORLD DOES, READ FROM CODE AND NOT RUN. Each home's boiler converts heat to gas at a fixed efficiency by boiler age (90% new, 86% mid, 80% old), with no dependence on flow temperature and no notion of whether it condenses. The new-boiler figure is above every measured in-home value. Thermostat settings are drawn around 20°C with a spread matching the 19-21°C range, adjusted by EPC band. Heating hours follow the published split by daytime presence. Combi hot water is converted at 80%, above the 73% measured.
WHAT THE COMPANY DOES, READ FROM CODE AND NOT RUN. It assumes one seasonal boiler efficiency of 85% for every home, which the field trial supports. Its customer advice text still says a smart thermostat 'could save 10-15%', which the measured evidence does not support.

residuals.heading: Where our picture is still weak
residuals.body: Twelve things are weak. (1) No authoritative GB boiler lifetime distribution. (2) No GB stock by boiler age band, and the survey's combination and condensing-combination categories need defining. (3) No independent GB measurement of savings from power flushing, filters, balancing or bleeding; only an industry 'up to 15%'. (4) No published efficiency gain from servicing. (5) No winter trial of flow-temperature advice. (6) No independent GB field trial of weather compensation. (7) No validated way to infer flow temperature, efficiency, setpoint or schedule from meter data alone. (8) No GB distribution of radiator oversizing. (9) Rebound after controls advice is not quantified. (10) The energy advice body's pound figures run two to three times the arithmetic at the 2026 cap, and their basis is not stated. (11) The 2005 condensing mandate's month and the jurisdictions it covered come from a secondary source. (12) The 70% efficiency cut-off for the old G band is unconfirmed.

scope_delta.heading: What this page does not yet establish
scope_delta.body: It does not grade the simulated world's gas against these bands; that is owed. It does not explain how a household chooses its schedule and setpoint or what health floors bind advice, which are on the heating behaviour page, nor heat pumps and insulation, which have their own page. It does not cover oil, LPG or electric storage heating.

meta.title: How households heat their homes, how warm they actually are, and the temperatures advice must never go below
meta.subtitle: Households set about 20°C and live about a degree below it, heat for about seven hours a day, and a tenth of homes sit below 16°C in the coldest weeks. After 2022 the average setting fell a degree and the cut fell hardest on those who could least afford it. Any advice to save heat has to respect a health floor first.

Every figure comes from a published source and was checked against it on 25 October 2026 where the advisor's pack could not fetch it; figures still unconfirmed are named as gaps. The statements about the simulation and the company are about their code and are marked as read, not run.

claim_freshness.source: EFUS 2017 heating patterns and thermal comfort reports; Huebner et al. 2013 and 2015 (CaRB living-room temperatures); SERL panel (Hanmer and Zapata-Webborn 2023; Zapata-Webborn et al. 2024; SERL statistical report vol. 2); DESNZ domestic hot-water use from connected devices (2024); EST hot water measurement (2008) and BRE's analysis; PHE minimum home temperature thresholds (2014); WHO Housing and Health Guidelines (2018); NICE NG6; HSE legionella guidance; Ofgem SLC 27A decision (2020)
claim_freshness.note: Drafted from the advisor's cited evidence pack of 25 Oct 2026 for the advice roadmap and the personalised asset world. Its headline bands are calibration for the whole population, never targets for one home.

headline.heading: The claim, in one sentence
headline.body: English households set a median thermostat of 20°C (interquartile range 19-21°C), run their living rooms about a degree cooler than that, and heat for a median of 7 hours on a weekday; in winter 2022/23 the mean setting fell from 20.2°C to 19.2°C and the share set below 18°C more than doubled to 15%, concentrated in homes that felt fuel poor; and published health guidance puts 18°C as the floor no advice should push a living room below.

plain.heading: In plain terms
plain.body:
Most homes heat at set times: twice a day is the commonest pattern (a short morning burst and a longer evening block), and about a quarter of centrally heated homes heat irregularly. A home with a pensioner in it heats for about 9 hours, a single person under 60 for about 5.5. The heating season lasts about 5.7 months, typically October to April.
What homes actually reach differs from what they set. In February 2018 the average living room was 18.5°C and the average bedroom 18.1°C; the coldest tenth of homes were below 15.7°C and 15.0°C. Homes in the worst energy bands were about 2°C colder than the best. About 12% of households say their living room is uncomfortably cold often or always, and that rises to 23% among the fuel poor.
When prices rose in 2022, households turned down: the median household cut gas by about 11%, about 3.8% for each degree off the thermostat. The households that cut most were twice as likely to say they could not keep warm. Health guidance says 18°C carries minimal risk for most people, that older and ill people need slightly more, and that risk rises again below 16°C. Ofgem sets no temperature rule; a supplier's duty is to spot customers who ration themselves and support them.

theory.heading: How it works
theory.body:
SETPOINT AND ACHIEVED TEMPERATURE. A thermostat ends heating at its setting; the room then falls back during the off periods. Measured living rooms run about 1°C below the stated setting while heating is on, and further below it in leaky homes, where the system cannot keep up or the household sets lower. The survey measures the sum of those two effects, not the split.
SCHEDULES. Among homes that heat regularly, 58% heat twice on a weekday, 23% once and 19% three or more times. Once-a-day heating is long: its median period is about 14.5 hours, mostly starting at wake-up. Whole-day flat temperature profiles appear in about 31% of measured homes, far more than the 4-6% who report heating all day or all year, because low setbacks and long hours look flat too.
HOT WATER. A household draws a fixed amount plus an amount per person: about 36 + 25 litres per person per day in the national model, a median of 90 litres in 45,000 combi homes with a range of 19-222. Small taps are 85% of draws but showers and baths are 45% of the volume. About 37% of showers are electric, 47% in fuel-poor homes, and their energy is on the electricity meter.
HEALTH FLOORS. WHO proposes 18°C as a safe indoor temperature, more for older people, children and the chronically ill. PHE: 18°C poses minimal risk to sedentary, clothed people; over-65s and the ill benefit from slightly more and 18°C overnight; infants' rooms 16-20°C; below 16°C blood-pressure risk rises sharply. Stored hot water must be kept at 60°C or above against legionella, and water above 44°C at the tap is a scald risk for vulnerable people.

expected_shape.heading: What the data should look like
expected_shape.body:
A credible simulated population should show these shapes against the record:
• Thermostat settings with a median of 20°C and interquartile range 19-21°C before 2022; a mean near 19.2°C in 2023 with about 15% below 18°C.
• A February living room near 18.5°C and bedroom near 18.1°C, with the coldest tenth below 15.7°C and 15.0°C.
• EPC F and G living rooms about 1.5-2°C colder than A to D.
• Weekday heating of median 7 hours (5-10), and at any half-hour no more than about 74% of homes heating.
• At least half of homes using no heating gas overnight.
• Median gas use of about 26 kWh a day, or about 9,500 kWh a year, in 2023.
• Hot water about 19% of heat demand, with a median of 90 litres a day in combi homes.
• About 12% of households reporting an uncomfortably cold living room.

live_evidence.heading: Live evidence
live_evidence.body:
WHAT IS SOURCED. Setpoints, measured temperatures by home and household type, schedules, season, flow temperature, controls, room-by-room heating, hot water volumes and events, the 2022/23 response, and the health guidance, with every link and the outcome of each check made on 25 October 2026, are in the research note behind this page.
WHAT THE WORLD DOES, READ FROM CODE AND NOT RUN. Each home draws a thermostat setting around 20°C with a spread matching the published range, offset by its energy band so leaky homes run colder, and a schedule whose length follows the published hours by daytime presence. Once-a-day homes are given a single evening block of the same 6-8.5 hours, whereas the survey's once-a-day period is a median of about 14.5 hours. There is no irregular or all-day pattern for boiler homes. Hot water follows the national fixed-plus-per-person volume, anchored to the measured combi median. The 2022 response scales each home's whole gas use by a published per-household elasticity rather than lowering its thermostat. No home has an electric shower.
WHAT THE COMPANY DOES, READ FROM CODE AND NOT RUN. Its one zero-cost heating advice, a one-degree turn-down, is refused wherever the home's band would put it below 18°C, and refused when the band is unknown. It carries no higher floor for older, ill or registered-vulnerable households, no rule against advising homes already rationing, and no hot-water floor.

residuals.heading: Where our picture is still weak
residuals.body: Nine things are weak. (1) No published overall distribution of measured winter temperatures, only deciles and group means. (2) The share of homes heated round the clock is uncertain: reported about 4-6%, a flat measured profile about 31%. (3) The flow-temperature distribution rests on one trade-journal report of telemetry; the primary paper was not found. (4) Hot water by occupancy has only a mean line with very wide scatter. (5) No GB figures for coping behaviours such as extra clothing, heating one room or going to bed early. (6) No measurement of how radiator valves are actually set. (7) Electric showers and immersion use are missing from the connected-device data. (8) Whether lowering a combi's hot-water setting is low legionella risk is not a formal HSE position. (9) Access to the SERL in-home temperature data for calibration is unconfirmed.

scope_delta.heading: What this page does not yet establish
scope_delta.body: It does not grade the simulated world's temperatures or schedules against these bands; that is owed. It does not set the health floors as policy; that is a design decision for the advice build, which this page informs. It covers how boilers convert gas to heat only in passing; that is on the boilers page.

meta.title: What a heat pump and insulation really deliver in GB homes, and what they cost and save
meta.subtitle: A typical air-source heat pump in a GB home delivers about 2.8 units of heat per unit of electricity over a year, close to break-even with gas at today's prices but cutting carbon by two thirds or more. Insulation saves less than modelled: about 3% for a loft top-up, 7-10% for cavity walls and 16-19% for solid walls, as measured.

claim_freshness.source: DESNZ heat pump deployment statistics and Household Energy Efficiency detailed release (Mar 2026); Ofgem Boiler Upgrade Scheme annual reports (2024-25, 2025-26); Energy Systems Catapult Electrification of Heat results; DECC RHPP final report (2016); NEED reports 2018-2026; English Housing Survey 2023-24; Ofgem cap announcement for Oct-Dec 2026; Octopus Cosy tariff page; EST insulation and controls advice pages; SMETER competition summary; Sunikka-Blank and Galvin (2012)
