headline.heading: The claim, in one sentence
headline.body: Air-source heat pumps installed under the Electrification of Heat trial achieved a median seasonal performance factor of 2.80 (2.44 on the coldest days), which at the October 2026 price cap is almost exactly the 2.77 at which they break even on unit cost against an 84%-efficient gas boiler, while cutting the home's heating carbon by about 67-85%; and the government's measured median gas savings from insulation are about 2-4% for lofts, 7-10% for cavity walls and 16-19% for solid walls.

plain.heading: In plain terms
plain.body:
Heat pumps are still rare. About 53,000 were fitted to existing homes in 2025, almost all air-source, against a target of over 450,000 a year by 2030. The government grant is £7,500, and the average air-source quote under it was about £13,400 before the grant.
How well they work depends on the house and the installation more than on the weather. The best recent field trial found a median of 2.80 units of heat per unit of electricity over a year, up from about 2.44 a decade earlier; enthusiasts who monitor their own systems report nearer 3.9. At today's capped prices electricity costs 3.3 times as much per unit as gas, so a typical heat pump saves little on running cost alone. Most of the money comes from a heat-pump tariff with cheap periods and from dropping the gas standing charge. The carbon saving is large at every efficiency.
Insulation has been widely fitted: 71% of cavity-walled homes and 67% of lofts have it, but only 11% of solid-walled homes. Measured savings are smaller than models predict, and loft savings fade by about a tenth over five years. At today's gas price a cavity wall saves about £80 a year for an installation costing about £2,200.

theory.heading: How it works
theory.body:
PERFORMANCE. A heat pump's seasonal performance factor is the heat it delivers over a year divided by the electricity it uses, measured at a stated boundary. It falls as the flow temperature it must deliver rises, so emitter size and weather compensation matter. In the Electrification of Heat trial the mean flow temperature was 38°C, detached homes did best, and much of the spread was unexplained. Hot water is a harder duty: the earlier RHPP trial measured 2.31 for hot water against 2.74 for space heating, and immersion heaters used about 12% of electricity, more at poor sites.
RUNNING COST. Break-even on unit cost is the price ratio times the boiler's efficiency: 3.30 times 0.84 gives 2.77 at the October 2026 cap (electricity 26.32p with VAT at zero until March 2027, gas 7.97p). On Octopus's Cosy tariff the cheap periods are 51% below the day rate, which lowers break-even to about 2.2 on an assumed 60/40 split.
INSULATION. The government's NEED analysis compares the weather-corrected gas of homes that had a measure fitted with a comparison group that did not, and reports the median. Combined measures save less than the sum of their parts: cavity plus loft about 9%, solid wall plus loft about 14%.
IN THE METER DATA. A heat pump shows as gas falling to zero (or to cooking) from a date, with electricity rising by roughly the heat demand divided by the performance factor, strongly in winter. Insulation shows as a lower slope of gas against heating degree-days with the baseload unchanged. A 3% change is below what one home's year-to-year noise reveals, so loft savings can only be shown across many homes.

expected_shape.heading: What the data should look like
expected_shape.body:
A credible simulated population and its heat-pump homes should show these shapes against the record:
• Air-source seasonal performance with a median near 2.8 (interquartile range about 2.5-3.1), near 2.4 on the coldest days, and hot water near 2.3.
• Hybrid systems near 2.4.
• 71% of cavity-walled homes insulated, 67% of lofts at 125 mm or more, 11% of solid walls.
• EPC registrations in England in 2025 about 15% A-B, 48% C, 30% D, 5% E and 1.5% F-G; about half the whole stock A-C.
• Air-source 97-99% of new installs, about 52-53 thousand retrofits in 2025.
• Measured median gas savings of about 2-4% for a loft, 7-10% for a cavity wall and 16-19% for a solid wall, with loft savings about a tenth lower by year five.

live_evidence.heading: Live evidence
live_evidence.body:
WHAT IS SOURCED. Deployment, grant levels and costs, field performance, prices, carbon factors, insulation coverage, measured savings and their decay, and the economics, with every link and the outcome of each check made on 25 October 2026, are in the research note behind this page.
WHAT THE WORLD DOES, READ FROM CODE AND NOT RUN. In the half-hourly physics a heat pump's efficiency rises with outdoor temperature, from 2.2 at -2°C to 3.5 at 7°C. That matches the measured coldest-day figure but sits above the measured 2.8 annual median at mild winter temperatures. A ground-source pump is the same curve scaled up by a quarter. In the settlement path every heat-pump home adds a fixed 5,500 kWh a year whatever its size or fabric, about twice what a typical home would use at the measured performance.
WHAT THE COMPANY DOES, READ FROM CODE AND NOT RUN. It assumes a seasonal performance of 2.8, which matches the trial. Its offer book prices insulation at £6,000 removing 30% of the fabric's heat loss, above every measured median, and a heat pump at £12,000 with a performance of 2.6.

residuals.heading: Where our picture is still weak
residuals.body: Twelve things are weak. (1) The heat-pump install series 2016-2021 on one counting basis. (2) The Electrification of Heat final report, so no final distribution or metered hot-water figure. (3) The self-monitored systems' published paper, so no cycling, defrost or flow-temperature curve. (4) Modelled insulation savings to set against the measured ones. (5) Recent kWh medians, which NEED shows only in charts. (6) The measured rise in electricity after a heat pump. (7) Cosy's absolute rates, which vary by region; only the windows and ratios are confirmed. (8) Winter and marginal carbon intensity of heat-pump load. (9) Heat-pump pathways from the CCC and NESO. (10) Savings-measurement thresholds. (11) Installation time and the replacement-boiler cost. (12) Heat-loss estimation from meter data is unvalidated for heat-pump and A/B homes.

scope_delta.heading: What this page does not yet establish
scope_delta.body: It does not grade the world's heat pumps or insulation against these bands; that is owed. It does not set the advice roadmap's order. How a gas boiler and its controls work is on the boilers page; where a home's carbon sits overall is on the household carbon page; how houses gain measures on their own timeline is on the houses-change page.

meta.title: Solar panels and home batteries: what they generate, what the home keeps, and what the settings are worth
meta.subtitle: A GB rooftop array makes about 800 to 1,100 kWh a year for each kilowatt of panel. A home without a battery uses roughly 40-45% of that itself and exports the rest. A battery's value depends less on its size than on how it is set and which tariff it sits on.
meta.wall_placement: Public-reality commons only. Every figure comes from a published source: DESNZ cost and load-factor statistics, Ofgem's Feed-in Tariff and Smart Export Guarantee reports, BRE's SAP self-use method, peer-reviewed field studies, manufacturer datasheets and trade press marked as such. PVGIS figures are © European Union, JRC. The statements about this project's world and company are about their code and are marked as read, not run.

claim_freshness.source: DESNZ Solar PV cost data (May 2026) and FiT load factor analysis 2024/25; Ofgem FIT annual report SY15 and SEG annual report Year 5; BRE S10TP-07 (SAP 10.2 self-use factor); McKenna et al. 2018 and 2019; Luthander et al. 2015; NREL degradation review; IEA PVPS Task 12; Tesla Powerwall 3 datasheet; PVGIS v5.2 (run 25 Oct 2026); MCS and Solar Power Portal citing DESNZ for battery counts and costs
claim_freshness.note: From the advisor's cited evidence pack of 25 Oct 2026 (advice roadmap). The pack's unverified items were checked at source on the same day: 1 confirmed, 0 corrected, 8 still open. The supplier-side view of the same kit is on the EV, solar and batteries page.

headline.heading: The claim, in one sentence
headline.body: A GB rooftop solar array produces about 800 to 1,100 kWh a year per kilowatt of panel depending on place and orientation, a home without a battery uses about 37-57% of that itself (typically 40-45%), and a battery adds roughly 13-25 percentage points of self-use, so most of a battery's money comes from the tariff it is set to work against, not from the solar.

plain.heading: In plain terms
plain.body:
There are about 2.1 million solar installations in Britain, roughly 41% of them from the Feed-in Tariff years of 2010 to 2019 and most of the rest installed since 2023. A typical older system is 2-4 kW; new ones are about 5 kW. Batteries were rare before 2023 and now come with about one new solar system in six or seven, at a mean of about 8.6 kWh.
A panel only makes power in daylight, mostly in spring and summer, while a home uses most of its power in the evening. So a home keeps less than half of what it generates unless someone is in during the day or a battery stores the surplus. What is not used is exported, and is worth whatever export tariff the household has: from about 1p to 25p a unit in 2026.
A battery can also charge from the grid at night and discharge at the evening peak. On a tariff built for that, the same 5 kWh battery is worth two to three times as much as on a flat export rate. How it is set (mode, reserve, schedule) decides most of what it earns.

theory.heading: How it works
theory.body:
GENERATION. Output is irradiance on the panel's plane times its size times a performance ratio (about 0.77-0.80 measured), less shading, inverter clipping and ageing of about 0.5-0.8% a year. The fleet's median yield ran 806-920 kWh per kW a year in 2011-2025; 2024/25 was the lowest year on record.
SELF-USE. SAP's method gives the monthly share used on site as exp(-C1·(C2·E/D)^C3), where E is generation and D demand, with coefficients that move with usable battery capacity up to 15 kWh. For a 2.5 kW array on a 3,100 kWh home it gives 0.40 without a battery, 0.65 with 5 kWh and 0.86 with 10 kWh. Daytime occupancy moves it more than anything else: at equal generation and demand, from about 20% to about 80%.
BATTERY. Round trip about 89%. The levers are self-consumption mode, timed grid charging to a target, timed export and a reserve floor. On a peak/off-peak import-export tariff one 5 kWh cycle a day is worth roughly £210-330 a year; left in self-consumption mode on a flat export rate it adds about £150-180.
COST. DESNZ's median installed cost for 0-4 kW systems was £1,780 per kW in 2025/26, down from £2,263 in 2023/24 and at a record low in real terms; batteries cost about £590-1,020 per kWh by size. Both are zero-rated for VAT until 31 March 2027.

expected_shape.heading: What the data should look like
expected_shape.body:
A credible simulated population of solar homes should show:
• About 41% of installations from 2010-2019 at 2-4 kW, and a 2023-26 cohort near 5 kW, 60% of it at 0-4 kW.
• Annual yield per kW in the 806-920 range across years, about 35% of it in April-June and about 15% in October-December for a south-facing array.
• Self-use without a battery mostly 37-57%, higher where someone is home in the day.
• Self-use 13-25 points higher with a battery of about 5 kWh.
• Batteries almost absent before 2022, then attached to roughly 15-20% of new solar by 2025, averaging about 8.6 kWh.
• Exports measured, not deemed: homes export 55-63%, more than the Feed-in Tariff's assumed 50%.

live_evidence.heading: Live evidence
live_evidence.body:
WHAT IS SOURCED. Installation counts and the cost series by size band (DESNZ, re-read at source on 25 Oct 2026), Feed-in Tariff and Smart Export Guarantee counts and payments (Ofgem, re-read the same day), SAP's self-use coefficients (BRE, re-read), measured self-use from GB field studies, degradation, lifetimes, battery datasheets and warranty terms, and a PVGIS grid run the same day for seven GB sites. Every figure and URL is in the research note solar_pv_and_home_batteries_2026-10-25.md.
WHAT THE WORLD AND COMPANY DO, READ FROM CODE AND NOT RUN. The world's half-hourly solar output uses one fixed array size for every home, with no orientation, tilt, shading or ageing, and a separate older annual figure. Panel sizes and battery sizes are drawn from flat ranges unchanged across the years. The battery charges only from surplus solar and discharges 4pm-8pm; it never charges from the grid or follows a tariff. The company assumes 50% self-use without a battery, at the top of the measured range, and one export price per year.

residuals.heading: Where our picture is still weak
residuals.body: Eight things are missing. (1) Measured inverter efficiency and real-world battery round trip and standby losses in GB homes. (2) The Feed-in Tariff rate by year of installation, and how often a FiT licensee receives generation readings. (3) How export meters are registered and settled, and what share of solar homes have one. (4) Day-to-day cloud variability and how common shading is. (5) The uplift in self-use from a diverter or an electric car. (6) Marginal carbon factors and the embodied carbon of panels. (7) A GB protocol for proving solar and battery savings. (8) The DESNZ battery cost release itself; its figures were read through trade press.

scope_delta.heading: What this page does not yet establish
scope_delta.body: It does not cover what solar and batteries do to a supplier's margin, export competition between suppliers or EV tariffs; those are on the EV, solar and batteries page. It does not give the distributions of roof orientation, tilt and system size across the fleet; those are on the roofs page. It does not cover connecting the kit to the network or local flexibility payments. It does not grade the simulated world's solar homes against these bands.

meta.title: A roof's solar array: which way it faces, how steep, how big, how old, and the sky above it
meta.subtitle: Two identical panels on two GB roofs can differ in output by half. Facing, tilt, size, age, shade and the local sky each move it, and each can be drawn per home from published data.

Every figure comes from a published source: DESNZ load-factor and cost statistics, Ofgem Feed-in Tariff reports, peer-reviewed fleet studies, the Open Climate Fix uk_pv dataset card (© Open Climate Fix, made possible by Sheffield Solar, CC-BY-4.0, DOI 10.57967/hf/0878), PVGIS (© European Union, JRC; run on 25 Oct 2026, calibration only) and CM SAF SARAH-3 (© EUMETSAT). The statements about this project's world are about its code and are marked as read, not run.

claim_freshness.source: DESNZ Feed-in Tariff load factor analysis 2011/12-2024/25; DESNZ Solar PV cost data (May 2026); Ofgem FIT annual report Year 10; Open Climate Fix uk_pv dataset card; PVGIS v5.2 grid of seven GB sites × eight facings × three tilts (run 25 Oct 2026); Killinger et al. 2018; Dhimish et al.; PEARL PV fleet study; Pfeifroth et al. 2024 (SARAH-3); ENA EVCP and heat pump form v3.3
claim_freshness.note: From the advisor's cited evidence pack of 25 Oct 2026, one of six supplying the personalised asset world. Checked at source the same day: of 6 unverified items, 2 confirmed and 4 still open; three sourced figures corrected (the 2-4 kW share of the OCF sample, and the east/west and north factors).

headline.heading: The claim, in one sentence
headline.body: Across seven GB sites PVGIS gives a south-facing 35° array 886 to 1,145 kWh per kW a year, an east- or west-facing one 0.76 to 0.81 of that and a north-facing one about half, while the real fleet's median has run 806 to 920 kWh per kW a year since 2011, so where a roof faces and where it is matter as much as what is on it.

plain.heading: In plain terms
plain.body:
No two solar roofs are the same. One facing south in Cornwall makes about a third more than the same panels facing south in Manchester, and a fifth more again than the same panels facing east or west. A north-facing roof makes about half. Steepness matters less: anything from about 15° to 50° stays close to the best for its direction.
Size and age matter too. Most systems fitted under the Feed-in Tariff (2010-2019) are 2-4 kW; most fitted since 2023 are 4-6 kW, and about a third of those are on new-build homes, which get smaller arrays. Panels lose about 0.7-0.9% a year, and inverters fail: about a third of them by year 15 in one large survey.
The weather each home sees is available at street scale. A satellite record gives sunshine every half hour on a grid about 4 by 5 km, so neighbouring homes share their sky, and a cloudy afternoon hits a whole street at once.

theory.heading: How it works
theory.body:
ORIENTATION AND TILT. The PVGIS grid run for this page (seven sites from Penzance to Aberdeen, eight facings, three tilts, SARAH-2 satellite weather 2005-2020) gives east or west at 0.81-0.84 of south at 25°, 0.76-0.81 at 35° and 0.73-0.78 at 45°; south-east and south-west 0.92-0.96; north 0.41-0.65. The year-to-year standard deviation is 3.4-4.1% of the annual yield.
WHAT IS NOT PUBLISHED. No GB-wide distribution of which way solar roofs face has been published. The best source is the Open Climate Fix dataset of over 30,000 GB systems, whose metadata gives each system's orientation, tilt and size; its access terms were accepted on 25 Oct 2026 and the metadata has not yet been read. Until it is, the world's orientation shares are a named assumption.
SIZE. The same dataset's card shows 81.5% of its systems at 2-4 kW. DESNZ data for 2025/26 put 60% of new domestic systems at 0-4 kW and 36% at 4-10 kW.
THE MEASURED FLEET. DESNZ's median load factor for Feed-in Tariff solar ran 9.2-10.5% (806-920 kWh per kW) a year from 2011/12 to 2024/25, with the spring quarter near 13.6% and the autumn quarter near 4.7% in 2024/25; the South West ran about 20% above Scotland in 2020/21.
THE SKY. CM SAF SARAH-3 gives half-hourly global and direct irradiance from 1983 to the present on a 0.05° grid, free with attribution, and within about ±2 W/m² of ground stations on average.

expected_shape.heading: What the data should look like
expected_shape.body:
A credible simulated fleet should show:
• Median annual yield per kW in 806-920 in each year, moving with that year's sunshine, about 4% year to year.
• The South West about a fifth above Scotland.
• East- or west-facing homes at about 0.76-0.81 of south-facing ones at the same place and a 35° tilt.
• Older systems at 2-4 kW; systems from 2023 on near 5 kW, with a new-build group near 1-2 kW.
• Output falling about 0.7-0.9% a year with age, and some systems producing nothing for months after an inverter fails.
• Neighbouring homes' output moving together from one half hour to the next.

live_evidence.heading: Live evidence
live_evidence.body:
WHAT IS SOURCED. The Feed-in Tariff fleet's load factors by year, quarter and region (DESNZ, re-read at source 25 Oct 2026), the system-size bins on the Open Climate Fix card (re-read), the DESNZ size split of new installations (re-read), degradation and inverter-failure studies, and a PVGIS grid of 168 runs made on 25 Oct 2026 for calibration only. Every figure and URL is in the research note pv_roofs_orientation_and_yield_2026-10-25.md.
WHAT THE WORLD DOES, READ FROM CODE AND NOT RUN. Which way a roof faces is a label by house type, and every drawn non-flat home is labelled east/west; the label only decides whether a home may install solar and never reaches its output. Output is computed on a flat surface from a clear-sky curve and a daily cloud figure, at a fixed size for every home, with no tilt, shading, ageing or inverter limit.

residuals.heading: Where our picture is still weak
residuals.body: Six things are missing. (1) The GB distribution of roof facing and tilt: in the Open Climate Fix metadata, not yet read. (2) How common east/west split arrays are. (3) How common shading is and how much it costs. (4) How closely cloud moves between nearby homes from day to day. (5) Panel size by house type and region, and battery uptake by region. (6) The share of systems that still work: only a third of Feed-in Tariff solar reported a valid reading in 2024/25, which is a reporting gap, not a failure rate.

scope_delta.heading: What this page does not yet establish
scope_delta.body: It does not cover what a home does with the power (self-use, batteries, export income, cost and carbon); that is on the solar panels and home batteries page. It does not cover connecting an array to the network. It does not grade the simulated world's arrays against these bands. The PVGIS runs are a calibration target and never an input the company reads.

meta.title: Connecting an EV charger, heat pump, solar or battery: the network's rules, the home's own supply and how long it takes
meta.subtitle: Most homes can fit one device and tell the network afterwards. A home on a shared service cable, with a small main fuse, or adding two devices at once has to apply first, and the cost of that is mostly time, not money.

Every figure comes from a published source: the ENA's common EV charger and heat pump form, DESNZ's unlooping research, the Smart Charge Point Regulations 2021, Ofgem decisions, DNO guidance and network studies, with vendor and trade sources marked as such. The statements about this project's world and company are about their code and are marked as read, not run.
