headline.heading: The claim, in one sentence
headline.body: A GB home may fit one EV charger or heat pump and notify its network operator within 28 days only if its supply is not looped, its cut-out rating is known and its maximum demand stays within 60 A per phase, and about 3.9 million homes (11-17%) are on looped services, so for a large minority the real cost of electrifying is weeks to months of waiting, not money.

plain.heading: In plain terms
plain.body:
Every home's electricity comes through a service cable and a main fuse (the cut-out), usually rated 60 to 100 amps on a single phase. Fitting an EV charger or a heat pump adds a big new load. If the home's supply is ordinary, the installer fits it and tells the network operator afterwards. If it is not, the installer must apply first and wait.
The commonest reason to wait is a looped service: one cable shared by two or more homes, often on 1970s and 1980s estates, in terraces and in rural areas. DESNZ estimates about 3.9 million GB homes are on one, and under 1% had been unlooped by January 2025. Unlooping is usually free to the household and takes 3-12 weeks, or six months to a year if a neighbour objects.
Since April 2023 a household rarely pays to reinforce the network for new demand; the exception is a move to three-phase, typically £3,000-7,000. Fitting two devices together, a heat pump and a charger, always means applying first, so the bundle a supplier would like to sell is the slowest to connect.

theory.heading: How it works
theory.body:
THE RULE. The ENA's common form, used by every DNO, lets an installer connect and notify within 28 days only if all hold: one additional device; a known cut-out rating; a metered supply; not a looped service; no safety concern; maximum demand below the cut-out rating and below 13.8 kVA (60 A) per phase, unless CT-metered or load-limited. A heat pump must also stay within 32 A including back-up heaters and be listed for connect and notify. Between 60 and 100 A the DNO should answer within 10 working days. A fail-safe load limiter holding the home at 60 A restores the quick route.
GENERATION. Type-tested solar and batteries up to 16 A per phase (about 3.68 kW single-phase) connect under G98 and notify; above that, G99 requires an application, up to 45 working days; export can be limited by a locked control under G100.
THE STREET. Network design adds a few kilowatts per home for each device after diversity: about 1.5-3 kVA for a gas-heated home, about 6-7 kVA with a heat pump and an unmanaged EV, about 5 kVA if the car charges smartly. Trials found at least 32% of low-voltage networks need intervention at 40-70% EV uptake, and that cars need only about 20% of their plug-in time to charge.
CHARGE POINTS. Since 2021 new home charge points come with default charging hours outside 8am-11am and 4pm-10pm on weekdays, which the owner may change, and a random start delay of up to 10 minutes, extendable to 30.

expected_shape.heading: What the data should look like
expected_shape.body:
A credible simulated world should show:
• About 11-17% of homes on looped services, varying 6-25% by network region.
• Most single-device installs connecting the same day, with a tail of applications, fuse upgrades of up to about 12 weeks and unlooping of up to 6-12 months.
• About a third to a half of heat pump installs needing a supply upgrade.
• Combined heat pump and charger installs always going through an application.
• Almost no reinforcement charged to households after April 2023, except three-phase upgrades at £3,000-7,000.
• Street-level demand rising by a few kVA per home per device, less where charging is managed.

live_evidence.heading: Live evidence
live_evidence.body:
WHAT IS SOURCED. The connect-and-notify conditions (the ENA form, re-read at source on 25 Oct 2026), the looped-service count, cost, timing and DNO practice (DESNZ, re-read), the charge point defaults (the Regulations, re-read), Access SCR charging rules, DNO lead times and upgrade costs, design demand per home, and network studies. Every figure and URL is in the research note network_limits_on_home_electrification_2026-10-25.md.
WHAT THE WORLD AND COMPANY DO, READ FROM CODE AND NOT RUN. Nothing in the world or the company holds a cut-out rating, a supply phase, a looped service or a connection rule, so every EV and heat pump connects instantly. The world draws a quarter of home EV chargers at 22 kW, which needs a three-phase supply most homes do not have.

residuals.heading: Where our picture is still weak
residuals.body: Seven things are missing. (1) The share of GB homes with a three-phase supply, and the spread of main-fuse ratings. (2) A national rate of installs that trigger an upgrade; only Octopus's 45% for its heat pump customers (not re-read at source) and WPD's 'about a third' exist. (3) A count of local substations needing reinforcement by 2030 or 2035. (4) How often home solar or battery applications are export-capped or refused. (5) Electric Nation's per-car peak after diversity. (6) Any right of a network operator to switch off home devices directly. (7) The 2024 and 2026 amendments to the wiring regulations, not read.

scope_delta.heading: What this page does not yet establish
scope_delta.body: It does not cover payments a network operator makes for local flexibility, virtual power plants or the Demand Flexibility Service; those belong to the flexibility page. It does not cover network charges on bills, which are on the regional supply cost page. It does not decide what the simulation builds: the cover steer sets a minimum viable layer (home supply, loop flag, the notify-or-apply rule, published delays) and optional layers above it, each with a trigger.

meta.title: Who else pays for a household's flexibility: aggregators, rival traders and the local network
meta.subtitle: A household's EV, heat pump or battery can earn money from more than its supplier: an aggregator can sell it to the grid operator, a rival can trade it in the wholesale market, and the local network pays for it in a few places. Each stream is real, most are small, and one of them can be taken from the supplier without asking.
meta.wall_placement: Public-reality commons only. Every figure comes from a published source: Elexon modifications and settlement data, NESO and DNO procurement reports, Ofgem decisions and aggregators' published offers. The statements about the company are about its code and are marked as read, not run. Which rival aggregator holds which meter is never visible to a real supplier until compensation arrives, and the page says so.

claim_freshness.source: Elexon (P415, P510 IWA slides, BL01, Market Facilitator rules), NESO flexibility onboarding and BM relaxation (Mar 2026), NGED flexibility market insights (Jun 2025, Jun 2026), SSEN, SP ENW and SPEN SLC31E reports 2025/26, UKPN DSO, Ofgem SSES implementation decision (Aug 2026), Cornwall Insight for Nesta (2024), Baringa/Eaton, CrowdFlex (NESO, Feb 2026), aggregator and supplier offer pages
claim_freshness.note: Written from the advisor's cited evidence pack on VPPs, third-party flexibility and local network payments, under the director's steer of 25 Oct that flexibility knowledge is thorough and the simulation layered. Knowledge only: it commits nothing to the build.

headline.heading: The claim, in one sentence
headline.body: A GB household's flexible devices can now be sold by its supplier, by an independent aggregator to the grid operator, or by a rival trader into the wholesale market without the supplier's consent; the supplier is compensated for that last route from a pot all suppliers pay into (£18.9m over September 2025 to February 2026), while local network payments reach most homes as single-digit pounds a year.

plain.heading: In plain terms
plain.body:
Until recently only a household's supplier could sell its flexibility, by moving its EV charging or heat pump into cheaper hours. Three things changed. Independent aggregators can now register household devices for the grid operator's balancing services; since November 2024 a rival 'virtual trading party' can sell the same household's turn-down into the wholesale market; and the local networks pay for flexibility in specific places where their cables are short of capacity.
For a household the money is modest. Aggregators pay about £6-25 a month. A local network may pay £120 once to every home in a constrained area, or a few pounds per event. For the supplier the rival route matters more than its size: when a rival turns down its customer, the supplier is left holding energy it bought and is paid back at a reference price from a shared pot, and if two aggregators claim one meter, the newer one wins.

theory.heading: How it works
theory.body:
ROUTES. A supplier optimises its own customers against wholesale and imbalance prices and can register Additional BM Units. A Virtual Lead Party registers Secondary BM Units (at least 1 MW, one GSP Group) for the Balancing Mechanism; a Virtual Trading Party can also trade in the wholesale market under P415. Every unit must be half-hourly settled, so the move to half-hourly settlement (about 36% migrated by June 2026) gates who can take part.
COMPENSATION. A VTP's action creates a deviation volume at the supplier's meter. The supplier is compensated at the Supplier Compensation Reference Price and the cost is shared by market share; P510 would make it a direct, two-way payment, and P511 (Aug 2026) keeps large generators out. In the Balancing Mechanism, P444 has compensated suppliers directly since November 2025.
LOCAL NETWORKS. DNOs buy standard products (Peak Reduction, Scheduled Utilisation, availability plus utilisation, Operational Utilisation) in zones keyed to postcodes and substations, at a 10 kW minimum aggregated in a zone. Since January 2026 delivery is settled per minute with a performance multiplier: at 5% grace and a multiplier of 3, payment reaches zero at 63% delivery.
RULES. From 2027-28 anyone controlling household devices for flexibility needs a load-control licence, with consent, override, honest rewards and capped exit fees.

expected_shape.heading: What the data should look like
expected_shape.body:
A world that holds third-party flexibility should show:
• Nearly all DNO-registered flexibility assets domestic (about 309,000 of 309,500 at NGED) but under 40% of the capacity.
• Tendered volume far above contracted, and contracted far above dispatched (NGED 2025/26: 198 GWh procured, 6.5 GWh dispatched).
• Domestic DNO value of single-digit pounds per asset per year outside short-notice low-voltage events.
• Household VPP payouts of about £6-25 a month.
• VTP supplier compensation concentrated in a few parties, rising through winter (£0.7m in September 2025 to £5.6m in February 2026).
• Turn-up drawing more than twice the response of turn-down.

live_evidence.heading: Live evidence
live_evidence.body:
WHAT IS SOURCED. Aggregator routes and counts, the P415 mechanics and compensation flows, P510 and P511, the Market Facilitator timetable and standard baselines, DNO products, prices and 2025/26 results for four of six DNOs, household payment offers, CrowdFlex trial results and load-control licensing. Every figure and link is in docs/market_research/vpps_and_local_flexibility_2026-10-25.md; NGED's 2025/26 figures were checked against its report on 25 October 2026.
WHAT THE PROJECT DOES, READ FROM CODE AND NOT RUN. The world dispatches flexibility on true system stress with a trivial baseline, and only dispatch instructions and settlement lines cross the wall. The company books DFS revenue only, refuses the Capacity Market leg with a reason, and counts flexible kW at the device's rated power (7.4 kW per charger) rather than the networks' standard baselines (1.67 kW). No rival aggregator exists anywhere, and the DNO tender register has no caller.

residuals.heading: Where our picture is still weak
residuals.body: Ten things are missing. (1) How the Supplier Compensation Reference Price is set. (2) Any published household income from the Balancing Mechanism or reserve services. (3) UKPN and Northern Powergrid 2025/26 results. (4) Piclo marketplace statistics. (5) Current Tesla, GivEnergy, Social Energy and Lunar VPP figures. (6) Incentive levels and measured kW per household in Power-ups and CrowdFlex. (7) The mapping from the old DNO products to the new ones. (8) The Balancing Mechanism baseline's lookback rule. (9) A study stacking every domestic revenue stream. (10) Domestic participation in Capacity Market units.

scope_delta.heading: What this page does not yet establish
scope_delta.body: It does not repeat the Demand Flexibility Service and Saving Sessions history, which is on the household flexibility page. It does not say which layer the simulation should build first; the director's steer proposes layers from a minimum viable core upward, and the roadmap rules them. It does not cover network connection limits on EVs and heat pumps, which have their own evidence pack.

meta.title: Household flexibility: what moving a home's demand is worth, how much households really move, and what else a supplier could advise on
meta.subtitle: The grid operator's paid events have fallen from about £3 to about 20p per kWh in three winters, and households move less than they sign up for. The value that remains is in shifting EV and heat-pump demand automatically into cheap half-hours, and around it sit a dozen other advice topics a supplier could offer.
meta.wall_placement: Public-reality commons only. DFS outturns, trial results and survey figures are published by NESO, Ofgem, suppliers and researchers; a real supplier could read every one. Which of its customers would respond to an event, and by how much, is not observable before the event, and the page keeps that distinction. Statements about the company are read from its code, not run.

claim_freshness.source: NESO DFS winter reviews (2022/23-2024/25), Octopus Saving Sessions releases, Centre for Net Zero (BIEE 2023), CrowdFlex closure report (NESO 2026), Ofgem Flexibility and Net Zero survey (2025), SPEN customer research, DESNZ SSES government response and Ofgem implementation decision (Aug 2026), Smart Charge Points Regulations 2021, Drax, Cornwall Insight, CMA final report (2016), DESNZ smart meter statistics (Jun 2026), gov.uk scheme pages
claim_freshness.note: Written from the advisor's cited evidence pack on household flexibility and the advice roadmap, one of six under the director's steer of 25 Oct that the advice roadmap needs its knowledge first. Part 2's roadmap scan was mostly unverified; what was checked on 25 October is listed in the research note.

headline.heading: The claim, in one sentence
headline.body: The grid operator's Demand Flexibility Service fell from about £3,300 to about £241 per MWh delivered in three winters (48p per registered meter in 2024/25), and households that opt in cut 38-40% in an event but only about 9% against a fair comparison group, so a supplier's flexibility value now lies in automated, tariff-embedded shifting rather than paid events.

plain.heading: In plain terms
plain.body:
In winter 2022/23 the grid operator paid up to £3 for every kWh a household avoided in a short peak window, and suppliers like Octopus passed most of it on. Two winters later the same service paid about 20p per kWh and was used all year as an ordinary balancing tool. Households also moved less than the headlines suggested: a natural comparison group shows a 9% cut where the raw figure said 38-40%, and the official baseline overstated it by 13%.
What remains valuable is quieter. A supplier settled on each half hour of its customers' actual use buys less expensive power when an EV charges at 3am instead of 6pm. That is worth tens to hundreds of pounds a year per EV or heat pump, and it needs automation and consent rather than a text message before each event.
Around flexibility sit other things a supplier could advise on: the right tariff, data consent, storage heaters on Economy 7, prepayment safeguards and grants come first in the scan, ahead of hot water, landlords, home moves and cooling.

theory.heading: How it works
theory.body:
EVENTS. DFS pays providers per MWh turned down against a baseline of recent similar days. In 2024/25 it became a year-round merit tool, stackable with local network and capacity payments. Saving Sessions paid customers per kWh in OctoPoints. Opt-in falls with short notice (44% same-day against 63% day-ahead) and with repetition (about 49% to 33% of sign-ups per session), and delivery runs at about 72% of what is bid.
SHAPING. Under half-hourly settlement a supplier pays for each half hour its customers actually use, so shifting demand from expensive to cheap periods lowers its purchase cost directly; the value scales with shiftable kWh and the price spread.
CAPTURE. Since November 2024 an independent trader can sell a household's flexibility in the wholesale market and the supplier is compensated from a shared pot. The balancing mechanism opened to standard domestic devices in March 2026.
CONTROL. From March 2028 controlling EV chargers, smart electric heating up to 45 kW and home batteries for flexibility needs a licence. EV chargers already must ship with off-peak default hours and a random start delay of up to 600 seconds.
CONSENT. Only 16% of people are comfortable with a company controlling their heating, against 55% of EV users for charging.

expected_shape.heading: What the data should look like
expected_shape.body:
A world that holds household flexibility should show:
• Event response of about 24-26% among signed-up households and 38-40% among those who opt in, but only about 9% against a natural comparison.
• Opt-in falling with repetition (about half to a third of sign-ups per session) and with short notice.
• Delivery at about 65-82% of what is bid, lowest in midwinter.
• Load moved into the hours around an event, not only removed.
• Comfort with third-party control far higher for EV charging than for heating.
• Event revenue per registered meter well under £5 a winter, against a stated household expectation of about £150 a year.

live_evidence.heading: Live evidence
live_evidence.body:
WHAT IS SOURCED. Three winters of DFS outturns, two of Saving Sessions, the response and opt-in studies, the value streams a supplier can capture with their bands, the SSES licensing timetable and consumer terms, and the value-sharing models in use. The 2024/25 DFS figures, the Smart Charge Points Regulations, the CMA detriment figure, the restricted-meter count, the radio teleswitch switch-off, the smart-meter share and four scheme figures were checked against primary sources on 25 October 2026; eighteen roadmap-scan figures remain unverified and are not used as claims. Every figure is in docs/market_research/household_flexibility_and_the_advice_roadmap_2026-10-25.md.
WHAT THE COMPANY DOES, READ FROM CODE AND NOT RUN. It books DFS revenue from 2022 for any household with an EV, heat pump or battery, from the published per-winter record, and refuses the capacity leg with a reason. Nothing values a household's shifted demand against the company's own half-hourly costs, nothing models opt-in, notice or fatigue, and no rival trader exists. Its advice modules have no recipient.

residuals.heading: Where our picture is still weak
residuals.body: Ten things are missing. (1) The value of imbalance avoidance per household. (2) Balancing Mechanism revenue for aggregated domestic devices. (3) Domestic capacity-market de-rating; the band assumes 0.5 kW. (4) DFS 2025/26 outturn. (5) Saving Sessions 2024/25 and 2025/26. (6) A direct measure of event fatigue. (7) Fetches not made: Axle, OVO Charge Anytime, Piclo, ENA Open Networks and FES 2025 flexibility capacity. (8) Eighteen roadmap-scan figures, including electric-heating homes, prepayment meter counts, the smart data access defaults, the private rented share and heat-network counts. (9) The SSES legal-force date is stated two ways. (10) The CrowdFlex report's own figures disagree between sections.

scope_delta.heading: What this page does not yet establish
scope_delta.body: It does not cover rival aggregators, local network payments or load-control licensing in depth; those are on the VPPs and local flexibility page. It does not cover boilers, EVs, solar and batteries, heat pumps or how savings are proven, which have their own pages. It ranks the advice topics but does not set the build order, which the director's steer and the roadmap decide.

meta.title: Proving a household saved, and showing it so they believe it
meta.subtitle: A saving is the difference between what a home used and what it would have used, and the second number is never observed. Industry methods estimate it with known biases, a single home can only show a saving above about 4%, and the advertising regulator has twice ruled against suppliers' savings claims.
meta.wall_placement: Public-reality commons only. Every method, threshold and result is published. A real supplier never observes a household's counterfactual; the simulation does, and that is what lets this project grade a supplier's estimate. The page keeps the two apart, and the statements about the company are read from its code, not run.

claim_freshness.source: CalTRACK methods (readthedocs), EVO M&V Focus #5, ASHRAE Guideline 14 summary, Ofgem ECO measures table (2014) and ECO4/GBIS guidance, DESNZ SMETER evidence annex and ECO4 mid-scheme assessment (2024), BIT/DESNZ smart meter meta-analysis (2023), Early Learning Project (2015), NEED (2025), BRE solid-wall trial (2016), Allcott (2011), Allcott & Rogers (2014), Kemper (ACEEE 2015), NESO/ERM-CSE DFS evaluation (2025), ASA rulings on British Gas (2026) and Octopus (2025), CMA Green Claims Code, Ofgem Standards of Conduct
claim_freshness.note: Written from the advisor's cited evidence pack on proving and showing household savings, with the CalTRACK and in-use-factor sections of the gap-closure pack, under the director's steer of 25 Oct that the advice roadmap needs its knowledge first.

headline.heading: The claim, in one sentence
headline.body: A household's saving can only be estimated, because what it would have used is never observed: deemed savings deliver about 0.7 of what they predict, studies without a comparison group find about 9.6% where controlled ones find about 2%, a single home's hourly data can detect a saving only above about 3.6%, and the advertising regulator has ruled that an 'up to' saving must be achieved by a significant share of customers.

plain.heading: In plain terms
plain.body:
To say a home saved money you need two numbers: what it used, and what it would have used without the change. The second can only be estimated. Schemes such as the Energy Company Obligation give each measure a fixed 'deemed' saving and then cut it, because measured savings come in lower: a solid-wall trial achieved about 73% of the prediction, and the least efficient homes already use far less than models assume.
Measured savings have their own traps. A cold winter, a price rise or a new baby all change a bill. Without a comparison group, studies find savings about four times larger than with one. For one home, a smart meter can only reliably show a saving bigger than about 4%; smaller savings need hundreds or thousands of homes.
Showing a saving has rules too. In 2026 the advertising regulator upheld a complaint against 'save up to £546 with a heat pump' because only 34% of customers achieved it, and in 2025 against a claim that hid its basis behind 'learn more'.

theory.heading: How it works
theory.body:
METHODS. Deemed savings assign each measure a fixed value (ECO1 cut it by an in-use factor: 35% for cavity and loft, 33% for older solid brick walls). Modelled savings come from SAP or an engineering model. Metered savings compare actual use with a counterfactual built from the home's own history, normalised for weather (IPMVP Option C).
CALTRACK, the open method used in US pay-for-performance, fits a 365-day daily or billing baseline with heating and cooling degree days at a searched balance point, or an hourly time-of-week and temperature model; it reports fractional savings uncertainty and combines homes by root-sum-of-squares, which shrinks noise but not bias.
DETECTION. Uncertainty falls roughly with the square root of the number of homes: about ±4.5 points with 300 per arm, ±0.8 with 10,000. Weather and price shocks cancel in a randomised comparison but not in one home's before-and-after. ASHRAE Guideline 14 requires savings uncertainty below 50% of the saving at 68% confidence.
BIASES. Prebound (homes already under-heat), rebound (comfort taken back, 10-30% for heating), Hawthorne (being watched saves about 2.7% that vanishes) and persistence (report-driven savings decay 10-20% a year once reports stop).
CLAIMS. Ofgem's Standards of Conduct require complete, accurate, plain information; the CMA's Green Claims Code requires substantiation; the ASA requires the basis in the claim itself.

expected_shape.heading: What the data should look like
expected_shape.body:
A world in which savings are measured honestly should show:
• Smart meter and in-home display savings of about 2-3.5% electricity and 1.5-3% gas, lower for prepayment gas.
• Home energy reports saving about 2% on average, far more for high users (about 6%) than low (about 0.3%), decaying 10-20% a year after they stop.
• Measured fabric savings at about 0.7 of modelled, with the shortfall largest in the least efficient homes.
• Single-home detection impossible below about 3.6% with hourly data and about 10% with monthly.
• Flexibility-event savings net of load moved into the following hours, which exceeded the baseline in 14 of 18 events in 2022/23.

live_evidence.heading: Live evidence
live_evidence.body:
WHAT IS SOURCED. Deemed, modelled and metered methods; CalTRACK and the Guideline 14 thresholds; comparison-group and detection-size evidence from GB trials; flexibility baselines and their gaming; measured savings for smart meters, home energy reports and insulation; prebound, rebound, Hawthorne and persistence; the ASA rulings and the rules on claims. The CalTRACK rules, the Guideline 14 uncertainty rule and the ECO in-use factors were checked against their primary sources on 25 October 2026. Every figure is in docs/market_research/proving_and_showing_household_savings_2026-10-25.md.
WHAT THE PROJECT DOES, READ FROM CODE AND NOT RUN. The company's household-side figure is what a home would have paid on the default tariff minus what it paid: a price comparison, not a measured change in use. The world models the prebound effect. Nothing implements a savings estimator, a detectable-saving calculation or a claim audit, the world's flexibility baseline is trivial, and advice reaches no household yet.

residuals.heading: Where our picture is still weak
residuals.body: Nine things are missing. (1) EVO's own IPMVP text. (2) Guideline 14's calibration clause (the standard is sold, not published). (3) LBNL's M&V 2.0 acceptance criteria. (4) In-use factors for ECO3 and ECO4, which replaced them with a treated-share adjustment. (5) The cross-programme range for home energy reports. (6) Ofgem rules specific to estimated savings in sales. (7) How suppliers' apps present savings, and any trial of whether 'you saved £X' is believed. (8) A GB measure of flexibility-baseline error against a true counterfactual. (9) Any GB savings-share or heat-as-a-service tariff with measured savings.

scope_delta.heading: What this page does not yet establish
scope_delta.body: It does not set how this project will measure savings; the savings grader is a roadmap item and its eight tests are listed in the research note as proposals. It does not cover what each measure saves in carbon, which is on the household carbon page, or how advice is chosen for each customer, which is on the next-best-action page.

meta.title: How GB gas and power prices move: volatility at every time scale, the forward curve's shape and the spark spread
meta.subtitle: Gas and power prices in Britain are calm for long stretches and then violent, worst in autumn and winter, and the forward curve and the gas-to-power margin change shape with them. A supplier's hardest job is forecasting through that, and a simulated future that is too smooth or too wild would score every decision for the wrong reason.
meta.wall_placement: Public-reality commons only. Every figure comes from a published source: Elexon, Ofgem's commissioned UCL study, the Oxford Institute for Energy Studies, EnAppSys, Electricity Maps, Timera, S&P Global and others named in the research note. The statements about the simulated world are about its code and the price files it replays, read and measured on 25 October 2026; no figure from the company appears.

claim_freshness.source: OIES NG60 (Alterman 2012); Elexon BSC insight on 2021 price spikes; UCL for Ofgem (Gissey et al. 2018); EnAppSys GB 2021 annual summary; Electricity Maps GB grid in review 2025; Timera on GB clean spark spreads (Jan 2023); S&P Global, MNI, ECIU, Electric Insights as cited in the note
claim_freshness.note: The page the director's steer of 25 Oct 2026 asks for first: the forward years must reproduce the record's volatility and calm at every time scale, and these bands are what they are graded against. Seven of the pack's sources were re-fetched and confirmed on 25 Oct; five items remain open and are not used as claims.

headline.heading: The claim, in one sentence
headline.body: Between 2016 and 2025 GB gas and power prices were calm for long stretches and violent in bursts: front-month gas typically moved 8-15% a month, a third more in winter than summer, power spikes above £500/MWh came in autumn and spring and never in summer, and when prices rose the forward curve tipped into backwardation and the gas-to-power margin swung from a few pounds to hundreds.

plain.heading: In plain terms
plain.body:
Energy prices do not wobble evenly. Most weeks they barely move; then a cold, still spell, a pipeline outage or a war moves them several-fold in days, and the turbulence lasts. Between 1997 and 2011 the month-ahead gas price typically moved about 8-15% a month, rising over the period, and about a third more in the heating months than in summer. In 2021-22 it went far beyond that: month-ahead gas hit 800 pence a therm in March 2022, against an average of about 42 pence a therm (£14.24/MWh) before 2021.
Power follows gas, because gas plant usually sets the price, and adds its own spikes. The half-hourly balancing price passed £500/MWh 50 times in 2016-2020, almost all in autumn and spring when plant is on maintenance and the wind can drop, and never in summer. Since 2019 power has also gone below zero when the wind blows hard at night: 190 hours in 2025.
The shape of the future moves too. When prices are high and rising, near-term contracts cost more than later ones; when they fall, the reverse. A supplier hedging a fixed tariff, a household deciding when to run a heat pump and a forecaster projecting a cash balance all live inside that uncertainty, which is why the simulated future has to have it.

theory.heading: How it works
theory.body:
VOLATILITY. Measured as the spread of daily log returns, scaled to the horizon. It clusters: calm periods persist and so do turbulent ones, which is why a model of uniform noise is wrong at every scale. Gas volatility rises in winter, when demand is uncertain and storage is finite.
SPIKES AND NEGATIVES. Power spikes when the margin of available plant is thin and the wind is low; in 2021's spike periods wind supplied 1.1 GWh per half hour against 3.4 GWh otherwise. Negative prices come from high wind and low demand, when subsidised generators pay to keep running.
THE FORWARD CURVE. A forward is not a forecast: it carries a risk premium that is positive, grows with horizon and is larger in winter. Its slope follows the spot level. High spot usually means backwardation (near dates dearer) and a compressed or inverted seasonal spread; in February 2025 next summer's gas traded above next winter's. Falling spot restores contango.
THE SPARK SPREAD. Power price minus the gas a typical plant burns (at 49.13% efficiency) and, for the clean spread, its carbon (0.411 t/MWh). It was about £4-10/MWh at peak before 2021, reached about £280 base and £610 peak month-ahead in 2022, and fell back to £16 and £46 by January 2023. Gas set the power price 65% of the time in 2017 and about 85% in 2024.
LINKS. Cold and still weather tightens gas and power together, so a cold, still, gas-tight week is one event, not three coincidences.

expected_shape.heading: What the data should look like
expected_shape.body:
A credible price world, past or generated, should show these shapes:
• Monthly realised gas volatility mostly in the 8-15% range in normal years, about 1.3 times higher in winter than in summer, with clustered spikes well above it.
• Annual day-ahead power means of about £35-46/MWh in 2015-2020, £118 in 2021, about £200 in 2022 and £72-81 in 2024-25.
• A daily standard deviation of day-ahead power of about £6-13/MWh in normal years, and a mean daily high-to-low swing of about £68/MWh by 2025.
• Balancing prices above £500/MWh a few to a few dozen times a year, mostly autumn, never summer.
• Negative day-ahead hours rising from none before 2019 to about 190 in 2025.
• A forward curve that backwardates when spot is high and returns to contango when it falls, with a winter-over-summer spread that can collapse or invert.
• A peak clean spark spread of a few pounds in normal years and hundreds in a crisis.

live_evidence.heading: Live evidence
live_evidence.body:
WHAT IS SOURCED. The bands above, each with its publisher; seven sources were re-fetched and confirmed on 25 October 2026, among them Oxford's monthly gas volatility series, Elexon's count and seasonality of price spikes, UCL's day-ahead means and spreads for Ofgem, EnAppSys's 2021 summary, Electricity Maps' 2025 review and Timera's spark spreads.
WHAT THE SIMULATED WORLD DOES, MEASURED ON ITS OWN FILES. Its power price is the real half-hourly balancing price, replayed: its annual means sit on the day-ahead record (£113 in 2021, £200 in 2022, £71 in 2024), and its 50 balancing prices above £500/MWh in 2015-2020 match Elexon's count exactly. Its gas price is not NBP: it is a European monthly average converted at a fixed exchange rate and repeated every day of the month, so it moves 116 times in ten years. It therefore carries no daily or weekly gas volatility at all, its 2022 peak is a monthly £187/MWh against front-month prints near £273, and the July 2022 split between British and Dutch gas cannot happen in it.
WHAT THE COMPANY'S FORWARD QUOTE DOES, READ FROM CODE. A recent average of spot, times a fixed seasonal shape, times a premium that is always positive. Whether that reproduces the record's mix of backwardation and contango is not measured, because the record's own mix is unpublished.

residuals.heading: Where our picture is still weak
residuals.body: Nine things are missing. (1) Gas volatility by year for 2016-2025, the crisis included: no fetchable source, and the world's own gas file cannot supply it. (2) How fast a gas or power shock decays, and how fat the tails are: the studies are paywalled. (3) Official day-ahead annual means for 2016-2019 and 2022-2023. (4) How often the curve was backwardated: no study found. (5) A yearly spark spread series. (6) A daily gas-power correlation, and how much a gigawatt of wind moves the price. (7) How forecast error grows with horizon for gas and power forwards. (8) Annual NBP averages for 2022-2025 from a primary source. (9) A daily gas price history for the world itself, without which nothing below a month can be graded.

scope_delta.heading: What this page does not yet establish
scope_delta.body: It does not grade any forward generator against these bands; that grading is owed to the forward-years work, scale by scale. It does not explain how the gas price or the power price is set, which the gas, electricity and merit order pages do, nor why a supplier hedges, which the hedging page does. It does not give a forecast of future volatility, only the record's.

meta.title: What things cost a household, by date: fuel, energy, kit and carbon, 2016 to 2035
meta.subtitle: Every price a household weighs, from a litre of petrol to a heat pump to the carbon in a kilowatt-hour, is published as a dated series, and most of them moved a lot between 2016 and 2026. A constant in their place is wrong in most years, and wrong in a different direction each time.
meta.wall_placement: Public-reality commons only. Every figure comes from a published source: DESNZ weekly road fuel prices, Quarterly Energy Prices and greenhouse gas conversion factors, Ofgem's price cap pages, HMRC, the NESO carbon intensity service, Nesta's analysis of Boiler Upgrade Scheme data, DfT grant statistics and NESO's Future Energy Scenarios. The statements about the simulated world and company are about their code, read on 25 October 2026 and not run.

claim_freshness.source: DESNZ weekly road fuel prices (CSV 2003-2017 and 2018-), QEP September 2026, 2026 GHG conversion factors methodology paper (Tables 9 and 1.6), Ofgem price cap rates page, HMRC VAT Notice 708/6 and Revenue and Customs Brief 10 (2026), NESO carbon intensity API (2025), Hoare Lea (Feb 2026), Nesta (Apr 2026), DfT EV charging grant statistics (Oct 2024), Ofgem on ECO and RO from April 2026
claim_freshness.note: One of six evidence packs behind the personalised asset world (director, 25 Oct 2026: "I'm worried you are using static costs and %"). Fifteen items were re-fetched and confirmed on 25 Oct, two were corrected, four remain open and are not used.

headline.heading: The claim, in one sentence
headline.body: Every cost a GB household weighs is a dated series, and between 2016 and 2026 petrol ran from about 101p to 192p a litre, the electricity unit rate more than doubled and fell back, the median heat pump fell 11% in real terms after 2022, and the carbon in a grid kilowatt-hour fell by more than half, so any fixed figure is wrong in most years.

plain.heading: In plain terms
plain.body:
Whether an electric car, solar panels, a battery or a heat pump saves a household money depends on what the alternatives cost at the time. Those costs move. Petrol averaged 109p a litre in 2016, peaked at 192p in July 2022, fell to about 136p in 2025 and was back at 175p in October 2026. Electricity went from about 15p a kWh in 2015 to 34p under the 2022 price guarantee, and sat near 26p in late 2026, when the government took VAT off electricity for six months. Kit got cheaper: a typical small solar system cost £1,876 per kW of capacity in 2024/25, down a fifth in a year, and the median heat pump about £13,000 before a £7,500 grant.
Carbon moved most of all. A kilowatt-hour from the grid carried about 0.28 kg of CO2 in 2016 and about 0.13 kg in 2025, and in 2025 it ranged from 24 to 293 grams half-hour by half-hour, and from 47 grams in the north of Scotland to 252 in South Wales over the year.
So the honest way to tell a household what it could save is to use the price that applied on the date in question, for that household's region and payment method, and to say how wide the spread between households is.

theory.heading: How it works
theory.body:
WHERE EACH SERIES COMES FROM. Pump prices are weekly UK averages from 2003, with duty and VAT, and no regional split. Retail energy prices come from Ofgem's cap (quarterly since October 2023, six-monthly before, from January 2019, by 14 regions, payment method and meter type) and from DESNZ's Quarterly Energy Prices, which go back further. PV costs are £ per kW by size band from 2013/14, battery costs £ per kWh by size band from 2024/25, heat pump costs from the Boiler Upgrade Scheme from 2022. Chargepoints have only grant amounts, and insulation only occasional point estimates.
POLICY DATES MOVE PRICES. Fuel duty fell 5p in March 2022. Energy-saving materials were zero-rated for VAT from April 2022 to March 2027, batteries from February 2024. Bill-funded energy efficiency (ECO) left the cap in April 2026 and most of the Renewables Obligation moved to taxation. Electricity was zero-rated for VAT from October 2026 to March 2027, while gas kept 5%.
CARBON HAS TWO CLOCKS. The government's annual conversion factors describe grid data one or two years older than the year they are published for, and one data year (2024) was skipped when the lag shortened. The same methodology paper publishes a consistent series by data year, and that series differs from the factors as first published by up to about 10%. The National Energy System Operator's carbon intensity service gives measured half-hourly values by region from September 2017.

expected_shape.heading: What the data should look like
expected_shape.body:
A credible household world should show these shapes:
• Petrol and diesel prices that follow the weekly record: about 101-117p a litre in 2016, a peak near 191-199p in July 2022, and a second rise in 2026.
• Electricity and gas prices that change on the cap's dates and differ by region and payment method, with standing charges ranging from about 42p to 72p a day across regions in early 2025.
• Kit costs that fall over time and fall with size: battery £ per kWh roughly halving from the smallest to the largest band.
• Heat pump costs net of a grant that changed on 23 October 2023.
• Grid carbon falling from about 0.28 to 0.13 kg per kWh over 2016-2025, varying several-fold by region and half-hour.
These are calibration properties of the population and the record, never a target for any one home.

live_evidence.heading: Live evidence
live_evidence.body:
WHAT IS SOURCED. The series register, representative values and policy dates in the research note, with 15 items re-fetched and confirmed on 25 October 2026 and two corrected: the half-hourly carbon range in 2025 is 24 to 293 grams, and indexing grid carbon by data year should use the consistent series the government now publishes rather than the factors as first issued.
WHAT THE SIMULATION DOES, READ FROM CODE AND NOT RUN. No petrol or diesel price exists anywhere in the code, so no saving against a petrol car can be computed. The company's retrofit offers carry four fixed costs (insulation £6,000, heat pump £12,000, solar £7,000, a time-shift measure £300), the same in every year. One of its two price cap tables is annual, with a fixed value for every year after 2025 that is well below the published 2026 caps, and three company modules read it. An Economy 7 rate table carries no source and nothing calls it. Grid carbon is read by the year a factor was published, as a reporting company would, which the code states as its choice.

residuals.heading: Where our picture is still weak
residuals.body: Ten things are missing. (1) Solar costs and their spread before 2024/25. (2) The spread of heat pump costs by region and size. (3) Ofgem's 2019-2021 unit rates by region. (4) Battery costs before 2024/25. (5) What a home chargepoint costs to install, as opposed to the grant. (6) Insulation costs in 2019 and 2022, with any spread. (7) Price deflators and car price indices. (8) The government's own retail price projections. (9) NESO's technology cost assumptions to 2035. (10) A daily exchange-rate series for converting gas prices.

scope_delta.heading: What this page does not yet establish
scope_delta.body: It does not change any cost in the simulation, and it does not grade the population against these series; both are owed to the personalised asset world. It does not say what any one household paid, only what was published for the market. It does not project bills to 2035, because no published source does.

meta.title: How GB households are priced: the fixed deal, the default tariff, the cap and time-of-use
meta.subtitle: Most of what a GB household pays is decided by which tariff it sits on, and most households who never act sit on the default. This page sets out how fixed deals end, how the default is capped, how far apart the two have been, and how few homes are on a time-of-use tariff.
meta.wall_placement: Public-reality commons only. Every figure comes from a published source: CMA 2016, Ofgem decisions, letters and State of the Market reports, House of Commons Library briefings, Which?, MoneySavingExpert, and Octopus's own product pages. The statements about the world and the company are about their code and are marked as read, not run.

claim_freshness.source: CMA Energy Market Investigation final report (Jun 2016) and restricted-meters appendix 9.5; Ofgem SVT trends (Sep 2017), default tariff cap decision (Nov 2018), cap letters (Feb 2021, Feb 2024), SLC 22C notice (2017), SLC 22G consultation (2020), BAT decisions (Jul and Nov 2024), State of the Market (Apr 2025, Jan 2026); Commons Library CBP-8081, CBP-9714, CBP-7543; Which?; MSE; Octopus; Elexon (MHHS)
claim_freshness.note: Step 4 of the owed pages in the director's map steer of 24 Oct 2026, from the advisor's cited evidence pack. Its eight [unverified] items were checked while drafting: 2 confirmed, 1 partly, 3 corrected, 2 still open. The price-cap page has the cap's method; this one has the tariffs around it.

headline.heading: The claim, in one sentence
headline.body: A GB household that does nothing at the end of a fixed deal moves to its supplier's default tariff, which since 1 January 2019 has been capped by Ofgem per fuel, payment method and region; the default's share of households has ranged from about 54% (August 2021) to about 90% (mid-2023), and the gap to the cheapest fix has been about £140-£330 a year in a normal market and close to nothing in 2022.

plain.heading: In plain terms
plain.body:
A household is on one of two kinds of tariff. A fixed deal locks the unit rate and standing charge for 12, 18 or 24 months, may charge a fee to leave early, and ends with a renewal letter 42-49 days before it expires. A default (standard variable) tariff has no end date and its price changes when the cap changes. Anyone who does nothing at the end of a fix lands on it.
In 2016 the CMA found about 70% of the big six's customers on a default tariff and put the cost of that inertia at about £1.4bn a year. The cap followed in 2019. In 2022 wholesale prices rose past the cap, fixed deals priced below it disappeared, and about nine households in ten ended up on the default. Fixes came back from late 2023, and by July 2025 about a third of customers were on one.
Time-of-use is still small: about 835,000 accounts, 2.8%, in July 2025, most of them on EV tariffs. About 4 million homes have an older restricted meter such as Economy 7.

theory.heading: How it works
theory.body:
END OF A FIX. SLC 22C (from December 2017) requires the end-of-term notice no earlier than 49 and no later than 42 days before the end. No exit fee may be charged in the final 49 days. A household that does nothing moves to the default, or to a fixed default that is no dearer than the supplier's cheapest evergreen tariff and carries no exit fee.
EXIT FEES. No rule caps them. Before 2021 they were about £5-£30 per fuel. In 2022-23 they were typically £75 per fuel on a 12-month fix and up to £200 on a two-year fix.
THE CAP. The Tariff Cap Act 2018 has Ofgem set a cap for each fuel separately, by payment method and for each of 14 regions, with its own multi-register cap. Levels are quoted at typical consumption: 3,100 kWh electricity and 12,000 kWh gas at first, later revised down. The cap started at £1,137 (direct debit, dual fuel) and was reset every six months, then every quarter from October 2022. It peaked at £3,582 in Q1 2023 on current consumption values. Prepayment joined the default cap when the CMA's prepayment cap expired at the end of 2020. Standing charges were levelised from April 2024, so prepayment paid about £49 a year less and direct debit about £10 more.
THE EPG. From 1 October 2022 to 30 June 2023 the household paid 34.0p/kWh for electricity and 10.3p/kWh for gas, including VAT, whatever the cap said. Government paid the supplier the difference. Standing charges were not reduced.
ACQUISITION-ONLY TARIFFS. Banned from April 2022, with a market-wide derogation letting suppliers offer fixed retention tariffs to their own customers. The ban has been extended each year, most recently to 31 March 2027.
TIME-OF-USE. Restricted meters (Economy 7 about 3.7m in 2015) are covered by SLC 22G. Modern products such as Agile (half-hourly, tied to wholesale) and Go (a night window for EVs, launched June 2018) need a smart meter in smart mode.

expected_shape.heading: What the data should look like
expected_shape.body:
A credible world should show these shapes against the record:
• Default share at large legacy suppliers in 2016-17 of 57-70%, lower across the whole market.
• Fixed share of about 45-48% in August 2021, about 9-11% at the mid-2023 low, 25-30% in January 2025 and 30-35% in July 2025.
• A gap between the cheapest fix and the default of £140-£330 a year for typical dual fuel in a normal market, and at most about £100 in 2022, when many fixes cost more than the cap.
• Exit fees of £5-£30 per fuel before 2021 and up to £75-£200 per fuel in 2022-23, with none in the final 49 days.
• Restricted meters on 14-17% of electricity accounts.
• Modern time-of-use on 2.5-3% of accounts in mid-2025, about three quarters of them EV tariffs.
These are calibration checks on what the world produces. They are never targets for a single home.

live_evidence.heading: Live evidence
live_evidence.body:
WHAT IS SOURCED. Tariff shares 2016-2025, the end-of-fix and rollover rules, exit fees, the loyalty-penalty gap, the cap's structure and levels, the EPG, restricted meters and modern time-of-use, and the RMR and BAT rules. Every figure and URL is in docs/market_research/tariffs_and_the_default_tariff_2026-10-25.md, with the outcome of each [unverified] item checked on 25 October 2026. The default-share series with its prepayment basis is tools/published_tariff_mix.py, written up in gb_domestic_default_tariff_share_2016_2025.md. Payment-behaviour drift on the default is in svt_drift_by_payment_behaviour.md.
WHAT THE WORLD AND COMPANY DO, READ FROM CODE AND NOT RUN. The world settles a default-tariff account at the published cap, in cap periods, with no renewal decision, and charges the EPG rate in 2022-23. The published split checks its output and is never an input. The company offers smart-metered fixed-term customers a peak/off-peak pair that splits its flat rate revenue-neutrally; there is no Agile- or Go-shaped product and no restricted meter. The company's exit-fee module waives a fee within 42 days, not the licence's 49, prices it per kWh where every published fee is flat, and nothing calls it.
GRADED. The once-per-stint letter to default-tariff households, with a re-fix, costs the company on all three book seeds (C30, 25 October 2026), and households who stay gain about £0.9k-£1.4k a book.

residuals.heading: Where our picture is still weak
residuals.body: Eight things are missing. (1) Ofgem's monthly tariff-type series for 2016-2025 exists only as charts. (2) The share of fixes by length. (3) A regulatory limit on exit fees: none was found. (4) The current wording of SLC 22C after 2022-24. (5) Nil-consumption cap values by region, and the EPG standing charges by region. (6) Customer numbers for each time-of-use product. (7) A current Economy 7 count, after 2020. (8) The date the RMR simpler rules were formally removed, and the third permitted discount.

scope_delta.heading: What this page does not yet establish
scope_delta.body: It does not grade the world's fixed/default split against these bands; tools/svt_generated_share_check.py is the check that does that. It does not repeat the cap's method, which has its own page. It does not grade the company's peak/off-peak split against any published time-of-use product, and the world has no restricted-meter household to price.

meta.title: Smart meters and half-hourly settlement: what the meter reports, what settlement uses, and when it changes
meta.subtitle: A smart meter can report every half hour, but what a supplier is charged for a home's energy has, until now, rested on a profile and an annual read, corrected over 14 months. This page sets out the rollout, how settlement worked before MHHS, what MHHS changes, and who may see half-hourly data.
meta.wall_placement: Public-reality commons only. Every figure comes from a published source: DESNZ/BEIS smart meter statistics, Elexon's BSC pages and MHHS programme updates, Ofgem decisions (MHHS 2021, CR022 2023, settlement data access 2019, SLC 47 2022, billing performance 2026), DECC's 2012 data access framework and POST. The statements about the world and the company are about their code and are marked as read, not run.

claim_freshness.source: DESNZ/BEIS Smart Meters in Great Britain quarterly reports (Q3 2016, Q1 2019, Q4 2019, Q4 2021, Q4 2022, Q1 2024, Q4 2024, Q4 2025, Q1 2026); Elexon profiling, settlement-run glossary, MHHS programme pages (2025-26); Ofgem MHHS decision (Apr 2021), CR022 (Jun 2023), HH data for settlement (Jun 2019), SLC 47 (Sep 2022), domestic billing performance (Jul 2026); DECC data access and privacy (2012); POST smart meters briefing
claim_freshness.note: Step 5 of the owed pages in the director's map steer of 24 Oct 2026, from the advisor's cited evidence pack. Its six unverified or secondary items were checked while drafting: 2 confirmed, 1 corrected, 3 still open, one of them a conflict between two Elexon sources on when R2 runs.

headline.heading: The claim, in one sentence
headline.body: By the end of 2025, 71% of GB domestic meters were smart and 65% were in smart mode. Until migration to market-wide half-hourly settlement began on 22 October 2025, almost every home was settled on a profile and corrected over reconciliation runs ending 14 months later. That window falls to 7 months from April 2027 and 4 months from July 2027.

plain.heading: In plain terms
plain.body:
A smart meter records use every half hour and sends it to the supplier over the national network. The rollout began in earnest in 2016. About 8% of large suppliers' domestic meters were smart in 2016, 29% in 2019, half in 2022 and 71% by the end of 2025. Not every smart meter works as one. About one in twelve is in 'traditional mode', often a first-generation meter that stopped talking after a switch.
Even where a supplier had half-hourly data, settlement (how the market charges each supplier for its customers' energy) mostly did not use it. A domestic home was settled on a standard profile shape scaled to an annual estimate, and the bill was corrected as real reads arrived, run by run, over 14 months. Market-wide half-hourly settlement (MHHS) replaces that with each home's actual half-hours. Migration began in October 2025 and is due to finish in May 2027.
Half-hourly data is personal data. From November 2022 a newly installed or newly contracted home shares half-hourly data by default and may opt down to daily. Older arrangements default to daily.

theory.heading: How it works
theory.body:
PROFILES. Elexon's Profile Class 1 is domestic unrestricted and Profile Class 2 is domestic Economy 7. A non-half-hourly meter's annual quantity (EAC or annualised advance) is spread over half-hours with regression coefficients, refreshed twice a year from about 2,500 sample sites.
RUNS. Interim Information at 1 week (no money moves), Initial Settlement at about 1 month, R1 at 2 months, R2 at 4 or 5 months (two Elexon sources differ), R3 at 7 months, RF at 14 months, and Dispute Final at 28 months for disputes only. Each run replaces estimates with actual reads as they arrive. In 2014 about 30% of non-half-hourly energy was on actual data at R1, 60% at R2, 80% at R3 and 97% at RF, the performance target.
MHHS. Approved by Ofgem on 20 April 2021, replanned in June 2023 (CR022) because the first timetable was 'unrealistic and unachievable'. Central systems went live in September 2025 and migration began on 22 October 2025. More than 11.3 million meters had migrated by June 2026. Completion is due on 7 May 2027 and the shorter timetable from 2 July 2027. Non-communicating meters are settled with Load Shaping Service shapes.
DATA ACCESS. DECC's 2012 framework: monthly data for billing without consent, daily data for any purpose except marketing with an opt-out, half-hourly only with opt-in. Ofgem's 2019 decision made settlement use of half-hourly data an obligation with an opt-out. SLC 47 as modified from 3 November 2022 sets half-hourly by default for 'New System' customers, daily for 'Old System', and no opt-out for half-hourly time-of-use customers.
READS. SLC 21B requires all reasonable steps to read a meter at least once a year. The two-yearly duty some sources quote was the meter-inspection duty, removed in April 2016.

expected_shape.heading: What the data should look like
expected_shape.body:
A credible world should show these shapes against the record:
• Domestic meters smart in any mode: about 37% at end 2019 [derived], 50% at end 2021, 55% at end 2022, 66% at end 2024 and 71% at end 2025 (band 68-74%).
• Smart meters in smart mode: 90-94% of smart and advanced meters. Traditional mode: 4-8% of domestic meters in 2024-25.
• SMETS1 to SMETS2 at about 1:2 by end 2025 (13m to 27m).
• About 2.4-3.2m domestic installs a year. About 11% of domestic smart meters in prepayment mode.
• Every domestic home settled on a profile through 2025, with reconciliation ending at 14 months.
• About 81% of bills on actual reads at first issue (2024).
These are calibration checks on what the world produces. They are never targets for a single home.

live_evidence.heading: Live evidence
live_evidence.body:
WHAT IS SOURCED. The rollout at year ends 2016-2026, operating modes, SMETS1 and SMETS2, profile classes, the run timetable and its MHHS transition, MHHS milestones and progress, the data access rules, read duties and estimated bills. Every figure and URL is in docs/market_research/smart_meters_and_half_hourly_settlement_2026-10-25.md, with the outcome of each unverified item checked on 25 October 2026. The run timetable the world uses is read from Elexon's 2014 slides in elexon_settlement_run_timetable_verified.md. Half-hourly load-shape clustering and data consent are in hh_load_shape_clustering_2026.md and smart_meter_hh_data_consent_2026.md.
WHAT THE WORLD AND COMPANY DO, READ FROM CODE AND NOT RUN. The world draws which premise has a smart meter from DESNZ Table 5a, linearly interpolated (10.6% in 2016 to 68.9% in 2024), with 90% communicating. That is within about 5 points of the record. A second copy in saas/smart_meter_rollout.py runs 4-10 points higher, derived by dividing meters by households, and it gates the company's time-of-use offer. The world settles every home on a profile with R1, R2, R3 and RF at 2, 4, 7 and 14 months. It has no MHHS, because the run ends before migration, no elective half-hourly settlement and no data-consent choice.

residuals.heading: Where our picture is still weak
residuals.body: Seven things are missing. (1) The quarter-by-quarter rollout series in DESNZ's data tables was not read, so 2017, 2018 and 2023 rest on gaps or secondary sources. (2) MPAN counts by profile class. (3) Elective domestic half-hourly settlement uptake: no published count. (4) Actual half-hourly data opt-out rates under SLC 47. (5) Whether R2 runs at 4 or 5 months: two Elexon sources disagree. (6) Intermediate run timings under the MHHS target timetable. (7) Estimated bills split by meter type.

scope_delta.heading: What this page does not yet establish
scope_delta.body: It does not grade the world's smart-meter share against these bands beyond the year-end comparison in the note. It does not settle which of the two penetration series should be the one home; that is filed as a finding. It does not cover read cadence and estimated bills in depth, which belong to the metering-and-reads page.

meta.title: Vulnerable customers: the Priority Services Register, ability to pay, prepayment and self-disconnection
meta.subtitle: A supplier must identify customers in vulnerable situations, give them free priority services, set debt repayments by what they can afford and never leave a prepayment household cut off without help. Most of what it needs to know, it only learns if the household tells it.
meta.wall_placement: Public-reality commons only. Every figure comes from a published source: Ofgem decisions, reports and the Consumer Vulnerability Strategy progress report, DESNZ and the Scottish Government's fuel poverty statistics, Citizens Advice, Energy UK, and the Warm Home Discount consultation. The statements about the world and the company are about their code and are marked as read, not run.

claim_freshness.source: Ofgem PSR review (2015) and press release (2016); Vulnerable consumers in the energy market (2019); self-disconnection and self-rationing decision (Oct 2020); ability-to-pay review (Sep 2022); involuntary PPM Code of Practice (Apr 2023) and licence decision (Sep 2023); Consumer Standards decision (Oct 2023); PPM compensation (May 2025); Consumer Vulnerability Strategy (Apr 2025) and progress report (Jul 2026); DESNZ fuel poverty statistics (2025, 2026); Scottish House Condition Survey 2024; Citizens Advice (2023, 2025); WHD 2025/26 consultation; Energy UK Vulnerability Commitment
claim_freshness.note: Step 6 of the owed pages in the director's map steer of 24 Oct 2026, from the advisor's cited evidence pack. Its four unverified items were checked while drafting: 1 confirmed, 1 partly, 2 still open. Debt collection itself has its own page.

headline.heading: The claim, in one sentence
headline.body: By the end of 2025 about 32% of GB electricity customers were on a supplier's Priority Services Register and just under 7% were in debt or arrears, 58% of those with no repayment plan; since December 2020 a supplier must set repayments by ability to pay and identify prepayment customers who self-disconnect, and since November 2023 it may not force a prepayment meter on a household of over-75s, under-twos or with a health need for continuous supply.

plain.heading: In plain terms
plain.body:
Some households are much less able to protect themselves when things go wrong: older people living alone, people who rely on powered medical equipment, families with very young children, people who are seriously ill, or people in a temporary crisis. Suppliers keep a Priority Services Register of them and offer free services such as password schemes, accessible bills and advance warning of power cuts. Registration has grown from about 13% of customers in 2015 to about a third in 2025, but it depends on the household telling its supplier.
The other kind of vulnerability is money. Energy debt reached a record £4.79bn in early 2026. A supplier must contact a customer after two missed monthly payments, set repayment by what the household can afford, and consider pausing repayments.
Prepayment is where the two meet. In 2022 about 600,000 households were moved to prepayment for debt, some by force under warrant, and 3.2 million people ran out of credit. After a newspaper exposed forced installs in February 2023, Ofgem stopped them, made a code of practice mandatory and later had suppliers pay £18.6m in compensation and write-offs.

theory.heading: How it works
theory.body:
THE REGISTER. Since January 2017 eligibility covers anyone 'in a vulnerable situation', permanent or temporary; networks must also cover households with children under five. Suppliers must take reasonable steps to identify eligible customers and share needs data with the network, using common needs codes, with consent.
ABILITY TO PAY (SLC 27). From 15 December 2020 suppliers must give due consideration to ability-to-pay principles: repayment rates set on ability to pay, no large upfront payment before reconnection, and re-engagement after a failed arrangement. From 14 December 2023 they must make contact no later than after two missed monthly payments (SLC 27.5B), consider repayment pauses, and offer free contact to customers who are struggling.
PREPAYMENT AND SELF-DISCONNECTION (SLC 27A). Emergency and friendly-hours credit for every prepayment customer; additional support credit for vulnerable households who are self-disconnecting; all reasonable steps to identify self-disconnection on an ongoing basis. Self-rationing carries no identification duty.
INVOLUNTARY PREPAYMENT. Frozen from February 2023, governed by a mandatory code from November 2023. It needs at least £200 of debt per fuel and at least three months outstanding, at least ten contact attempts and a welfare visit. Never for households of only over-75s, with children under two, or with a health need for continuous supply.
FUEL POVERTY. England: an energy-efficiency band of D-G and income after housing and energy costs below the poverty line (LILEE). Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland use spending shares of 10% or more.
WARM HOME DISCOUNT. £150 a year, by data matching. It reached about 3.4m households before 2025/26 and about 6.1m after the high-cost-to-heat test was removed.

expected_shape.heading: What the data should look like
expected_shape.body:
A credible world should show these shapes against the record:
• About 24% of electricity accounts on a PSR at end 2018, about 25% at end 2020 and about 32% at end 2025.
• Just under 5% of customers in debt or arrears at end 2020 and just under 7% at end 2025. Of those in arrears, 49% (2020) to 58% (2025) with no repayment plan.
• Average electricity debt when a plan is agreed of about £700 (2020) to £1,050 (2025).
• Prepayment customers self-disconnecting in a year: about 1 in 7 (2019) to 29% (2024/25 survey).
• Fuel poverty in England falling from 16.2% (2016) to 9.9% (2024), and about 1.5-2.5 times the direct-debit rate among prepayment customers.
These are calibration checks on what the world produces. They are never targets for a single home.

live_evidence.heading: Live evidence
live_evidence.body:
WHAT IS SOURCED. The Consumer Vulnerability Strategy, PSR eligibility, services and registrations 2014-2025, the ability-to-pay rules and the 2022 review, debt outcomes 2018-2026, the prepayment moratorium, code and compensation, self-disconnection prevalence, fuel poverty definitions and series, and the Warm Home Discount. Every figure and URL is in docs/market_research/vulnerability_psr_and_ability_to_pay_2026-10-25.md, with the outcome of each unverified item checked on 25 October 2026. The world's two vulnerability states are set out in debt_and_collections.md section 10; Ofgem's licence background is in ofgem_regulation.md.
WHAT THE WORLD AND COMPANY DO, READ FROM CODE AND NOT RUN. The world draws PSR-type and financial vulnerability as hidden household states, independently. Only a disclosed PSR registration crosses to the company, and nothing else reads either state yet. At its defaults the world registers about 16% of households, about half the 2025 register share, though the denominators differ (households against accounts). The company decides PSR eligibility and disconnection protection in one module from the published vocabulary. The world also draws silent self-rationing: a household that keeps paying and stops heating, visible only as a fall in consumption that a company detector looks for. The world has no prepayment meter, so the prepayment rules have no household to act on. Several company registers (prepayment, fuel poverty, Warm Home Discount) have no caller.

residuals.heading: Where our picture is still weak
residuals.body: Nine things are missing. (1) The final SLC 26 text and the current needs-code list. (2) PSR counts after 2018, beyond percentages, and how many registrations sit with a supplier but not the network. (3) Ofgem's 2022 expectations letter. (4) Any regulatory measure of self-rationing. (5) A cross-tabulation of fuel poverty against arrears. (6) Friendly-hours and emergency credit amounts. (7) How the Warm Home Discount reaches prepayment customers. (8) The Energy UK Commitment's launch year and signatories. (9) Involuntary prepayment volumes for 2022 and after the 2024 restart.

scope_delta.heading: What this page does not yet establish
scope_delta.body: It does not grade the world's registration share, arrears or fuel poverty against these bands; the 16% registration figure is arithmetic on the world's defaults, not a run. It does not cover debt collection itself, which has its own page. It does not describe a prepayment world, because the world has none.

meta.title: Seven markets against GB: what transfers from the build and what a second market would need
meta.subtitle: Australia, France, Germany, Italy, Spain, Belgium and Japan set against GB on sixteen dimensions. The weather-to-demand engine, the asset advice and the wholesale replay transfer well; prepayment, the fixed direct debit, the all-supplier price cap, supplier-owned meters, the deemed contract and the mutualised SoLR levy are GB peculiarities.
meta.wall_placement: Knowledge only -- not on the roadmap. Public-reality commons; nothing here is read by the world or the company, and nothing is built from it (director, 25 Oct 2026, 07:17).

claim_freshness.source: the seven country evidence packs of 25 Oct 2026 and the advisor's synthesis across them
claim_freshness.note: The synthesis is the advisor's; the closeness ranking is judgement, not a measured distance. Items the packs tag [unverified] were spot-checked on the country pages; this page adds no check of its own.

headline.heading: The claim, in one sentence
headline.body: Most of what the GB build does to model households transfers to other markets, but most of what it does to model the GB supplier's commercial rules does not, because prepayment at scale, a fixed direct debit that builds a credit balance, one price cap over every supplier's default tariff, supplier-owned meters, a deemed contract on move-in and a mutualised supplier-of-last-resort levy are each unusual outside GB.

plain.heading: In plain terms
plain.body: The director asked how transferable the GB build is, and where a second market would need new world and new supplier features. The advisor compared seven countries with GB on the same sixteen dimensions, from weather to where a household's debt sits. This page is the summary; each country has its own page. It is knowledge only: nothing is built from it and no priority changes.

theory.heading: How it works
theory.body:
TRANSFERS WELL ALMOST EVERYWHERE.
• The weather to building to demand engine. Every market except Germany and Belgium needs a cooling term.
• Advice and asset offers (EV, PV, battery, heat pump), strongest in Australia, Germany and Spain.
• The wholesale replay mechanism: High for Germany and Belgium. Australia (5-minute pricing across 5 regions), Italy (zonal) and Japan (9 area prices) need regional prices.
TRANSFERS POORLY ALMOST EVERYWHERE: GB FEATURES THAT ARE UNUSUAL, NOT STANDARD.
• Prepayment at GB scale is absent or negligible in all seven. Debt is handled by power limitation (France reduces power; Italy limits to 15% for 15 days; Spain falls back to a 3.5 kW minimum supply), hardship plans (Australia), the DSO as social supplier with prepaid meters (Belgium), or disconnection (Germany about 239k a year; Japan around day 51).
• Fixed monthly direct debit building a credit balance. Germany, Belgium and France use monthly advances plus an annual true-up; Spain, Italy and Japan bill monthly or bimonthly on actual readings; Australia bills quarterly in arrears.
• A price cap over every supplier's default tariff. France, Spain and Japan have a regulated tariff only the incumbent may sell (still dominant at about 55-65% in France and Japan); Australia's DMO/VDO caps standing offers only and serves as an advertising reference; Italy auctions its default service; Germany's default supplier is not price-capped; Belgium has only a social tariff.
• Supplier-owned meters through the DCC. In six of seven the network operator owns the meter; Australia uses a metering coordinator appointed by the retailer. Data arrives from the DSO.
• The deemed contract on move-in. Only Australia (a designated retailer's standing offer) and Germany (basic supply) have a default supplier. France, Italy, Spain and Japan require the new occupant to contract; Belgium routes unclaimed points to the DSO.
• SoLR with a mutualised levy. No other market socialises failure costs this way. Australia and Germany move customers to large retailers or the default supplier; Japan's last-resort supply covers high-voltage customers only; in Belgium the network absorbs the debt of social-supply customers.

expected_shape.heading: What the data should look like
expected_shape.body:
How far each market is from GB, closest first (the advisor's judgement, not a measured distance):
• Germany and Belgium: similar climate and wholesale; they differ in billing, settlement and debt.
• Australia: asset offers transfer very well, but market and settlement mechanics are far apart.
• France and Spain: a regulated-tariff benchmark, capacity subscription, electric heating and cooling.
• Italy: all of the above, plus legal heating seasons, CMOR and 3 kW limits.
• Japan: room-based heating, a three-fuel world, ampere tariffs and an incumbent-dominated market.

live_evidence.heading: Live evidence
live_evidence.body:
WHAT A SECOND MARKET WOULD NEED, ACROSS THE SEVEN.
• A configurable settlement clock: 15 minutes across the EU markets (DE, BE, FR imbalance, IT, ES), 5 minutes in Australia, 30 minutes in Japan.
• Contracted capacity or a breaker per home: kVA subscription (France 3-36 kVA; Spain two contracted powers), kW subscription (Italy, 3 kW typical, trips at 3.3), ampere breaker (Japan 10-60 A), and a peak-based network charge (Flanders, on the 12-month average of 15-minute peaks with a 2.5 kW floor).
• Network time-of-use calendars as a constraint on households: Spain's 2.0TD, France's per-home off-peak hours, Germany's §14a dimming, Australian network tariffs.
• An incumbent regulated tariff as a competitor price signal, with a published formula: France's TRVE cost stack, Spain's PVPC futures blend, Japan's tiers plus fuel cost adjustment.
• A debt path with power limitation and DSO execution, with rules for where debt sits: Italy's CMOR lets arrears follow the customer; Belgium moves debtors to the DSO; everywhere else the debt stays with the old supplier.
• Cooling demand: air-conditioning ownership about 90%+ in Japan, about 74% in Australia, 56% in Italy, 43%+ in Spain and about 25% in France; it drives summer peaks.
• Cooking and heating fuels the GB build lacks: kerosene and LPG (Japan), oil (Belgium, Germany), district heating (Germany), building-level gas heating (Italy, Spain, France), bottled butane (Spain).
• PV export regimes: per-phase limits and dynamic exports (Australia); monthly netting capped at consumption (Spain); legacy net-metered cohorts (Belgium, Italy); post-FIT buy-back (Japan); the 60% feed-in cap and no payment at negative prices (Germany); regulated purchase of surplus (France).
WHERE THE GB BUILD HARD-CODES THESE. Rows 8 to 16 of the portability register, docs/design/PORTABILITY_DEBT.md, note each of these GB assumptions as a parameter a second market would need opened; row 3 already covered the settlement clock. Nothing is built from it.

residuals.heading: Where our picture is still weak
residuals.body: (1) Every figure on this page comes from the seven packs. Their items tagged [unverified] were spot-checked while each country page was drafted, and most remain open; the director's verification steer of 25 Oct ranks these packs last, after the GB-market packs. The count of confirmed, corrected and open items for each pack is at the foot of the Knowledge index. (2) The GB comparison figures in the packs were not re-checked by the advisor. (3) The closeness ranking is judgement. (4) The packs record blocked fetches (Eurostat's API, several statute sites) that a later pass could make.

scope_delta.heading: What this page does not yet establish
scope_delta.body: It builds nothing and changes no world or supplier priority. It does not say any market is worth entering. It does not check the GB build's own code against the list beyond naming where each assumption sits. Language is out of scope (director, 07:17).
